p: The world into which he was born was divided between two great empires. The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire ruled Sham, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa from Constantinople; its Christians were split by bitter disputes over the nature of Isa, and the Copts of Egypt were persecuted for their beliefs. The Sasanian Persian Empire, mostly fire-worshipping, ruled Iraq and Iran. The two had fought each other for generations, a rivalry the Quran later mentions in Surah ar-Rum. Further east, in India, worship of idols and a rigid caste system held sway.

Arabia itself lay outside both empires. Its people worshipped idols of stone, wood, even dates; Umar later recalled making an idol of dates and eating it when he was hungry. They believed in omens and consulted fortune-tellers, and most denied any life after death. Tribes fought feuds over a single camel that lasted forty years, until later generations no longer knew why they fought. Some buried infant daughters alive out of shame (16:58–59, 81:8–9). Marriage took several corrupt forms besides proper marriage, as Aisha described (Bukhari), and a man could divorce and take back his wife without limit (2:229). Interest was common in trade.

Yet the Arabs had virtues that Islam would later build on: remarkable memories, so that they knew the lineages of their families and even their camels; generosity to guests, such as Hatim at-Ta'i, who would slaughter his own riding camel for a visitor; courage; faithfulness to their word; and a deep love of eloquent poetry, so that a single great poem could raise a man to honour. Quraysh lived by trade, with caravans to Yemen in winter and to Sham in summer, which no one dared to attack because of their guardianship of the Ka'bah (106:1–2). They still performed a form of Hajj inherited from Ibrahim, mixed with idol worship, and held great markets at Ukaz, Majannah and Dhul-Majaz.

Makkah in the year 570 CE was a city of traders built around the Ka'bah, the house Ibrahim and Isma'il (peace be upon them) had raised for the worship of Allah. Over the centuries it had filled with idols, yet Quraysh were still respected across Arabia as its guardians.

That same year Abrahah, the Abyssinian ruler of Yemen, came with an army and an elephant to destroy the Ka'bah, and Allah destroyed his army with flocks of birds (see the event 'Abrahah's army and the elephant'). The Arabs called it the Year of the Elephant.

A few weeks later, on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal, Aminah bint Wahb gave birth to a son. His father Abdullah, the son of Abd al-Muttalib, had died at about 25 in Yathrib, on the way back from a trading journey to Sham, when Aminah was some months pregnant. Aminah said the pregnancy was the easiest she could imagine, and that at the birth she saw a light leave her by which the palaces of Sham were lit up (Ahmad). He was born in a house in the quarter of Banu Hashim near Safa; the spot is now marked by a library building near the Masjid al-Haram.

Other signs are reported on the night of his birth: the sacred fire of the Persians, which had burnt for a thousand years, went out; fourteen balconies of Khosrow's palace fell; and the idols around the Ka'bah toppled. Some reports also say he was born already circumcised, with his umbilical cord cut; others say Abd al-Muttalib circumcised him on the seventh day and held a feast. Scholars regard several of these reports as weak. Mufti Menk warns against invented stories, such as minarets of the Haram bowing at his birth, since there were no minarets then: 'there is no need to fabricate anything, because what is correct is already there.'

The first to hold the newborn, it is reported, was ash-Shifa bint Amr, who served as midwife; she was the mother of Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, later one of the wealthiest and most generous of the Companions. Umm Ayman (Barakah), Aminah's Abyssinian servant, was also there and helped care for the baby from his first days, and Thuwaybah, a freed slave of Abu Lahab, nursed him for a few days before the women of Banu Sa'd arrived.

Abd al-Muttalib carried the baby into the Ka'bah, thanked Allah, and named him Muhammad, 'the praised one', a name rarely used among the Arabs. When asked why, he said he hoped his grandson would be praised in the heavens and on earth.
Years later, when asked about fasting on Mondays, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'That is the day on which I was born, and the day on which revelation came to me' (Muslim).

He was born an orphan, and in Islamic usage a yatim is precisely a child who has lost his father; losing a mother alone does not make one a yatim in that sense. That the best of creation was chosen to grow up this way is a lasting comfort to every orphan: it is not a sign of Allah's displeasure, and Allah often surrounds such a child with others who care for him, as He did with Muhammad ﷺ. The Arabs of the time had no fixed calendar and dated events by great happenings, so his birth year became known as 'Am al-Fil, the Year of the Elephant. Most scholars give the date as the 12th of Rabi' al-Awwal; other days (the 2nd, 8th and 9th) are also reported. A report in the history books (Ibn Kathir, from Ikrimah, with a weak chain) says Iblis cried out in grief four times: when he was cursed, when he was cast out of Paradise, when the Prophet ﷺ was born, and when Surah al-Fatihah was revealed.
birth.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 1–2.

p: It was the custom of the noble families of Makkah to send their infants to the desert, where the air was clean and the Arabic purest. Women of Banu Sa'd came to Makkah looking for babies to nurse, hoping for a good reward from the fathers. None wanted the orphan Muhammad, since there was no father to pay them.

Halimah as-Sa'diyyah and her husband al-Harith arrived late: the donkey she rode was weak (in one telling, injured and bleeding at the knee) and kept falling behind, so by the time they reached Makkah the other women had already taken the babies of rich and noble families. Only the orphan was left. Rather than return empty-handed she took him, and from that moment, she later said, everything changed: her breasts, which had not had enough milk even for her own crying son, filled for both children; their old she-camel gave milk; and the slow donkey now led the whole caravan. Back home, in a year of drought, her flocks returned full while her neighbours' sheep came back hungry.

She remembered him as an unusual child: calm, never quarrelling over small things like other children, quick to speak clear and eloquent Arabic. Some narrations add that before sleeping he would gaze up at the sky, and that he would cry when his clothes were taken off to bathe him until he was covered again. The house and the whole encampment, she said, seemed full of blessing while he was with them. The Arabs sent their children to the desert not only for clean air and pure milk but to learn the purest language and good manners; parents parted with their infants for years for the sake of their upbringing.

He stayed with Banu Sa'd for about four years. One day, while he was out with the flocks and playing with other boys, including his foster brother (Halimah's son, who shared her milk), angels in white came. Muslim's narration names Jibril: he laid him on his back, opened his chest, took out his heart and removed a clot from it, saying 'This was Shaytan's share of you.' He washed the heart in a basin of gold with Zamzam water and returned it. The foster brother ran to Halimah and her husband crying that his brother was being killed; they found him standing, his colour changed, but unhurt. Anas later said he had seen the mark of the stitching on his chest (Muslim). Scholars explain that the heart was cleansed of the qualities Shaytan works through: envy, hatred, pride, deceit and anger for the self. Aishah said he never took revenge for himself, only when the limits of Allah were violated (Bukhari, Muslim).

Frightened for his life, Halimah and her husband took him back to Makkah. At first she offered excuses for returning him early, but Aminah pressed her until she told the whole story. Aminah was not alarmed: she said that signs had accompanied this child from his conception, and that Shaytan had no way to him. Halimah remained dear to him all his life, and years later he spread his cloak for her to sit on.
halimah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: When he was about six, his mother Aminah took him to Yathrib to visit her husband's maternal relatives, Banu an-Najjar, and to see Abdullah's grave. With them travelled Umm Ayman (Barakah), the servant who cared for him.

They stayed about a month. Years later, when he arrived in Madinah after the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ pointed out the house where they had stayed and the pool where he had learnt to swim with the boys of Banu an-Najjar.
yathrib-visit.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: On the journey home from Yathrib, Aminah fell ill. At al-Abwa, a stopping place between Madinah and Makkah, she died and was buried there. The boy of six had now lost both parents.
Umm Ayman brought him the rest of the way back to Makkah. She cared for him like a mother, and he later called her 'my mother after my mother'.

Many years later, on the way to Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ visited his mother's grave at al-Abwa and wept, and those with him wept too (Muslim). Surah ad-Duha recalls this stage of his life: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?'

Umm Ayman stayed with him. When he married Khadijah he freed her, and she was among the very first women to believe when prophethood came, saying in effect that she had watched him from the day he was born. He said: 'Whoever would be pleased to marry a woman of the people of Paradise, let him marry Umm Ayman' (Ibn Sa'd). Zayd ibn Harithah, his beloved freed servant and much younger than her, married her, and she bore Usamah ibn Zayd, who as a young man would command a Muslim army. Zayd was fair and Usamah very dark, and some people spoke ill of it, until a known expert in lineage, Mujazziz al-Mudliji, saw their feet sticking out from under a sheet as they slept and said: 'These feet are from one another.' The Prophet ﷺ was delighted (Bukhari, Muslim). Umm Ayman outlived him and died in Madinah in the time of Uthman.
orphan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: After Aminah's death his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib took him into his home. The old chief loved him more than his own sons.

Abd al-Muttalib had a special carpet spread for him in the shade of the Ka'bah, where no one, not even his sons, would sit out of respect. When the uncles tried to move the boy away, Abd al-Muttalib would say: 'Leave my son alone; by Allah, he has a great future,' and seat him beside him. He had some ten or eleven sons, yet none was treated like this grandson; he would stroke the boy's back and was pleased with whatever he did.
This care lasted only two years. When the boy was eight, Abd al-Muttalib died, and before his death he entrusted him to his son Abu Talib, the full brother of the boy's father Abdullah.
abdulmuttalib.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: Abu Talib was not a wealthy man and had many children, but he took his nephew in and loved him deeply, often keeping him closer than his own sons. Abu Talib noticed that his household seemed to have more blessing once the boy joined it. At meals his own children grabbed for the best pieces, while the young Muhammad waited calmly for his share, like an adult (Ibn Sa'd).

The boy helped where he could. He later said: 'Every prophet herded sheep, and I herded them for the people of Makkah for a few qirats' (Bukhari). Shepherding trained the prophets in patience with creatures that cannot speak, in humility (dust, dirt and hard work), and in care: a shepherd goes after the one animal that strays from the flock.
Abu Talib's protection would last more than forty years. Though he never accepted Islam, he defended his nephew against all of Quraysh until his death in the tenth year of prophethood.
abutalib-care.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: When he was about twelve, Abu Talib prepared to take a trade caravan to Sham. The boy clung to him, and Abu Talib took him along.

At Busra, on the edge of Sham, lived a Christian monk called Bahira. The caravans had passed his cell many times without his paying attention, but this time he came out and invited them all to a meal. He looked closely at the boy, asked him questions, and found the signs he had read of in his books, including a mark between his shoulders. At the meal the boy came last, from minding the camels, and the shade had already been taken; as he sat, the branches of the tree leaned over to shade him. 'Look at the shade of the tree, it has inclined to him,' said Bahira (Tirmidhi).

Bahira told Abu Talib: 'This is the master of the worlds; Allah will send him as a mercy.' He urged him to take the boy home and guard him: Tirmidhi's narration warns of the Romans, and Ibn Ishaq's of the Jews, who would recognise him from their books and wish him harm. Abu Talib cut the journey short and returned to Makkah. The incident is reported by at-Tirmidhi and in the Seerah works; scholars discuss details in some versions.

This was the first clear sign, from outside his family, that pointed to his prophethood. It shows that some of the People of the Book had not hidden the truth they knew, as the Quran says of those who believe among them; later, Waraqah ibn Nawfal would be another.
busra-1.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: The Harb al-Fijar, the 'sacrilegious war', broke out between Quraysh with their ally Kinanah and the tribe of Qays Aylan. It was so named because it was fought in the sacred months, when the Arabs normally forbade fighting.

He was in his teens. He later said that he used to hand arrows to his uncles in the battle. The war ended in a settlement in which blood money was paid. It showed him early the cost of tribal feuding.
fijar.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After the war, a merchant from the tribe of Zubayd in Yemen sold goods in Makkah to al-As ibn Wa'il of Banu Sahm, the father of the Companion Amr ibn al-As, who took them and refused to pay. Al-As was one of the nobles of Quraysh, and when the stranger asked people for help they would not believe him or dared not act. He had one weapon left, his tongue: he climbed the hill of Abu Qubays beside the Ka'bah and recited verses calling Quraysh oppressors. For a people who lived by poetry and reputation, such verses could shame them for generations.

Az-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, called the clans together. Five clans (Hashim, al-Muttalib, Asad, Zuhrah and Taym) met in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an, a once-poor man who had grown rich and was famous for his generosity, and swore to stand with anyone wronged in Makkah, local or stranger, against the wrongdoer until his right was returned. Then they went together to al-As's door and made him hand over what he owed. The pact was called Hilf al-Fudul, the Alliance of the Virtuous.

He attended it as a young man. Years later, as Prophet, he said: 'I witnessed in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an a pact I would not exchange for red camels. If I were called to it in Islam, I would answer' (reported by Ibn Ishaq and al-Bayhaqi).
The Quran later set the same principle for Muslims: 'Do not let your dislike of a people lead you to injustice. Be just; that is nearer to piety' (al-Ma'idah 5:8).
fudul.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: By his mid-twenties he was known in Makkah as al-Amin, the trustworthy. Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a noble and wealthy widow who traded through agents, heard of his honesty and offered him double the usual share to take her goods to Sham.

He travelled with her servant Maysarah. Maysarah saw how he treated a servant with the respect due to any man, and how he accounted for every coin. The trade went well and the profits were greater than ever. Maysarah came back full of praise: of his honesty in every sale, his gentle manners, and things he had noticed on the way, such as a cloud that shaded him from the heat throughout the journey, and a monk who said only a prophet would sit under the tree where he rested.

Khadijah, impressed by his honesty and character and by what Maysarah described, felt there was something great about this man, and began to think of him as a husband. She chose an orphan who had little wealth, only honesty, dignity and a spotless name.
The route to Sham passed by Yathrib, so the city that would one day shelter him became familiar to him from his early life.
busra-2.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 3–4.

p: Khadijah sent her friend Nafisah bint Munyah to ask whether he would marry her. He agreed, and spoke to his uncles; most reports say Abu Talib, and some that Hamzah went with him to her family to ask for her hand. Abu Talib gave the marriage sermon, praising his nephew's character. He was 25. Most reports give her age as 40, though another report says 28. She had been widowed twice, from Abu Halah and then Atiq ibn A'idh, and had children from those marriages, among them Hind and Halah. He was a young man of the most honoured family of Quraysh and could have married any girl in Makkah; he chose a mature widow, and Allah had prepared in her the qualities he would need when revelation came.

Their marriage lasted 25 years, and he married no one else while she lived. She bore him all his children except Ibrahim, who was born much later in Madinah to Mariyah: two sons and four daughters. Al-Qasim died as a small boy, old enough, it is said, to ride a mount, and it is from him that the Prophet ﷺ was called Abu al-Qasim. Abdullah, also called at-Tayyib and at-Tahir, died in infancy. The four daughters, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah, lived to see his prophethood, accepted Islam and made the Hijrah.

Khadijah was his support when revelation began and the first to believe in him. Years after her death he still spoke of her with love and sent gifts to her friends. He said: 'She believed in me when people disbelieved, she trusted me when people called me a liar, and she supported me with her wealth when people denied me' (Ahmad).
marriage-khadijah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: When he was about 35, ten years into his marriage, the Ka'bah was in a poor state: an old fire had weakened it and a flood had cracked its walls. It still stood as Ibrahim and Isma'il had built it, of stones fitted one on another without mortar, a little above a man's height and without a roof. Quraysh decided to rebuild it, but they were afraid to pull down the House of Allah. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah took up a pickaxe and said: 'O Allah, we intend only good,' and knocked down part of it. The people waited that night to see if punishment would strike him; when morning came and he was well, they all joined in. They dug down until they reached the foundation of Ibrahim, green stones locked together like teeth, and stopped there.

They agreed that only pure wealth would go into the House: no money from interest, which even the pagans knew to be oppression of the poor, none from prostitution, and none taken by fraud or cheating. Pure money proved scarce. They could not rebuild the whole of Ibrahim's foundation, so they left out the curved area to the north, the Hijr (Hatim), marking it with a low wall, and built a cube. Each clan took a section. He and his uncle al-Abbas carried stones for Banu Hashim. Like the other men he wrapped his waist-cloth around his shoulder to cushion the stones, but when he did so he fell to the ground with his eyes turned to the sky, and he never uncovered himself again (Bukhari, from Jabir).

When the walls reached the place of the Black Stone, the clans quarrelled bitterly over who would have the honour of setting it. Some dipped their hands in blood and swore to fight. For days no one could agree. Some reports say the quarrel lasted four or five nights. Then the eldest of them, Abu Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah, proposed that the first man to enter through the gate of the masjid should judge.

The first man through was Muhammad. 'This is al-Amin; we accept him,' they said. He asked for a cloak, placed the stone on it, and had a leader of every clan hold its edges and lift it together. When it reached its place, he set it in the wall with his own hands. Bloodshed was avoided, and every clan shared the honour.

Quraysh raised the walls much higher than before, to about eighteen cubits, set a roof on six wooden pillars, and raised the door above ground level so that only those they allowed could enter and floodwater would not get in. Years later the Prophet ﷺ told Aishah: 'Were your people not so recently out of Jahiliyyah, I would have pulled down the Ka'bah and rebuilt it on Ibrahim's foundations, with two doors, one to enter and one to leave' (Bukhari, Muslim). He left it as it was so as not to unsettle new Muslims.

After the Ka'bah was damaged in the fighting of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah's time, Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, then ruling Makkah, rebuilt it as the Prophet ﷺ had wished, including the Hijr and with two doors. After his death, al-Hajjaj, on the orders of the caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, returned it to the shape Quraysh had given it, and that is the Ka'bah we see today. Later rulers, including the Ottomans after a flood in 1630 and the Saudi government in the 1990s, repaired and strengthened it, replacing worn pillars and roof, without changing its form.
kaaba.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 3–4.

p: Zayd ibn Harithah had been kidnapped as a boy from his tribe, Kalb, and sold in a market near Makkah. Khadijah's nephew bought him and gave him to her, and she gave him to her husband.

Years later Zayd's father and uncle found out where he was and came to Makkah to ransom him. The Prophet ﷺ said Zayd could choose: go with them freely, or stay. Zayd answered: 'I will not choose anyone over you.' His father was astonished that he preferred slavery to his family.

The Prophet ﷺ then took Zayd to the Ka'bah and declared him free and his son. He was called Zayd ibn Muhammad until the Quran later forbade calling adopted sons by their adopters' names. Zayd became one of the first Muslims and is the only companion named in the Quran (33:37).
zayd-joins.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: As he neared forty, signs of prophethood grew. Aishah said that his first revelation was true dreams: whatever he saw at night came true like the break of dawn (Bukhari). He also said: 'I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me with salam before I was sent; I know it even now' (Muslim). Then he came to love solitude. He would take provisions and spend nights in the cave of Hira on Jabal an-Nur, north-east of Makkah, reflecting on the state of his people and how they might be put right, and worshipping Allah alone in the way of Ibrahim. He never bowed to an idol, nor to any person. For a prophet, a dream is itself revelation, as with Ibrahim's dream of sacrificing his son, so these true dreams were the first stage of his prophethood.

He was forty. One night in Ramadan (many scholars say the 21st night, a Monday) the angel Jibril came to him in the cave and said: 'Read!' He replied: 'I am not a reader' (ma ana bi-qari'). He was unlettered, and he said so plainly. The angel embraced him and squeezed him until he could bear no more, then released him and said again: 'Read!' This happened three times. Then the angel said: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know' (96:1–5).

Scholars draw much from these first five verses. The first word revealed was 'Read', and it was revealed to an unlettered man, so that no one could say he had copied from the books of the Jews and Christians, which he could not read. Reading begins 'in the name of your Lord': the Prophet ﷺ taught that any important matter not begun with Allah's name is cut off from blessing. Rabb means more than 'Lord': the Creator, Sustainer, Provider and Protector in full control of every creature. Man is described as created from an 'alaq, a clinging clot; elsewhere the Quran speaks of dust, clay and a drop of fluid, which are different stages of the same creation, not a contradiction. And Allah 'taught man what he did not know': whatever knowledge people gain is a gift from Him, and only a little (17:85).

He hurried down the mountain, trembling and sweating, his heart pounding, to the person he trusted most, and said to Khadijah: 'Cover me, cover me.' When the fear left him he told her what had happened and said he feared for himself. She answered: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep ties of kinship, you carry the burdens of the weak, you help the poor, you honour guests, and you support people in hardship.' Khadijah was the first person after him to hear the words of the Quran.

He was forty and Khadijah, by most reports, about fifty-five. She took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, an old blind man who had become a Christian and knew the earlier scriptures. On hearing the story, Waraqah said: 'This is the Namus (Jibril) whom Allah sent to Musa. I wish I were young and alive when your people drive you out.' 'Will they drive me out?' he asked. 'Yes,' said Waraqah, 'no man has ever brought what you bring without being treated as an enemy.' 'If I live to see your day, I will support you with all my strength.' But Waraqah died soon after (Bukhari 3). Some narrations speak well of his end; Allah knows his state.
Khadijah believed at once, without needing to ask anything; she knew the man. She was the first to believe.
first-revelation.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 4–5.

p: After the first revelation came a pause (fatrat al-wahy). He kept going to Hira and waiting for the angel to return, and grew deeply anxious. Its length is reported very differently: Mufti Menk prefers about ten days, from the 21st of Ramadan to the 1st of Shawwal, and notes that it matches the last ten nights of Ramadan, the time of i'tikaf; other scholars give forty days, several months, or longer.

Jabir ibn Abdullah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'While I was walking I heard a voice from the sky. I looked up and saw the angel who had come to me at Hira, sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth. I was terrified, went home and said: Wrap me, wrap me.' Then Allah revealed: 'O you wrapped in your cloak, rise and warn, and magnify your Lord, and purify your garments, and shun idolatry, and do not give in order to gain more, and be patient for your Lord' (74:1–7). After that, revelation came regularly (Bukhari 4). Mufti Menk explains that this time he saw Jibril in his true form, filling the horizon. Scholars say he saw him in that form only twice: once at the start of his mission and once on the night of the Mi'raj (53:13); Ibn Mas'ud reports that he had six hundred wings (Bukhari). Usually Jibril came as a man, sometimes so that the Companions saw him too, as in the hadith of Jibril, when a man in brilliant white with jet-black hair, showing no trace of travel, sat knee to knee with the Prophet ﷺ and asked about Islam, Iman and Ihsan (Muslim).

These verses were the first command to preach. Iqra' had made him a prophet; Qum fa-andhir, 'Rise and warn', made him a messenger. 'Rise' calls for courage, and he would deliver most of his sermons standing. 'Magnify your Lord' means to declare the greatness of Allah alone. 'Purify your garments' means clean clothes, presentable according to one's means, and, scholars add, a pure character. 'Do not give in order to gain more' warns against doing favours and then reminding people of them or expecting a return (compare 2:264 and 76:9). 'Be patient for your Lord' already told him, as Waraqah had, that the road ahead would be hard.

Another short pause came at some point while he was unwell, and a woman mocked him that his 'devil' had left him. Surah ad-Duha answered: 'Your Lord has not abandoned you, nor is He displeased… What is to come will be better for you than what has passed.'
fatrah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 5.

p: Abu Bakr was a respected merchant, known for his gentle character and his knowledge of the lineages of Quraysh. When the Prophet ﷺ told him of the revelation he accepted at once, without hesitation. The Prophet ﷺ later said that everyone he invited hesitated except Abu Bakr.

Abu Bakr began inviting the people he trusted. Through him, five of the men later promised Paradise accepted Islam: Uthman ibn Affan, az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talhah ibn Ubaydillah. He brought them to the Prophet ﷺ, who recited the Quran to them and they believed. Talhah was still in his teens; on a trading trip to Busra he had heard a monk ask whether 'Ahmad' had appeared yet in Makkah, so when Abu Bakr spoke to him he believed at once. They were taught to worship Allah alone, to keep good character, to honour their parents even when they were not Muslim (but not to obey them in sin), to honour guests and give everyone his right, not to cheat or steal, and that there would be a resurrection, a reckoning, Paradise and Hell: the same belief taught by Musa and Isa.
These early years of da'wah were quiet and private. The Muslims prayed in secret in the valleys outside Makkah and met to learn. (Hayatus Sahaba 1:205, from Ibn Ishaq.)
abubakr-dawah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 6.

p: Amr ibn Abasa of Banu Sulaym had already turned away from idols before he heard of the Prophet ﷺ. Hearing that a man in Makkah was bringing news from heaven, he came and found him hiding from his people.

He asked: 'What are you?' 'A prophet.' 'What is a prophet?' 'Allah has sent me.' 'With what?' 'To join ties of kinship, break the idols, and that Allah alone is worshipped with nothing joined to Him.' 'Who is with you in this?' 'A free man and a slave,' meaning Abu Bakr and Bilal.
Amr accepted Islam and wanted to stay, but the Prophet ﷺ told him to return to his people and come back when he heard that Islam had prevailed. He came to Madinah years later (Muslim).
amr-abasa.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After about three years of private da'wah, when the Muslims numbered some thirty or forty, Allah commanded: 'Warn your nearest kinsfolk' (26:214), and then: 'Proclaim openly what you are commanded' (15:94).

The Prophet ﷺ climbed Mount Safa near the Ka'bah and called out to the clans of Quraysh one by one. No one had dared address all of them openly, and they came, some leaders sending a representative, wondering whether he would give it all up. When they gathered, he asked: 'If I told you that horsemen were in the valley behind this hill about to attack you, would you believe me?' They said: 'Yes, we have only known you to be truthful.' He said: 'Then I am a warner to you of a severe punishment ahead.' He called the clans and individuals by name, telling each to save themselves from the Fire, for being his relatives would not save them.

His uncle Abu Lahab, son of Abd al-Muttalib and a leader of Quraysh, shouted: 'May you perish (tabban laka)! Is it for this you gathered us?' Like many of the leaders, he could not bear to acknowledge anyone above himself. The others were silent. Allah then revealed Surah al-Masad, short and easy to memorise, so that it was soon repeated in the streets by Muslims and non-Muslims alike: 'May the hands of Abu Lahab perish, and he has perished. His wealth and what he earned will not avail him. He will burn in a blazing Fire, and his wife, the carrier of firewood, around her neck a rope of palm fibre' (Bukhari 4770).

His wife Umm Jamil, sister of Abu Sufyan, went among the women of Quraysh spreading lies and gossip about the Prophet ﷺ, kindling the fire in which both would burn: hence 'the carrier of firewood'. Proud of her necklace, she would wear a rope of fibre instead. Scholars note that when the Quran condemns someone by name in this way, he never accepts Islam, and Abu Lahab and his wife never did. Furious, she came to the Ka'bah with a stone to throw at him while he sat beside Abu Bakr; Allah took away her sight of him, and she asked Abu Bakr: 'Where is your companion? I have heard he mocks me…' and left. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'She did not see me; Allah took her sight from me' (Ibn Ishaq; al-Hakim).

He also invited his close relatives to a meal and called them to Islam, and he addressed his own family by name: 'O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, save yourself from the Fire; I cannot help you against Allah at all.' From this point the call was public, and so was the opposition.
public-dawah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 6.

p: Dimad of Azd Shanu'ah was known for treating people for madness and possession with incantations. Arriving in Makkah, he heard Quraysh calling the Prophet ﷺ mad and offered to treat him.

The Prophet ﷺ answered with the opening of his khutbah: 'All praise is for Allah; we praise Him and seek His help. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray, and whomever He leaves astray, none can guide. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.'

Dimad asked him to repeat the words three times, then said: 'I have heard the words of soothsayers, sorcerers and poets, but never words like these; they reach the depths of the sea.' He gave his hand in pledge to Islam on behalf of himself and his people (Muslim).
dimad.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Abu Dharr, whose name was Jundub ibn Junadah, was of the tribe of Ghifar, whose land lay on the caravan route between Makkah and Sham. He heard of a man in Makkah claiming prophethood and sent his brother Unays to find out. Unays came back saying the man called to good character, but Abu Dharr was not satisfied and came himself, with a little water and provisions. Afraid to ask anyone openly, he stayed in the masjid, drinking Zamzam. Ali noticed the stranger and gave him a place to sleep. The Arabs did not ask a guest his business for three days, a custom Islam confirmed: a guest's right is three days (Bukhari). On the third day Ali asked, and Abu Dharr told him once he had promised to keep it secret. Ali said: 'He is truly the Messenger of Allah. Follow me; if I see danger I will stop as if to fix my sandal, so walk on.' So he brought him to the Prophet ﷺ.

He accepted Islam on the spot. The Prophet ﷺ told him to keep it secret and return to his people, but Abu Dharr said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, I will shout it among them.' He went to the Ka'bah and declared the shahadah aloud. Quraysh fell on him and beat him until al-Abbas threw himself over him and warned them that Ghifar lay on their trade route to Sham. The next day Abu Dharr did the same again.
He returned home and called Ghifar to Islam; half of them accepted before the Hijrah and the rest after it (Bukhari, Muslim; Hayatus Sahaba 1:304).
abudharr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 6.

p: One day the Prophet ﷺ was speaking earnestly with leaders of Quraysh, hoping they would accept Islam. Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, a blind companion, came and asked repeatedly to be taught. The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned back to the leaders.

Allah then revealed: 'He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him. How do you know that he might be purified?…' (80:1–16). The ayat taught that a sincere seeker deserves attention before the powerful who turn away.

Scholars point to two lessons. The reproach is recorded in the Quran for all to recite, which no man would write about himself; this too shows it is not his own words. And the Prophet ﷺ accepted correction at once, without anger or excuse, leaving an example for anyone, however learned, who is corrected.

Afterwards, whenever the Prophet ﷺ saw Ibn Umm Maktum, he would honour him, saying: 'Welcome to the one for whose sake my Lord reproached me.' He later made him his deputy in Madinah more than once and appointed him a mu'adhdhin alongside Bilal (reported in at-Tirmidhi, graded sahih).
abasa.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 8.

p: As Islam spread, the leaders of Quraysh turned their anger on the believers. Some say the first Muslims were only the weak and the poor; in fact most came from good families of Quraysh, which is exactly why their relatives felt shamed and fought to bring them back. But those with no tribe or master to protect them (slaves, freed slaves and outsiders) suffered the worst.

Bilal, an Abyssinian slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, was laid on the burning sand at midday with a heavy rock on his chest and told to renounce Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-Uzza. He was whipped until he bled and dragged over the hot stones, yet he only repeated: 'Ahad, Ahad' (One, One): one God, and your idols are nothing. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, a blacksmith, was pressed onto hot coals until the fat of his back put them out.

Yasir, his wife Sumayyah and their son Ammar were tortured together in the heat of Makkah. Passing by, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Patience, family of Yasir; your meeting place is Paradise.' Abu Jahl killed Sumayyah with a spear, making her the first martyr of Islam; Yasir also died under torture.

Ammar, overwhelmed by torture, said words against Islam. He came to the Prophet ﷺ weeping. 'How do you find your heart?' he asked. 'At peace with faith.' 'If they return, do it again.' Allah revealed that there is no blame on one 'forced while his heart remains firm in faith' (16:106).

Even free Muslims of noble families suffered. Uthman ibn Affan, then about thirty-four, was tied up by his uncle al-Hakam ibn Abi al-As, who disowned him unless he gave up Islam; Uthman answered that he would never abandon it, and in the end his uncle gave up. Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, only a boy (about twelve, some say), was wrapped in a mat by his uncle, who lit a fire beneath him so the smoke would choke him: 'I will never return to disbelief.' Mus'ab ibn Umayr was the most pampered young man in Makkah: dressed in the finest clothes, his perfume noticed before he was seen. He kept his Islam secret until someone saw him praying and told his mother. She locked him in the house and cut off everything, until his clothes were rags and his once-soft skin cracked and peeled, and still he would not turn back. He later went to Abyssinia, taught Islam in Madinah, and was martyred at Uhud; there was not enough cloth to shroud him: covering his head left his feet bare, and covering his feet left his head bare (Bukhari).

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, about seventeen, loved his mother dearly. When she learnt of his Islam she swore she would neither eat nor drink nor shelter from the sun until he renounced Muhammad. Day after day she stayed out, until she fainted. Sa'd said: 'Mother, even if you had a hundred souls and they left you one by one, I would not leave this religion; eat or do not eat.' Allah revealed: 'We have enjoined on man kindness to his parents; but if they strive to make you associate with Me what you have no knowledge of, do not obey them' (29:8; also 31:14–15). Muslims are to treat parents with kindness even when they are not Muslim, and obey them in everything except sin (Muslim, from Sa'd).

They gained nothing worldly from Islam, neither wealth nor status, and lost a great deal; they held firm because they believed. Islam was far from the religion of their fathers: Quraysh did not even believe in a life after death ('There is only our life in this world; we die and we live,' 45:24).
persecution.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 6–7.

p: As the number of Muslims grew and the hostility of Quraysh rose, the Prophet ﷺ chose the house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam, a teenager from a noble family who had accepted Islam early, as their meeting place. It stood on Mount Safa, near the Ka'bah but out of sight, and Arqam's clan, Banu Makhzum, was not expected to host the Muslims.

Among those who had entered Islam by then were Sa'id ibn Zayd and his wife Fatimah bint al-Khattab, Umar's sister; Khabbab ibn al-Aratt; Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-As; Ubaydah ibn al-Harith; and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Many were protected only by their families, since Quraysh hesitated to strike someone with a powerful clan, or trade ties, behind him.

There the Prophet ﷺ taught the Quran as it came down, a few verses at a time. The verses of this period were mostly about belief: the Oneness of Allah, the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell, and that idols can neither harm nor benefit. explained the faith and prayed with the companions. Many accepted Islam inside its walls, including Ammar and Suhayb and, in the sixth year, Umar ibn al-Khattab. Dar al-Arqam remained the centre of the Muslims until Umar's Islam allowed them to pray openly at the Ka'bah.
arqam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 6.

p: Ammar ibn Yasir and Suhayb ar-Rumi, a freed slave who had grown up among the Byzantines, each decided separately to visit the Prophet ﷺ. They met at the door of Dar al-Arqam. 'What do you want?' each asked the other. 'I want to go to Muhammad and hear what he says.' They entered together and accepted Islam. Both later endured heavy persecution for their faith (Ibn Sa'd; Hayatus Sahaba 1:104).
ammar-suhayb.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Abu Bakr used his wealth to rescue the weakest believers. Passing Umayyah ibn Khalaf as he tortured Bilal, he said: 'Do you not fear Allah over this poor man?' He bought Bilal and set him free.

He did the same for six others, men and women, among them Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Zinnirah, an-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, and a slave woman of Banu Mu'ammal. His father Abu Quhafah told him to free strong men who could defend him instead. Abu Bakr replied that he did it only for the sake of Allah. Mufassirin link the closing ayat of Surah al-Layl to him: 'And the most righteous will be kept away from it, the one who gives his wealth to purify himself… seeking only the Face of his Lord the Most High.'

Zinnirah, a Roman slave woman, was beaten by Abu Jahl and others until she lost her sight, yet she kept saying she believed in one God, not in al-Lat and al-Uzza. When Abu Bakr bought her freedom, they jeered: 'It is al-Lat and al-Uzza who took your sight.' She answered: 'By Allah, they can neither harm nor benefit. This is from Allah, and He can return it if He wills.' Her sight was restored the next morning, and Quraysh said it was Muhammad's magic (Ibn Ishaq).
Umar later said: 'Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master,' meaning Bilal (Bukhari).
freeing.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 7.

p: As the Muslims grew, Quraysh tried bargaining. Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, a calm and respected elder, went to the Prophet ﷺ while he sat alone in the masjid.

'You are one of us, of noble lineage, but you have split our people. If you want wealth,' he said, 'we will gather it until you are the richest of us. If you want honour, we will make you our chief. If you want kingship, we will make you king. If you want women, choose any you like. And if what comes to you is something you cannot repel, we will find you a cure.' The Prophet ﷺ listened, then asked: 'Have you finished, Abu al-Walid?' and recited the opening of Surah Fussilat.

When he reached 'If they turn away, say: I warn you of a thunderbolt like that of Ad and Thamud' (41:13), Utbah put his hand over the Prophet's mouth and begged him to stop. He returned to Quraysh so changed that they said: 'Abu al-Walid has come back with a different face.' He advised them to leave Muhammad alone; they refused (Ibn Ishaq).

These are the opening verses of Surah Fussilat (Ha Mim as-Sajdah), up to the warning about Ad and Thamud. Mufti Menk urges every listener to read their meaning: if an enemy admitted their power, a Muslim should at least know what they say.
utbah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 7.

p: When threats failed, leaders of Quraysh, including al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and al-As ibn Wa'il, offered a compromise: 'Muhammad, let us worship what you worship for a year, and you worship what we worship for a year.' (Some reports say a day in turn.) They saw his numbers growing and wanted to stop losing their sons to Islam.

Allah answered with Surah al-Kafirun: 'Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship what I worship… To you your religion, and to me mine.' The surah ended any idea of mixing tawhid with idol worship (Ibn Ishaq, at-Tabari).

Mufti Menk notes that the sweetness of iman lies in worshipping the One who made us and none besides Him; worship cannot be shared out in turns. The surah's last line, 'To you your religion, and to me mine,' also teaches Muslims to let others live by their faith while holding firmly to their own.
compromise.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 8.

p: Around 614–615 CE the Persians crushed the Byzantine armies and took Jerusalem. The idolaters of Makkah, who felt closer to the fire-worshipping Persians, rejoiced, while the Muslims were saddened, since the Byzantines were People of the Book.

Allah revealed: 'The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will be victorious within a few years' (30:2–4). Abu Bakr was so certain that he made a wager with Ubayy ibn Khalaf, before wagering was forbidden, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to extend the time to within nine years (Tirmidhi).
Within that time Heraclius defeated the Persians decisively. Many reports say the news came around the time of Badr, when the believers also rejoiced at their own victory, as the ayat had said.
romans.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 1.

p: In the fifth year of prophethood, with persecution at its worst, the Prophet ﷺ told the companions: 'In Abyssinia there is a king under whom no one is wronged. Go there until Allah grants relief.'

A first group of about ten or twelve men and four or five women left secretly, led by Uthman ibn Maz'un, among them Uthman ibn Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter, and Mus'ab ibn Umayr. None was a slave; all were from leading families. Quraysh sent men after them to the coast, but by the time they arrived the Muslims had already sailed. After about three months a rumour reached them that Quraysh had accepted Islam, and some came back, only to find it false; they re-entered Makkah in secret or under the protection (jiwar) of a man of Quraysh, as was the custom. A larger second group then left, harder to arrange than the first: eighty-two or eighty-three men (depending on whether Ammar was among them) and eighteen or nineteen women, led by Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. Islam thus found a home in Africa, under a Christian king, before it reached Madinah.

Quraysh sent Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah with gifts to the Negus (an-Najashi), asking him to hand over the runaways. The Negus called the Muslims. Ja'far spoke: 'O King, we were a people of ignorance, worshipping idols, eating carrion, committing shameful deeds, cutting ties of kinship and the strong devouring the weak, until Allah sent us a Messenger whose lineage, truthfulness and chastity we knew. He called us to worship Allah alone, to speak the truth, keep trusts and join ties of kinship, be good neighbours, and give up idols, the shedding of blood, shameful deeds, false witness and consuming the orphan's wealth. He commanded us to pray, give charity and fast. We believed him, and our people turned on us to force us back to idols.'

The Negus asked to hear something of the revelation. Ja'far recited the opening of Surah Maryam. The Negus wept until his beard was wet, and said: 'This and what Musa brought come from the same lamp.' The next day Amr tried again, saying the Muslims spoke ill of Isa. Ja'far answered: 'He is the servant of Allah, His messenger, His spirit and His word cast into Maryam the virgin.' The Negus picked up a twig and said: 'Isa is no more than what you said, not even by this much.' He returned the gifts, saying he would not take a bribe for something he had not done, and gave the Muslims full protection (Ahmad, from Umm Salamah). Of such Christians the Quran says: 'When they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognise. They say: Our Lord, we believe, so write us among the witnesses' (5:83).

The Negus, whose name was Ashamah (an-Najashi was his title), believed but kept his Islam from his people. When he died, in the ninth year after the Hijrah (some say the eighth), the Prophet ﷺ told the Companions in Madinah: 'Your brother Ashamah has died; stand and pray for him,' and led them in the funeral prayer in his absence (Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah and Jabir). Amr ibn al-As later returned to Abyssinia, and the Negus told him that the angel who came to Musa and Isa had come to Muhammad. Some reports say Amr accepted Islam there; the better-known account is that he came to Madinah with Khalid ibn al-Walid shortly before the Conquest of Makkah and accepted Islam at the Prophet's hand.
abyssinia.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 8–9.

p: As the persecution grew, Abu Bakr set out to emigrate to Abyssinia. On the way he met Ibn ad-Dughunnah, chief of the Qarah tribe. 'A man like you should not leave or be driven out,' he said. 'You help the destitute, keep ties of kinship, carry the burdens of the weak and honour guests.' He brought Abu Bakr back under his protection.

Quraysh accepted on condition that Abu Bakr worship inside his house. Instead he built a small masjid in his courtyard and recited the Quran there, weeping. Women and children gathered to listen, and Quraysh complained: the sons and daughters of their leaders were already turning to these words. By now nearly every chief had a son, brother or close relative in Islam, and they feared losing their power and wealth. Ibn ad-Dughunnah asked him to stop or give back the protection. Abu Bakr said: 'I return your protection to you, and I am content with the protection of Allah' (Bukhari; Hayatus Sahaba 1:293). From then on he was openly attacked.
dughunnah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 9.

p: One day Abu Jahl met the Prophet ﷺ near Safa and insulted and abused him (one report says he struck him and drew blood); the Prophet ﷺ did not reply. A servant woman saw it.

That evening Hamzah, the Prophet's uncle and a strong, proud hunter, came back from hunting with his bow over his shoulder. The woman told him what had happened. In fury, Hamzah went straight to Abu Jahl among the men of Quraysh, struck him on the head with his bow and said: 'Do you insult him when I follow his religion? I say what he says. Hit me back if you can!' Men of Abu Jahl's clan rose, but Abu Jahl stopped them, admitting he had wronged the nephew.

Hamzah had spoken in anger, but he reflected and his Islam became firm. Quraysh knew the Prophet ﷺ now had a powerful protector, and for a time they eased their attacks on him. He began coming to Dar al-Arqam to learn the religion. The Prophet ﷺ prayed that Allah strengthen Islam with one of two men, and within days the answer came.
hamza-islam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 8.

p: Umar ibn al-Khattab was among the fiercest enemies of Islam. In the sixth year of prophethood he set out with his sword to kill the Prophet ﷺ. On the way Nu'aym ibn Abdullah stopped him: 'Look first to your own family. Your sister Fatimah and her husband Sa'id have become Muslims.'

Umar burst into his sister's house, where Khabbab was teaching them Surah Ta-Ha. He struck his brother-in-law and, when Fatimah stood between them, hit her and she bled. She said: 'Do what you will; we have become Muslims.' Seeing her blood, Umar softened and asked for the page. She made him wash first. He read: 'Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Quran to you to cause you distress…' and said: 'How beautiful and noble these words are!'

He went to Dar al-Arqam. The companions were alarmed, but Hamzah said: 'Let him in; if he comes for good, we will give it; if for evil, we will kill him with his own sword.' The Prophet ﷺ seized his garment: 'Will you not stop, Umar?' Umar said: 'I have come to believe in Allah and His Messenger.' The Prophet ﷺ cried out 'Allahu akbar' so loudly that the people in the house heard it.

Umar wanted everyone to know. He asked who in Quraysh spread news fastest, and was told Jamil ibn Ma'mar al-Jumahi. He went and told him he had become a Muslim; Jamil ran to the Ka'bah and shouted: 'Umar has left his religion!' Umar, behind him, called out: 'He lies; I have become a Muslim.' Some reports say he was the fortieth to accept Islam. He asked the Prophet ﷺ: 'Are we not on the truth?' 'Yes.' 'Then why hide?'

The Prophet ﷺ had prayed: 'O Allah, strengthen Islam with whichever of the two men is dearer to You, Umar or Abu Jahl.' After Umar's Islam the Muslims went out in two rows, one led by Hamzah and one by Umar, and prayed openly at the Ka'bah. Ibn Mas'ud said: 'We have been strong ever since Umar accepted Islam' (Bukhari 3684).
umar-islam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 8.

p: With Hamzah and Umar now Muslim and Abu Talib still protecting his nephew, Quraysh decided to break Banu Hashim. In the seventh year of prophethood they wrote a pact: no one would marry their women or give them women in marriage, buy from them or sell to them, make treaties with them, sit with them, speak with them or enter their homes, until they handed Muhammad over to be killed. The pact was hung inside the Ka'bah. The man who wrote it, Mansur ibn Ikrimah, is reported to have had his hand paralysed afterwards.

Abu Talib led Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, into the narrow valley known as Shi'b Abi Talib. Only Abu Lahab sided with Quraysh. For about three years they endured siege. Food ran so short that they ate leaves and boiled skins, and the cries of hungry children could be heard outside. A few relatives smuggled in food by night; Hakim ibn Hizam was caught bringing wheat to his aunt Khadijah. Abu Talib moved his nephew to a different place to sleep each night so that no one could reach him, since his murder would have meant open war.

In time some men of Quraysh felt ashamed. Hisham ibn Amr, whose relatives were among the besieged, reasoned that had the boycott been against Abu Jahl's own family, he would never have obeyed it. He went quietly, one by one, to men he trusted, appealing to them simply as human beings: 'Are you content to eat and dress and marry while your kin starve?' Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah agreed, then al-Mut'im ibn Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari and Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad. They planned to raise it at the Ka'bah as if they had not agreed in advance. Zuhayr stood up and declared that he would tear up the unjust pact; Abu Jahl shouted that it would never be torn; then the others rose, one after another, to support Zuhayr.

Meanwhile Allah had told the Prophet ﷺ that termites had eaten the whole pact except the words 'In Your name, O Allah' (Bismika Allahumma). Abu Talib came to Quraysh and said: 'My nephew tells me this. If he is lying, I will hand him over to you; if he is right, end the boycott.' They agreed. When they took it down, they found it so. The boycott ended in the tenth year, after about three years, yet even this sign did not move them, nor Abu Talib himself. It had weakened Abu Talib and Khadijah, who both died soon after.
boycott.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 8–9.

p: The idolaters of Makkah demanded a sign. On a moonlit night at Mina, the Prophet ﷺ pointed and the moon was seen split into two parts, one part over the mountain and one beside it. He said: 'Bear witness.'

Ibn Mas'ud, who saw it, narrated it, as did Anas and Ibn Abbas (Bukhari, Muslim). The idolaters said: 'Muhammad has bewitched us,' but travellers arriving from other places confirmed they had seen it too. Allah revealed: 'The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split. Yet if they see a sign they turn away and say: continuous magic' (54:1–2).

Quraysh kept asking for more: 'We will not believe you until you make a spring gush from the earth for us, or have a garden of palms and grapes with rivers flowing through it, or bring down the sky on us in pieces, or bring Allah and the angels before us, or have a house of gold, or climb into the sky, and even then we will not believe in your climbing until you bring down a book we can read.' Allah told him to answer: 'Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?' (17:90–93). They even said: 'O Allah, if this is the truth from You, rain stones down on us from the sky,' and Allah said: 'Allah would not punish them while you are among them' (8:32–33). Scholars explain that had the demanded signs come and been rejected, destruction would have followed; Allah spared Quraysh, most of whom accepted Islam at the Conquest of Makkah.
moon.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 8.

p: Quraysh sent an-Nadr ibn al-Harith and Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the rabbis of Yathrib for a way to test Muhammad. The rabbis said: 'Ask him about young men who went away in ancient times; about a man who travelled to the east and west of the earth; and about the Ruh. If he answers, he is a prophet.'

Quraysh put the questions. The Prophet ﷺ said he would answer tomorrow, without saying 'in sha Allah'. Revelation then paused for about fifteen days, and Quraysh mocked him. Then Surah al-Kahf came, telling the story of the young men of the cave and of Dhul-Qarnayn, and the ayah on the Ruh: 'They ask you about the Ruh. Say: the Ruh is of my Lord's command, and you have been given only a little knowledge' (17:85).

The surah also taught: 'Never say of anything: I will do that tomorrow, except (adding) if Allah wills' (18:23–24). (Reported by Ibn Ishaq; a report in Bukhari places the question about the Ruh in Madinah.)
questions.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 8.

p: In the tenth year of prophethood, soon after the boycott ended, Abu Talib fell ill. As he lay dying, the Prophet ﷺ begged him: 'Uncle, say La ilaha illa Allah, a word I can plead for you with Allah.' Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah, sitting with him, said: 'Will you leave the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?' Quraysh made sure their leaders were at his bedside, afraid he would accept Islam at the last moment. He told his nephew: 'Were it not that Quraysh would say I said it out of fear of death, I would have pleased you with it' (Muslim). Abu Talib's last words were that he died on the religion of Abd al-Muttalib (Bukhari, Muslim).

The Prophet ﷺ was grieved and said he would seek forgiveness for him unless forbidden. Allah revealed: 'You cannot guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills' (28:56), and later 9:113. Scholars explain that guidance has two meanings. To show the path (irshad) was the Prophet's task: 'You guide to a straight path' (42:52). To give a heart the ability to follow it (tawfiq) belongs to Allah alone. Many know what is right and still do not walk on it.

Within weeks Khadijah also died, after 25 years of marriage. She had been the first to believe and his greatest support. The Prophet ﷺ felt both losses so deeply that the year became known as the Year of Sorrow. Abu Talib had shielded him from outside harm; Khadijah had comforted him at home. Now he had lost both. With Abu Talib gone, Quraysh harmed him as never before; once a man threw dust on his head, and his daughter wept as she washed it off. Allah later recalled their schemes: 'When the disbelievers plotted to confine you, kill you or drive you out; they plotted, and Allah plotted, and Allah is the best of planners' (8:30).
sorrow.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 9.

p: With Makkah closed to him, the Prophet ﷺ walked about 60 miles to Ta'if with Zayd ibn Harithah, on foot so that Quraysh would not notice them leave. He hoped the tribe of Thaqif would accept Islam and protect him, and that Makkah might follow. He went first to their three leading brothers, Abd Yalil, Mas'ud and Habib, sons of Amr ibn Umayr, and spent about ten days speaking to their leaders. They refused rudely. He asked them at least not to tell Quraysh he had come; they sent word to Makkah at once. Then they set their slaves and children on him. They lined the road and pelted him with stones until his feet bled and his sandals filled with blood. Zayd shielded him and was wounded in the head.

He took shelter in an orchard belonging to Utbah and Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah and made a moving dua: 'O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources and my humiliation before people… If You are not angry with me, I do not care… I seek refuge in the light of Your Face.' The owners sent their Christian servant Addas with a plate of grapes. When the Prophet ﷺ said 'Bismillah' and spoke of Yunus, 'my brother, a prophet like me', Addas kissed his head, hands and feet and accepted Islam. Utbah and Shaybah warned Addas not to let the man turn him from his religion; he replied that he had told him something only a prophet could know. (The Addas story is reported by Ibn Ishaq with a mursal chain, but it appears in most books of Seerah.)

On the way back, Aisha narrated, Jibril came with the angel of the mountains, who said: 'If you wish, I will bring the two mountains together on them.' The Prophet ﷺ replied: 'Rather, I hope Allah will bring from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone' (Bukhari 3231). Today there is hardly a non-Muslim in Ta'if. On the way back he stayed some days at Nakhlah. A party of jinn (seven, in one report) heard him reciting in the night prayer, fell silent to listen, believed, and went back to warn their people: 'We have heard a Book sent down after Musa, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth' (46:29–32). The jinn believed where the people of Ta'if had refused.

He could not re-enter Makkah without protection, and al-Mut'im ibn Adi, though not a Muslim, took him under his protection and escorted him to the Ka'bah with his sons, their swords drawn, while he performed tawaf. When Quraysh asked: 'Have you become his follower, or are you only protecting him?' he said: 'Only protecting him,' and they left him alone.
taif.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 9.

p: Every Hajj season, and at the fairs where the Arabs traded, boasted of their lineage and competed in poetry, tribes from across Arabia came to Makkah and to the markets of Ukaz, Majannah and Dhul-Majaz. The Prophet ﷺ went to their camps one by one, and visited their tents at night with Abu Bakr, saying: 'Who will shelter me and support me so that I may convey the message of my Lord?' By day he walked through the crowds calling: 'O people, say La ilaha illallah and you will succeed.' Often Abu Lahab followed behind him shouting: 'Do not listen to him; he is a madman and a liar!', looking more foolish than the man he mocked.

He spoke to Kindah, Kalb, Banu Hanifah, Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah and others. Banu Hanifah gave the harshest reply. A man of Banu Amir offered support on condition that power passed to them after him; the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The matter belongs to Allah; He gives it to whom He wills,' and they refused. Banu Shayban listened respectfully and praised what they heard, but explained they had a treaty with Persia they could not break.
Visitors from outside Makkah often listened more quietly than Quraysh: many had lived among Jews or Christians and already knew of the Resurrection and the reckoning, which Quraysh found laughable.
No tribe accepted. Yet in this search the Prophet ﷺ met six men from Yathrib, and through them Allah opened the way (Ahmad, Ibn Ishaq; Hayatus Sahaba 1:109–117).
hajj-tribes.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 10.

p: At-Tufayl ibn Amr, a chief and poet of the tribe of Daws, came to Makkah. Quraysh warned him to avoid Muhammad, whose words they said split families. He stuffed cotton in his ears before entering the masjid.

Yet Allah let him hear some of the recitation, and he thought: 'I am a poet who can tell good from bad; what stops me from listening?' He followed the Prophet ﷺ home, heard the Quran and accepted Islam. He asked for a sign to help him call his people, and was given a light. He called his father and wife, who accepted, but most of Daws refused.

He came back complaining and asked the Prophet ﷺ to curse Daws. Instead the Prophet ﷺ prayed: 'O Allah, guide Daws and bring them.' At-Tufayl returned with patience, and years later he brought some seventy or eighty families of Daws to Madinah, among them Abu Hurayrah (Abd ar-Rahman ibn Sakhr), who would narrate more hadith than any other Companion (Hayatus Sahaba 1).
tufayl.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 9.

p: After Khadijah's death, the Prophet ﷺ still spoke of her constantly; he never had a single quarrel with her recorded, and he kept sending gifts to her friends for the rest of his life. Khawlah bint Hakim, wife of Uthman ibn Maz'un, saw his house without a woman and his daughters still young, and asked: 'Will you not marry?' 'Whom?' 'A virgin if you wish, or a woman who has been married.' The widow she proposed was Sawdah bint Zam'ah. An early Muslim, Sawdah had emigrated to Abyssinia with her husband as-Sakran ibn Amr, and lost him after their return. Her brothers were idolaters and she badly needed protection. The Prophet ﷺ chose her. When Khawlah brought the news, Sawdah, astonished and relieved, sent her to her father, an old idolater, who was glad his daughter would be cared for by a man of her own faith. They married in the tenth year of prophethood, and she cared for his household and his daughters. Most of the women he married had suffered greatly and needed protection.

Khawlah's other suggestion was a virgin: Aisha, the young daughter of his closest friend. Early betrothal arranged by families was the custom of that society, as it still is in parts of the world, and Abu Bakr had earlier promised her to Jubayr, son of al-Mut'im ibn Adi. When he went to them, Jubayr's mother said she would not let her son leave his forefathers' religion by marrying into his family, so the promise lapsed. In the same period the nikah with Aisha, the daughter of Abu Bakr, took place in Makkah, when she was six or seven by the reports; she joined his household in Madinah after the Hijrah. Sawdah was known for her generosity and good humour, and in later years she gave her turn to Aisha.
sawdah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 11–12.

p: During the Hajj of the eleventh year of prophethood, the Prophet ﷺ met six men of the Khazraj from Yathrib at al-Aqabah in Mina: As'ad ibn Zurarah, Awf ibn al-Harith (ibn Afra'), Rafi' ibn Malik, Qutbah ibn Amir, Uqbah ibn Amir and Jabir ibn Abdullah ibn Ri'ab. He sat with them, asked where they were from, and asked if they would listen; they agreed. He recited the Quran to them and called them to Islam.

The men had heard their Jewish neighbours in Yathrib say that a prophet was about to appear. They said to each other: 'This is the prophet the Jews warn us about; let them not beat us to him.' They accepted Islam and said: 'We left our people with more enmity between them than any other. Perhaps Allah will unite them through you.' They returned home and spoke of Islam until there was no house in Yathrib where the Prophet ﷺ was not mentioned.
six-yathrib.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 10.

p: Its exact date is not authentically fixed; most scholars place it a year or so before the Hijrah, and reports name Rajab, Ramadan and Rabi' al-Awwal. Mufti Menk advises learning its lessons rather than arguing over the date. It came as a gift after the Year of Sorrow. One night Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was in Makkah, sleeping at the house of his cousin Umm Hani (another report says in the Hijr beside the Ka'bah; scholars reconcile them: he was taken from her house to the Hijr). His chest was opened again, as in his childhood among Banu Sa'd, and his heart washed with Zamzam and filled with faith and wisdom. Then al-Buraq, a white animal smaller than a mule and larger than a donkey, whose stride reached as far as its sight, was brought to him.

He rode it to Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem, tied it at the gate, and led all the prophets in prayer. Jibril offered him a cup of wine and a cup of milk; he chose the milk, and Jibril said: 'You have chosen the fitrah.' Muslims believe that Isa had already been raised alive, body and soul, before his enemies could kill or crucify him (4:157–158), and that he will return before the end of time; the difference is that the Prophet ﷺ came back and told us what he saw. Surah al-Isra opens with this journey: 'Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him some of Our signs' (17:1).

Then he was taken up through the heavens: the Buraq stayed behind, and the ascent (mi'raj, literally a ladder) was with Jibril. At each heaven a voice asked: 'Who is it?' 'Jibril.' 'Who is with you?' 'Muhammad.' 'Has he been sent for?' 'Yes.' And the gate was opened. In the first he met Adam; in the second Yahya and Isa; in the third Yusuf, who had been given half of all beauty (Muslim); in the fourth Idris; in the fifth Harun; in the sixth Musa, who wept as he passed, saying it was because more of this young man's followers would enter Paradise than his own (Bukhari); and in the seventh Ibrahim, leaning against al-Bayt al-Ma'mur, which seventy thousand angels enter daily, never to return to it. The angels glorify their Lord and seek forgiveness for those on earth (42:5), above all for those who believe and repent (40:7). He reached Sidrat al-Muntaha, the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, whose leaves were like the ears of elephants and whose fruit like great clay jars, and saw Jibril in his true form (53:13–18).

Allah prescribed fifty prayers a day. On his way down Musa told him: 'Your people cannot bear it; go back and ask for a reduction.' He returned again and again until they were reduced to five, and Allah said: 'They are five, and they are fifty' in reward (Bukhari 349, Muslim). On the same night he was told: whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, one good deed is written for him; if he does it, ten to seven hundred. Whoever intends an evil deed and does not do it, nothing is written against him (and if he leaves it for Allah's sake, a good deed); if he does it, only one evil deed is written (Muslim). Asked whether he saw his Lord, he said: 'Light; how could I see Him?' (Muslim, from Abu Dharr), and Aishah firmly denied that he saw Allah with his eyes (Bukhari, Muslim). Seeing Allah is the greatest reward kept for Paradise, the 'more' in 'For those who do good is the best, and more' (10:26; Muslim).

He was also shown Paradise and Hell. He saw how those who consumed interest, those who committed adultery and others were punished. In Paradise he heard footsteps ahead of him, and later asked Bilal what he did; Bilal said that whenever he made wudu he prayed two rak'ahs (Bukhari).

He returned the same night; one report, not strong, says his bed was still warm. Umm Hani begged him not to tell Quraysh, fearing they would mock him, but he went out and told them. They mocked him, and some weak believers wavered. When told, Abu Bakr said: 'If he said it, it is true. I believe him about news from heaven morning and evening.' From that day he was called as-Siddiq. When Quraysh tested the Prophet ﷺ by asking him to describe Jerusalem, Allah showed it to him and he described it gate by gate. They asked about their caravans on the road. He told them where he had passed each one, what had happened to it, and when it would arrive, led by a camel of a particular colour; it came exactly as he said (Ibn Ishaq). They called it soothsaying and magic, though the Quran he brought condemns both: 'Allah will make magic come to nothing' (10:81), and he said that whoever goes to a soothsayer and believes him has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad (Abu Dawud).

The five prayers became obligatory from that time. Jibril came on two consecutive days and led him in each prayer, the first day at the beginning of its time and the next day at its end, and said: 'The time is between these two' (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi). Before this the prayer had been two rak'ahs at a time (Aishah, Bukhari). Mufti Menk notes that praying at the start of the time is a great gift, since Shaytan's trick is to whisper that there is still time.
isra.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 9–10.

p: At the Hajj of the twelfth year, twelve men from Yathrib met the Prophet ﷺ at al-Aqabah and gave the first pledge. When they left, he sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr with them (one report says Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum went too) to teach the Quran and lead the prayer. Once the pampered youth of Makkah in the finest clothes, Mus'ab had given everything up for Islam.

In Yathrib he stayed with As'ad ibn Zurarah and taught in the gardens. Usayd ibn Hudayr came with his spear, angry. Mus'ab said: 'Sit and listen; if you like it, accept it, and if not, we will stop.' Usayd listened, his face changed, and he accepted Islam. He then sent Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, chief of Banu Abd al-Ash'hal, who came angry too and left a Muslim.

Sa'd went to his clan and said: 'What is my standing among you?' 'Our chief and the best of us.' 'Then I will not speak to man or woman of you until you believe in Allah and His Messenger.' By evening the whole clan had accepted Islam. Within a year Islam had spread through every household of the Ansar (Ibn Ishaq; Hayatus Sahaba 1:136, 208).
musab-madinah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 11.

p: The six men spread Islam among their people, helped by the silence that followed Bu'ath. At the Hajj of the twelfth year of prophethood, twelve men of Yathrib (five of the six and seven new men) met the Prophet ﷺ at al-Aqabah and gave what became known as the first pledge. They promised not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, commit adultery or kill their children, not to slander, and not to disobey him in good.
