Ubadah ibn as-Samit, who was there, said these were the same terms later taken from the women (60:12). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever fulfils this, his reward is with Allah. Whoever falls short and is punished in this world, it is an expiation; and whoever falls short and Allah conceals it, his matter is with Allah: He may forgive him or punish him' (Bukhari). He did not appoint himself their judge. Mufti Menk draws a lesson from this: we should not be quick to condemn others, since a sinner may end his life a saint.

Mus'ab returned before the next Hajj with good news: there was hardly a house in Yathrib without a Muslim. Jabir ibn Abdullah said the Ansar asked one another: 'How long will we leave the Messenger of Allah to be hunted and terrified in the mountains of Makkah?' The Prophet ﷺ had also been shown in a dream the land he would migrate to, a land of palms between two lava fields; he had thought it might be al-Yamamah or Hajar, until it became clear that it was Yathrib (Bukhari). So that year, 73 men and two women came. They met him secretly by night in the middle of the days of Tashriq, in the same valley, slipping away from their sleeping companions. Most were young. With him was his uncle al-Abbas, still not Muslim but now the family's protector after Abu Talib's death. Al-Abbas spoke first to make sure they were serious: Banu Hashim protected his nephew, and if they could not do the same, they should leave him now. They answered that they would.

The Prophet ﷺ first recited the Quran and called them to Allah. Then he set out two pledges: between them and Allah, to worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him; and between them and himself. They pledged to obey the Prophet ﷺ in ease and hardship, to spend in plenty and in poverty, to enjoin good and forbid evil, and to protect him as they protected their own wives and children. Abu al-Haytham ibn at-Tayyihan asked: 'If Allah gives you victory, will you return to your people and leave us?' The Prophet ﷺ smiled and said: 'Your blood is my blood; I am of you and you are of me.'

He asked them to choose twelve leaders (naqibs), nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws. Asked what they would get in return, he said: 'Paradise.' They said: 'A profitable trade; we will not cancel it or ask for it to be cancelled.' The way to the Hijrah was now open. At that moment a devil's voice cried out from the hill to Quraysh that Muhammad and the apostates were gathering to make war on them, and the Prophet ﷺ told them to return to their camps. In the morning leaders of Quraysh came to the elders of Yathrib and accused them. The elders, who had known nothing, swore honestly that nothing had happened, while the young men who had been there kept quiet. Islam had spread through the young.
aqabah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 11.

p: After the second pledge, the Prophet ﷺ gave the companions permission to emigrate to Madinah. They left in small groups, mostly in secret, leaving homes, families and wealth behind. Among the first were Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum; Hamzah went too. The Prophet ﷺ himself waited for Allah's permission to leave, staying until his followers were safe; the Companions would later say that when battle grew fierce, they sheltered behind him.

Abu Salamah, who had come back from Abyssinia and been persecuted again, set out for Yathrib with his wife Umm Salamah and their little son Salamah, about a year before the second pledge. Her clan, Banu al-Mughirah, seized her: 'You may go, but not with our daughter.' Then his clan, Banu Abd al-Asad, came and took the child: 'You will not keep our son's son.' The family was split three ways: the husband in Yathrib, the wife with her people, the child with his. For about a year Umm Salamah sat every day at the place where it had happened, weeping from morning to evening, until a cousin pitied her and persuaded her family to let her go. She got her son back, and set out alone on a camel with the boy. At at-Tan'im, the edge of the Haram where Masjid Aisha stands today, she met Uthman ibn Talhah of Quraysh, not yet a Muslim, who asked where she was going. 'To my husband in Yathrib.' 'With no one?' 'Only Allah and this little boy.' He took her camel's halter and led her the whole way, a journey of many days. At each stop he made the camel kneel and moved away until she had dismounted, and turned away again while she mounted; he barely spoke. At Quba he said: 'Your husband is in this village,' and turned back to Makkah. She said: 'I never saw a nobler companion than Uthman ibn Talhah.' He accepted Islam after Hudaybiyah. Mufti Menk's lesson: help those in need for Allah alone, wanting nothing in return.

A well-known report says Umar left openly, going round the Ka'bah with his sword and saying: 'Whoever wants his mother to lose him, his children to be orphans and his wife to be a widow, let him meet me behind this valley.' Mufti Menk notes that its chain is not authentic. The sounder report is that Umar arranged to leave with Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah and Hisham ibn al-As, meeting at a set place; whoever did not come would be taken as held back. Hisham was caught, and Umar and Ayyash reached Quba. Then Abu Jahl and al-Harith ibn Hisham, Ayyash's half-brothers, rode all the way to Quba and told him his mother had sworn not to comb her hair or leave the sun until she saw him. Umar warned him it was a trick and gave him his own fast camel, but on the road they asked to switch mounts, seized him, tied him up and paraded him into Makkah. Word spread that the two had left Islam. Then Allah revealed: 'Say: O My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; Allah forgives all sins' (39:53). Umar wrote the verses and sent them to Hisham, who understood at Dhu Tuwa that they were for him; in time both escaped to Madinah (Ibn Ishaq). Within a few months almost every Muslim had left; only the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, Ali and those held back by force remained. Makkah fell quiet.
companions-hijrah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 11–12.

p: Suhayb ar-Rumi had earned great wealth in Makkah as a craftsman and trader. When he set out to emigrate, men of Quraysh blocked his way: 'You came to us poor and penniless and became rich among us, and now you want to leave with your life and your wealth? By Allah, that will not happen.'

Suhayb said: 'If I give you my wealth, will you let me go?' They agreed, and he told them where it was buried. When he reached the Prophet ﷺ in Quba, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Your trade has profited, Abu Yahya.' It is reported that Allah revealed concerning him: 'And among people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah' (2:207) (Ibn Ishaq, al-Hakim; Hayatus Sahaba 1:361).
suhayb-hijrah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: The leaders of Quraysh met at Dar an-Nadwah, the house of Qusayy where their great decisions were made. One proposed to imprison him for life; others objected that his followers in Yathrib would come to free him. Another proposed to expel him; others said he would win over the Arabs and return with an army. Then Abu Jahl proposed that a strong young man from every clan strike him together, so his blood would be shared among all the tribes and Banu Abd Manaf could not take revenge on everyone, and would have to accept blood money. They agreed. Allah informed His Messenger and revealed: 'And when the disbelievers plotted against you to imprison you, kill you or drive you out… and Allah is the best of planners' (8:30).

Abu Bakr had long wanted to emigrate, but the Prophet ﷺ had told him: 'Do not hurry; perhaps Allah will give you a companion.' Understanding, Abu Bakr bought two camels and fed them well for months. Then one day at noon, when he never visited, the Prophet ﷺ came to Abu Bakr's house with his head covered. 'Send out whoever is with you.' 'They are only your family.' 'I have been given permission to leave.' 'Companionship, O Messenger of Allah?' 'Yes.' Aishah said she never knew anyone could weep from joy until she saw her father weep that day (Bukhari; Ibn Ishaq). It was near the end of Safar. They hired Abdullah ibn Urayqit, an idolater but trustworthy and an expert guide, gave him the two camels and told him to bring them to the cave of Thawr after three nights.

That night they surrounded his house. He told Ali to sleep in his bed under his green cloak and to return the trusts people had left with him. Even his enemies left their valuables with him for safekeeping, and his staying behind to return them also made Quraysh think he could not have gone. He went out through them, throwing a handful of dust and reciting from Surah Ya-Sin: 'We have put a barrier before them and a barrier behind them and covered them, so they do not see' (36:9). The dust fell on every one of them, and they did not see him. In the morning Ali came out of the bed, and they realised he had gone. He went to Abu Bakr's house, and the two left through a back window and headed south to the cave of Thawr instead of north toward Madinah.

They hid in the cave for three nights. Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr came each night with news of Quraysh; Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazed sheep over their tracks and brought milk; Asma bint Abi Bakr brought food, tying the bag with half of her waistband, and was called Dhat an-Nitaqayn.

Quraysh offered a hundred camels for each of them, and searchers reached the mouth of the cave. Abu Bakr whispered: 'If one of them looked down at his feet, he would see us.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'What do you think of two, the third of whom is Allah?' (Bukhari 3653). Allah recorded it: 'Do not grieve, Allah is with us' (9:40). Allah also says He 'supported him with forces you did not see.' The books of Seerah tell of a spider that spun a web across the mouth of the cave, so the searchers said no one could have entered it; scholars of hadith debate this report (there is a version in Ahmad), and the story of a dove nesting there is not authentic. Mufti Menk's conclusion: Allah protected them with His armies, whatever they were.
thawr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 12.

p: After three nights, the guide Abdullah ibn Urayqit came with two camels and led them along an unusual coastal route. Quraysh had offered a hundred camels, a fortune, for each of them. Suraqah ibn Malik was sitting with his people when a man said he had seen riders on the coast road. Suraqah told him it must be someone else, then slipped away wanting the reward, set out alone on his horse.

As he came close, his horse stumbled and threw him. He drew lots with his arrows, as the Arabs did, and they said no, but he rode on. Close enough to hear the Prophet ﷺ reciting (he never looked back, while Abu Bakr looked back often), his horse's forelegs sank into the ground up to the knees; when he freed it, smoke like a dust storm rose from the hoofprints. He realised the Prophet ﷺ was protected, called out for safety, and offered them provisions. The Prophet ﷺ asked only that he keep their whereabouts secret, and Amir ibn Fuhayrah wrote him a guarantee on a piece of leather (Bukhari).

It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ told him: 'How will you be when you wear the bracelets of Khosrow?' Suraqah returned and turned back anyone searching that way. He accepted Islam at Ji'ranah, after the Conquest of Makkah, and in Umar's time, when the treasures of Persia were brought to Madinah, Umar put Khosrow's bracelets on Suraqah's arms.
suraqah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 12.

p: The people of Madinah went out every morning to the lava fields to wait for him, returning only when the heat became too much. One day a Jewish man on a fort saw the riders and shouted: 'O people of the Arabs, here is the man you are waiting for!' The Muslims rushed out with their weapons, crying 'Allahu akbar'.

He arrived on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal: one report gives the 12th, the same date as his birth by the common view, others the 8th. He stayed in Quba, on the outskirts of Madinah, with Banu Amr ibn Awf in the house of their chief Kulthum ibn al-Hidm. Reports of the length vary: four days in some, fourteen in others; Mufti Menk gives fourteen to nineteen. There he founded Masjid Quba, the first masjid built in Islam, and carried stones for it himself with the Companions. It was a simple structure, but the hearts of those who prayed in it were beautiful. Allah praised it as 'a masjid founded on taqwa from the first day' (9:108), as many explain the ayah.

Ali, having returned the trusts in Makkah, caught up with him in Quba two or three nights after his arrival. The masjid was more than a place of prayer: there the Muslims met, learnt the Quran and the Prophet's teaching, settled their affairs and prepared to defend themselves. The Prophet ﷺ continued to visit Quba every Saturday, walking or riding, for the rest of his life (Bukhari 1193).
quba.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 12–13.

p: Before he came, As'ad ibn Zurarah had already been gathering the Muslims of Madinah on Fridays for prayer and remembrance. On Friday morning the Ansar came armed to escort him, ringing him to protect him from any enemy, and the Prophet ﷺ left Quba for Madinah. When the time of prayer came he was in the valley of Banu Salim ibn Awf, and there he led the first Jumu'ah prayer in Madinah, with about a hundred Muslims.

He delivered the first khutbah to the Ansar and Muhajirin, praising Allah and urging the believers to taqwa, to remember Allah and to prepare for the Day of Judgement, when Allah will ask each person what he did with the Messenger who came to him. In one version he told them: 'Whoever can protect his face from the Fire, even with half a date, let him do it; and whoever cannot find that, then with a good word' (the last words are also in Bukhari). No charity is too small to save a person from the Fire. A masjid, Masjid al-Jumu'ah, was later built on the spot (Ibn Ishaq; Hayatus Sahaba 3:407).
jumuah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 13.

p: After Jumu'ah, the Prophet ﷺ rode on into Madinah on his camel al-Qaswa. The whole city came out. Women climbed onto the rooftops; the boys and servants ran through the streets crying 'Ya Muhammad, ya Rasulallah!' (Muslim). The books of Seerah, though not of hadith, add that the girls sang: 'The full moon has risen over us from the valley of Wada'; gratitude is due from us as long as anyone calls to Allah.' Anas said he never saw a brighter day.

Every clan he passed took the camel's rein and begged him to stay with them. He said each time: 'Let her go, for she is under command.' The camel walked on and knelt at a drying ground for dates belonging to two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, near the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. Abu Ayyub carried his luggage inside, and the Prophet ﷺ stayed with him for some months. The house had two storeys. Abu Ayyub could not bear to live above the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but the Prophet ﷺ chose the ground floor so visitors would not pass through the family's rooms. Once a jar of water broke upstairs, and Abu Ayyub and his wife mopped it with their only blanket lest a drop fall on him (Muslim). The other emigrants were housed with the Ansar by drawing lots, so no one chose or was favoured (Bukhari, from Umm al-Ala). The Prophet ﷺ loved the Ansar: 'Were it not for the Hijrah, I would have been one of the Ansar' (Bukhari).

The Hijrah changed everything. The persecuted believers of Makkah became a community with a home, and Yathrib became al-Madinah, the City of the Prophet ﷺ. When Umar later set up the Islamic calendar, the companions chose the year of the Hijrah as its beginning, starting from Muharram. Ibn Hajar explains that the decision to emigrate followed the second pledge in Dhul-Hijjah, and the first new moon after it was Muharram. The Prophet ﷺ reached Quba around 20 September 622 CE. With the Hijrah began the Madinan revelation: fewer surahs, though long ones like al-Baqarah and Al Imran, now dealing with law and community; most surahs, on tawhid and the Hereafter, had already come in Makkah. Aisha narrated the whole journey in detail (Bukhari 3905).
hijrah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 13.

p: The land where the camel knelt belonged to two orphan boys. They offered it as a gift, but the Prophet ﷺ insisted on paying for it, and Abu Bakr paid the price. Graves of idolaters and palm trees on the site were cleared.

Until then the Muslims prayed wherever the time found them. The masjid was built of sun-dried mud bricks, with no carpet or tiles, so that their knees and foreheads bore the marks of the ground, with palm trunks for pillars and palm leaves for the roof, so low that a boy raising his hand could touch it. Companions who knew building were put to work mixing the clay. The Prophet ﷺ carried bricks with the companions, who sang as they worked: 'O Allah, there is no life but the life of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirin.' Ammar carried two bricks at a time.

At first the qiblah faced Jerusalem. Beside it were built simple, low rooms for the Prophet's family, first for Sawdah and Aishah; in Aishah's room he would die and be buried, and at the back a shaded platform, the Suffah, where poor Muslims with no homes lived and studied. The masjid became the centre of everything: prayer, teaching, judging disputes, receiving delegations and planning.

Some who had longed for this day did not live to see it completed. As'ad ibn Zurarah, among the first six believers, died while it was being built. Al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, one of the twelve naqibs, had died in Safar, just before the Prophet ﷺ reached Quba, and his host at Quba, Kulthum ibn al-Hidm, died soon after. In Makkah an old, sick man, Damrah ibn Jundub (named differently in some reports), had his family carry him out to emigrate, and died on the way; Allah revealed: 'Whoever leaves his home emigrating to Allah and His Messenger and death overtakes him, his reward is with Allah' (4:100).

Madinah was then known for a deadly fever that came every year, and many of the Muhajirin fell ill, Abu Bakr and Bilal among them. The Prophet ﷺ prayed: 'O Allah, make Madinah dear to us as You made Makkah dear, or more; make it healthy; bless us in its sa' and its mudd; and move its fever to al-Juhfah' (Bukhari). The fever left. He also said that whoever bears patiently the hardship of Madinah, he will be his intercessor or witness on the Day of Resurrection (Muslim).
nabawi.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 13.

p: Madinah now held several groups. The Muhajirin had lost homes and wealth in Makkah; faith there had cost so much that no hypocrite was among them, and Allah calls them 'the truthful' (59:8). The Ansar had opened their homes to them. Many of the Aws and Khazraj were still idolaters, and some would soon pretend to believe. Around the city lived three Jewish tribes: Banu Qaynuqa' inside Madinah, and Banu an-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah on its outskirts. Each was allied with one of the Arab tribes, Qaynuqa' with the Khazraj and an-Nadir and Qurayzah with the Aws. Few in number but skilled in trade, they controlled much of the market, including dates and wine, and lent to the Arab leaders at heavy interest, keeping them in debt.

The Muhajirin had arrived in Madinah with almost nothing. To help them, the Prophet ﷺ paired each emigrant with one of the Ansar as a brother. Many pairs shared homes, work and wealth, and the Muhajirin, who knew more Quran, taught their hosts the religion; at first they even inherited from each other, until the Quran later limited inheritance to relatives (8:75).

The Ansar offered: 'Divide our palm groves between us and our brothers.' The Prophet ﷺ said no. They said: 'Then let them share the work, and we will share the fruit with them,' and he agreed (Bukhari). The Ansar knew farming and the Muhajirin did not; dividing the land would have ruined the harvest, so ownership stayed with those who knew it and the produce was shared. Some of the pairs were Abu Bakr with Kharijah ibn Zayd, Umar with Itban ibn Malik, Abu Ubaydah with Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, az-Zubayr with Salamah ibn Salamah, Talhah with Ka'b ibn Malik, Sa'id ibn Zayd with Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mus'ab with Abu Ayyub (Khalid ibn Zayd), Ammar with Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Abu Dharr with al-Mundhir ibn Amr, and Salman with Abu ad-Darda'.

Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi' of the Ansar told his brother Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf: 'I am the richest of the Ansar. Take half my wealth, and I have two wives; see which you like and I will divorce her so you can marry her.' Abd ar-Rahman replied: 'May Allah bless your family and wealth. Just show me the market.' He traded and soon became wealthy himself (Bukhari).

Salman visited Abu ad-Darda' and found his wife in shabby clothes. 'Your brother Abu ad-Darda' has no need of this world,' she said. When food was served, Abu ad-Darda' said he was fasting; Salman said he would not eat unless he ate, so he ate. At night Abu ad-Darda' rose to pray, and Salman told him to sleep; again later, and again Salman sent him back. In the last third of the night Salman woke him and they prayed together. Then he said: 'Your Lord has a right over you, your body has a right over you, and your family has a right over you; give each its right.' Abu ad-Darda' told the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'Salman has spoken the truth' (Bukhari). Worship is to be kept up steadily and in balance, not in bursts at the cost of other duties.

The Ansar's generosity is praised in the Quran: 'They prefer others over themselves even though they are in need' (59:9). Many Muhajirin, being traders, would not live on handouts and asked only to be shown the market, and soon prospered.
muakhat.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 14.

p: When the Prophet ﷺ arrived, Madinah had been about to crown a king. After Bu'ath had killed most of the old leaders, the Khazraj and many of the Aws had settled on Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul as ruler. The Prophet's coming took that from him, and he never forgave it; later, seeing which way things were going, he declared Islam outwardly while keeping his resentment, and became the leader of the hypocrites. Now the Prophet ﷺ was the leader of the city, in religion and in government.
In his first year in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ had a written covenant drawn up for all its people: the Muhajirin, the Ansar of Aws and Khazraj, and the Jewish tribes and their allies.

Among the believers, the charter said: they are one ummah, distinct from other people; each clan pays its own blood money and ransoms as before, and all help a member weighed down with debt or ransom; the believers stand together against anyone who commits injustice, aggression or corruption, even if he is one of their own sons; the blood of the humblest believer is equal to that of the greatest; no believer may help a disbeliever against a believer; and no one may make a separate peace with Quraysh, since the peace of the believers is one. Any dispute was to be referred to Allah and to Muhammad ﷺ, and crimes were to be punished, not avenged by tribe.

With the Jews, it said: the Jews of Banu Awf and the other tribes are a community alongside the believers; the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs; each bears its own expenses, but the Jews share the cost of war while fighting alongside the believers; they owe each other sincere counsel and help against anyone who fights the parties to the treaty; the wronged are to be helped; the valley of Yathrib is sacred (haram) for the people of this document; and no one is to protect Quraysh or those who help them. Later the Prophet ﷺ declared Madinah a sanctuary like Makkah, where its trees were not to be cut nor its game hunted (Bukhari, Muslim).

The charter replaced old tribal feuds with a shared law, settled the city before Quraysh could stir trouble, and still reads as a lesson in building a nation, and later breaches of it by some tribes shaped events such as the expulsions of Banu Qaynuqa and Banu Nadir.
sahifah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 14.

p: In Madinah the Muslims gathered for prayer at the times they guessed, with no call; at first a man would go round calling out 'Prayer! Prayer!' The companions discussed what to use. Some suggested raising a flag, others lighting a fire; some a horn like the Jews, others a bell like the Christians, and each idea was rejected. Umar suggested a man be sent to call people to prayer.

Within days Abdullah ibn Zayd of the Ansar saw in a dream a man teaching him the words of the adhan. He told the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'It is a true dream, in sha Allah. Teach it to Bilal, for his voice is louder and more beautiful than yours.' One report adds that revelation had already come with the same words. When Bilal called it, Umar came running and said he had seen the same dream (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi; see Bukhari on the consultation).

From then on Bilal's voice called the believers to prayer five times a day, from the highest roof nearby, since there were no minarets. To the adhan of Fajr he added 'as-salatu khayrun min an-nawm' (prayer is better than sleep), and the Prophet ﷺ approved it (Ibn Majah). In Ramadan there were two calls before dawn: Bilal's, to wake people for suhur, and Ibn Umm Maktum's at true dawn (Bukhari). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The mu'adhdhins will have the longest necks on the Day of Resurrection' (Muslim), and: 'If people knew what is in the call to prayer and the first row, and could only get it by drawing lots, they would draw lots' (Bukhari). Mufti Menk adds that the caller receives the reward of everyone who answers his call. Later Uthman added a second call for Jumu'ah, given in the market at az-Zawra' as Madinah grew (Bukhari); Mufti Menk says the Umayyad caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik later had the call moved inside, before the imam. After him the adhan has been called in every Muslim land.
adhan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 13.

p: Abdullah ibn Salam was a learned rabbi of Madinah. When he heard the Prophet ﷺ had arrived, he came and looked at his face, and said he knew it was not the face of a liar. The first words he heard him say were: 'O people, spread salam, feed others, keep the ties of kinship, and pray at night while people sleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace' (Tirmidhi). He belonged to Banu Qaynuqa' and was among the most learned and honoured of the Jews of Madinah. He asked three questions which, he said, only a prophet would know: the first sign of the Hour, the first food of the people of Paradise, and why a child resembles its father or mother. The Prophet ﷺ answered each, and Abdullah accepted Islam (Bukhari, from Anas).

He then said: 'The Jews are a people who slander. Ask them about me before they learn of my Islam.' The Prophet ﷺ asked them, and they said: 'Our master and the son of our master, our most learned.' When Abdullah came out and declared the shahadah, they said: 'The worst of us and the son of the worst,' and insulted him. Many mufassirin say 46:10 refers to him.
ibnsalam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 1–4.

p: Seven months after the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ gave a white banner to his uncle Hamzah, the first banner in Islam, and sent him with thirty Muhajirin to the coast near al-Is to intercept a Quraysh caravan returning from Sham under Abu Jahl with about three hundred men.

The two sides met and lined up for battle, but Majdi ibn Amr al-Juhani, an ally of both, came between them until they parted without fighting. No blood was shed, but the march sent a message: the Muslims were no longer only patient victims. Like the expeditions that followed, it also gathered intelligence about the routes, wells and tribes around Madinah and the movements of Quraysh's caravans.
sr-sif.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Shawwal of 1 AH, Ubaydah ibn al-Harith led sixty Muhajirin to the valley of Rabigh, where they met a large party of Quraysh under Abu Sufyan (some say Ikrimah).

There was no real battle, but Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas shot an arrow, the first arrow shot in the cause of Allah. Two men from the Quraysh side, al-Miqdad and Utbah ibn Ghazwan, who had been Muslims in secret, crossed over to the Muslims; they had joined the Quraysh party as a way to reach Madinah.
sr-rabigh.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Dhu al-Qa'dah of 1 AH, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas led about twenty Muhajirin on foot to al-Kharrar near al-Juhfah to intercept a Quraysh caravan. The Prophet ﷺ told him not to go beyond al-Kharrar. They travelled by night and hid by day. When they arrived, the caravan had passed a day earlier, and they returned without fighting.
sr-kharrar.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Safar of 2 AH, the Prophet ﷺ himself led about seventy Muhajirin out of Madinah for the first time, leaving Sa'd ibn Ubadah in charge of the city. Hamzah carried the white banner, and the march lasted about fifteen days. He headed for al-Abwa and Waddan to intercept a Quraysh caravan.

The caravan was not met. Instead he spent time with the tribes on the way and made a treaty with Banu Damrah, who agreed not to fight the Muslims or help their enemies. These early marches secured the routes around Madinah and showed Quraysh that their trade with Sham could no longer pass safely. Mufti Menk notes that peace with the tribes did more than any battle to open the way for Islam.
waddan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 2 AH, the Prophet ﷺ led about two hundred companions toward Buwat, near Radwa, to meet a large Quraysh caravan led by Umayyah ibn Khalaf with about a hundred men. The caravan escaped and he returned without fighting.
buwat.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Jumada of 2 AH, the Prophet ﷺ led about 150–200 Muhajirin to Dhul-Ushayrah near Yanbu to intercept a Quraysh caravan going to Sham under Abu Sufyan. It had already passed; this was the same caravan whose return would lead to Badr.
He stayed some days and made a treaty of non-aggression with Banu Mudlij and their allies Banu Damrah.
The Muslims calculated when this richly laden caravan would return from Sham, and prepared to meet it on the way back; that plan led to Badr.
ushayrah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: Kurz ibn Jabir al-Fihri raided the pastures of Madinah and drove off the Muslims' camels and sheep. The Prophet ﷺ pursued him with about seventy men as far as the valley of Safwan, near Badr, but Kurz escaped. The pursuit is called the first Badr. Kurz later accepted Islam and was martyred on the day of the Conquest of Makkah.
The pursuit had a further benefit: the Muslims came to know the ground around Badr before the great battle there.
safwan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Rajab of 2 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abdullah ibn Jahsh with eight (some say twelve) Muhajirin and a sealed letter, to be opened only after two days. It told him to go to Nakhlah, between Makkah and Ta'if, and watch Quraysh.

At Nakhlah they met a small Quraysh caravan on the last day of Rajab, a sacred month. Unsure whether the month had ended, they attacked: Amr ibn al-Hadrami was killed, two men were captured, and the caravan was taken to Madinah. It was the first time a Muslim killed an enemy, took captives and took spoils.

The Prophet ﷺ was displeased: 'I did not order you to fight in the sacred month.' Quraysh made a great outcry. Then Allah revealed: 'They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: fighting in it is grave, but turning people from the way of Allah, disbelieving in Him and the Sacred Masjid, and expelling its people from it are graver in the sight of Allah' (2:217).
nakhlah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: For about sixteen or seventeen months after the Hijrah, the Muslims prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem. The Prophet ﷺ longed to face the Ka'bah, the house of Ibrahim, and often turned his face to the sky.

Allah revealed: 'We have seen you turning your face to the sky; We will turn you to a qiblah that pleases you. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (2:144). The change came during a prayer; he turned mid-prayer, and the companions turned with him. The masjid of Banu Salimah where this happened became known as Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the masjid of the two qiblahs.

A man who had prayed with him passed another group of the Ansar praying Asr toward Jerusalem and told them; they turned toward the Ka'bah while still in prayer (Bukhari 40). The hypocrites and some of the Jews mocked the change, and the Quran answered them: 'To Allah belong the east and the west' (2:142). People asked about those who had died praying toward Jerusalem, and Allah revealed that their faith would not be lost (2:143).

The old front of the masjid, now its back, was roofed and became the Suffah. Facing the Ka'bah also turned the Muhajirin's hearts to their home city, now in the hands of their enemies, and strengthened their longing to return to it.
qiblah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Sha'ban of 2 AH, Allah made fasting in Ramadan obligatory: 'O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may attain taqwa' (2:183).

At first those able to fast could feed a poor person instead, and in the early rules eating and relations were forbidden after sleeping at night. Some companions found this very hard; one fainted at work. Allah then revealed 2:187, allowing eating, drinking and relations until dawn, 'until the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread' (Bukhari).
Zakat al-Fitr was prescribed in the same year, and zakat on wealth became obligatory soon after. The first Ramadan fast coincided with the march to Badr, fourteen years after the first revelation.
siyam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Ramadan of 2 AH, the great Quraysh caravan that had slipped past the Muslims at Dhul-Ushayrah was returning from Sham under Abu Sufyan. Much of what it carried had been bought with the property Quraysh seized from the Muhajirin. The Prophet ﷺ sent Talhah ibn Ubaydullah and Sa'id ibn Zayd ahead to watch for it; they reported about a thousand camels carrying goods worth some fifty thousand dinars, guarded by about forty men. He called for volunteers, since no battle was expected and it was not obligatory for everyone, and he did not tell them more of the plan than they needed. Allah had already promised him one of two things: the caravan, or victory over Quraysh (8:7).

Some three hundred and forty set out. At Bi'r as-Suqya, just outside Madinah, he reviewed them and sent back those too young or needed at home, leaving about 313 (reports range from 311 to over 317). Uthman stayed to nurse his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter, who was gravely ill; the Prophet ﷺ told him he would have the reward and share of those who fought, and Bukhari counts him among the people of Badr. Ibn Umm Maktum was left to lead the prayer; at ar-Rawha the Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Lubabah back to govern Madinah. They had only two horses, ridden by az-Zubayr and al-Miqdad, and seventy camels, three men taking turns on each. The Prophet ﷺ shared one with Ali and Abu Lubabah (later Marthad), and when they offered to walk so he could ride, he said: 'You are no stronger than I am, and I am no less in need of the reward than you' (Ahmad).

He gave the general banner, white, to Mus'ab ibn Umayr, and two black banners to Ali for the Muhajirin and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh for the Ansar. Az-Zubayr led the right, al-Miqdad the left, and Qays ibn Abi Sa'sa'ah the rear. He had the bells cut from the camels' necks so their movement could not be heard, and revealed each stage of the route only when they reached it.

Abu Sufyan, shrewd and cautious, sensed danger. Finding the dung of camels where two riders had stopped, he broke it open and saw date stones: 'By Allah, this is the fodder of Yathrib.' He turned the caravan to the coast road and sent Damdam ibn Amr racing to Makkah, who arrived with his camel's nose cut and his shirt torn, crying that their goods were in danger. Quraysh marched out about 1,300 strong, with some hundred horses and six hundred coats of mail; nearly every chief came, and those who would not, like Abu Lahab, sent someone in their place. When the caravan was safe, Abu Sufyan sent word that they could go home. Banu Zuhrah, on al-Akhnas's advice, did turn back, and Quraysh were now about a thousand. But Abu Jahl swore: 'We will not return until we reach Badr and stay three nights, slaughtering camels, drinking wine and hearing singing girls, so that the Arabs will fear us forever.'

The caravan had escaped, and the Muslims now faced an army, not a caravan. The Prophet ﷺ consulted the companions; some felt they were not equipped for a battle, for they had come out lightly armed for a caravan, and Allah described them 'as though they were being driven to death while they watched' (8:5–6). Abu Bakr and Umar spoke well; al-Miqdad said: 'We will not say as the people of Musa said: go, you and your Lord, and fight, we will sit here. We will fight on your right and left, in front and behind.' But he was waiting for the Ansar, whose pledge was to protect him in Madinah, not beyond it. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: 'We have believed in you and testified that what you brought is the truth. If you plunge into the sea, we will plunge in with you; not one of us will stay behind.' The Prophet ﷺ rejoiced and said: 'Go forward, and have good news.'

He rode out with Abu Bakr to gather news and met an old Bedouin. 'Tell us of Quraysh and of Muhammad and his companions.' 'Not until you tell me who you are.' 'Tell us first, and we will tell you.' The old man told them precisely where each army had set out from and where it should be that day. 'Now, where are you from?' 'We are from water,' said the Prophet ﷺ, and they left. That evening he sent Ali, az-Zubayr and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas to the wells of Badr, where they caught two boys drawing water for Quraysh. 'How many are they?' 'We do not know.' 'How many camels do they slaughter a day?' 'Nine one day, ten another.' 'They are between nine hundred and a thousand.' 'Which of their nobles are with them?' The boys named Utbah, Shaybah, Abu Jahl, Umayyah and more. He turned to his companions: 'Makkah has thrown you the pieces of its liver' (Ibn Ishaq; see Muslim 1779).

He camped first at the nearest well. Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir asked: 'Is this a place Allah has chosen for you, which we may not leave, or is it opinion and war strategy?' 'It is opinion and strategy.' 'Then this is not the place. Let us move to the well nearest the enemy, stop up the others and build a cistern, so we drink and they do not.' The Prophet ﷺ accepted at once. At Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's suggestion a shelter of palm branches (al-Arish) was built as a command post on a rise overlooking the field; a masjid, Masjid al-Arish, stands there today.

That night, while Quraysh drank and made merry, Allah sent the believers a calm sleep, and rain that firmed the sand under their feet, washed them and took away the whispering of Shaytan, while it turned the enemy's ground to mud (8:11). He showed the Prophet ﷺ the enemy in a dream as few, for had He shown them many, the believers would have lost heart (8:43). In the Quraysh camp, Juhaym ibn as-Salt dreamt of a rider naming the chiefs who would be killed, and Abu Jahl laughed at him. The Prophet ﷺ spent the night in prayer. On the morning of 17 Ramadan, a Friday, he raised his hands toward the qiblah and prayed: 'O Allah, fulfil what You promised me. O Allah, if this small band is destroyed, You will not be worshipped on earth,' until his cloak fell from his shoulders and Abu Bakr put it back, saying: 'Enough; your Lord will fulfil His promise' (Muslim 1763). Allah answered: 'I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another' (8:9), and later promised three thousand, then five thousand if they were patient (3:124–125). Bukhari has a chapter on the angels who fought at Badr.

He drew the believers up in straight rows, like rows of prayer, walking along them with an arrow to straighten them, while Quraysh, unused to such order, stood in a mass: 'Allah loves those who fight in His cause in rows, as if they were a solid structure' (61:4). He told the archers: 'When they come near you, shoot at them, and save your arrows' (Bukhari), and the swordsmen not to draw until the enemy was upon them (Abu Dawud).

The battle began with single combat. Three of the Ansar stepped out, but Quraysh called for their equals from their own tribe. The Prophet ﷺ sent out Hamzah, Ali and Ubaydah ibn al-Harith against Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, his brother Shaybah and his son al-Walid. Hamzah and Ali quickly killed their opponents (reports differ on who faced whom); Ubaydah and his opponent wounded each other, and Hamzah and Ali finished his opponent and carried Ubaydah back, mortally wounded (22:19). Then Quraysh charged. The archers loosed their arrows at close range, bringing down many men and horses, and the armies clashed. The Prophet ﷺ threw a handful of pebbles at the enemy, saying 'May their faces be disfigured' (8:17).

Shaytan had come to Quraysh in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik, chief of Banu Kinanah, promising: 'No one can defeat you today; I am your protector.' When the armies met and he saw the angels, he turned on his heels: 'I am free of you. I see what you do not see. I fear Allah' (8:48). Mufti Menk draws the lesson: this is always Shaytan's way, making wrong seem right and promising support, then abandoning a person once he is in the mess. Allah warned the believers not to be 'like those who came out of their homes boastfully, to be seen by people' (8:47). The Muslims' war cry was 'Ahad, Ahad', Bilal's words under torture, and the Prophet ﷺ came out of the shelter in his armour reciting: 'The gathering will be defeated and will turn their backs' (54:45; Bukhari). Quraysh broke and fled.

Abu Jahl stood far behind his lines in a thicket of spears. Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf said two young boys of the Ansar, one on each side of him, each whispered: 'Uncle, show me Abu Jahl. I hear he insults the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. If I see him, I will not leave him until one of us dies.' When he pointed him out, they ran at him like hawks, slipped between the guards because they were small, and struck him down. They were Mu'adh ibn Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Mu'adh ibn Afra' (Bukhari; another report names Mu'adh and Mu'awwidh, the sons of Afra'). Abu Jahl's son Ikrimah slashed Mu'adh ibn Amr's arm until it hung by a strip of skin; he fought on dragging it, then put his foot on it and tore it off. Mu'adh ibn Afra' was martyred that day. After the battle Ibn Mas'ud found Abu Jahl breathing his last, and even then he spoke with pride and contempt. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'This was the Pharaoh of this ummah.' Pharaoh at least, when drowning, cried that he believed in the God of Banu Isra'il, too late (10:90–91).

Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Bilal's old torturer, was being led away as a captive by Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, his friend from their trading days in Makkah, who had agreed to protect him. Bilal saw him and cried out: 'The head of disbelief, Umayyah ibn Khalaf! May I not survive if he survives!' A party of the Ansar gathered; Abd ar-Rahman threw himself over Umayyah to shield him, but they struck at him from beneath and killed him (Bukhari). Allah had brought the two armies together, though neither had planned it, 'so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained: that whoever perished would perish upon clear evidence, and whoever lived would live upon clear evidence' (8:42).

Seventy of Quraysh were killed and seventy were captured. Fourteen Muslims were martyred, six of the Muhajirin and eight of the Ansar; 313 had come and 299 went home. Quraysh fled leaving their goods on the field, and the Muslims gathered the spoils. The Prophet ﷺ sent Abdullah ibn Rawahah and Zayd ibn Harithah ahead with the news. The believers of Madinah rejoiced; the hypocrites and many of the Jews, who had hoped for the Muslims' defeat, were dismayed, and began whispering that the Muslims had gone out only for plunder.

On the way home two captives, Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt and an-Nadr ibn al-Harith, were executed for their long record of persecution, as Mufti Menk explains it. The Prophet ﷺ ordered the rest treated well, and the Companions fed their captives bread while they themselves ate dates (Ibn Ishaq; at-Tabarani). Suhayl ibn Amr had been one of Quraysh's most eloquent speakers against Islam; Umar asked to knock out his front teeth so he could never speak against it again. The Prophet ﷺ refused: 'I will not mutilate him, lest Allah mutilate me, though I am a prophet' (Ibn Ishaq).

The army stayed three days at Badr: to make sure Quraysh did not regroup, to bury the fourteen martyrs and to throw the dead of Quraysh into the old well (al-Qalib), to gather the spoils, and to rest before marching home. On the way, at as-Safra', the Companions disputed over the spoils, and Allah revealed: 'They ask you about the spoils. Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set things right between you, and obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers' (8:1). The Prophet ﷺ divided them equally, and gave a share to the eight or nine men who had stayed behind or been sent elsewhere on his orders. Among the captives was Abu Aziz, brother of Mus'ab ibn Umayr. Seeing an Ansari tying him, Mus'ab said: 'Tie him tight; his mother is rich and will pay well for him.' 'Brother, is this your advice about me?' 'He is my brother now, not you' (Ibn Ishaq).

The Prophet ﷺ consulted about the captives: Abu Bakr advised ransom, Umar advised execution. Most of the Companions agreed with Abu Bakr, and he accepted ransom, set according to each captive's means: the wealthy paid the maximum, those who had shown kindness in the past were treated leniently, some of the poor were freed without payment, such as Abu Azzah, who pleaded for his daughters and promised never to fight the Muslims again, and those who could read were allowed to ransom themselves by teaching ten Muslim children to write. Allah then revealed 8:67–69.

Some captives had family stories of their own. Abu Sufyan refused to pay for his son Amr, until he seized Sa'd ibn an-Nu'man of the Ansar, who had come to Makkah for umrah, and exchanged him for his son. Abu al-As ibn ar-Rabi', husband of the Prophet's daughter Zaynab, was among the captives. Zaynab sent from Makkah her necklace to ransom him, the necklace Khadijah had given her on her wedding day. When the Prophet ﷺ saw it he was deeply moved and said to the Companions: 'If you think fit to release her captive and return her necklace to her, do so.' They did, on condition that Abu al-As let Zaynab go to Madinah, and he kept his word (Abu Dawud). He had refused Quraysh's pressure to divorce her, saying no woman of Quraysh could replace her; when he accepted Islam years later, before the Conquest, the Prophet ﷺ returned her to him (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi).

Al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Khalid's brother, was ransomed by his family and accepted Islam only after he returned to Makkah, so that no one could say he had become Muslim out of fear while a captive. Al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle, was also captured; the Prophet ﷺ had told his men not to kill him, since he had come out under pressure. When told to pay for himself and his nephew Aqil, al-Abbas protested that he had nothing. 'Then where is the money you left with Umm al-Fadl, telling her: if I am killed, this is for my sons?' 'By Allah, no one knew of that but she and I.' He paid (Ibn Ishaq), and later accepted Islam, joining the Prophet ﷺ on the road just before the Conquest of Makkah.

Those who fought at Badr were known ever after as al-Badriyyun, with a rank above others. Uthman was counted among them. Years later, when Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a veteran of Badr, wrote secretly to Quraysh before the Conquest, Umar asked to kill him as a hypocrite. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'He was at Badr. How do you know that Allah did not look at the people of Badr and say: Do as you wish, I have forgiven you?' (Bukhari). He also said: 'Do not revile my Companions. If one of you spent gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach a handful of theirs, or even half of it' (Bukhari). Surah al-Anfal was revealed about the battle, calling it the Day of the Criterion (Yawm al-Furqan, 8:41).
badr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 15–18.

p: Some weeks after Badr, Umayr ibn Wahb sat with Safwan ibn Umayyah by the Ka'bah, mourning their dead. Umayr's son was a captive in Madinah. He said: 'If not for my debts and my family, I would go and kill Muhammad.' Safwan said: 'Your debts are on me and your family is with mine.' Umayr poisoned his sword and rode to Madinah.

Umar saw him arrive with his sword and brought him to the Prophet ﷺ. 'Why have you come?' 'For my son the captive.' 'Then why the sword?' 'What good were swords to us at Badr?' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Tell me the truth. You sat with Safwan in the Hijr and said such-and-such, and he took on your debts and family so that you would kill me, and Allah stands between you and that.'

Umayr was stunned: 'No one was with us but Safwan. By Allah, only Allah could have told you.' He accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Teach your brother his religion and free his captive.' Umayr returned to Makkah and openly called people to Islam, and many accepted at his hands, while Safwan swore never to speak to him again (Ibn Ishaq, at-Tabarani; Hayatus Sahaba 1:211). (Mufti Menk adds that he was later held back in Makkah and only reached Madinah some years afterwards.)
umayr-wahb.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 17.

p: After the first Ramadan of fasting and the victory at Badr, the Muslims celebrated the first Eid al-Fitr on 1 Shawwal, 2 AH. The Prophet ﷺ went out to the open prayer ground (musalla) and led the Eid prayer, then gave a khutbah.

Zakat al-Fitr, a small measure of food from every Muslim, was paid before the prayer so the poor could share in the joy of the day. When he came to Madinah, the people had two days of play from jahiliyyah; he told them: 'Allah has replaced them with two better days: al-Adha and al-Fitr' (Abu Dawud).
eid.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: When the Prophet ﷺ marched to Badr, his daughter Ruqayyah, wife of Uthman, lay seriously ill with measles. He told Uthman to stay behind and nurse her, and promised him the reward and share of those who fought at Badr.

Ruqayyah died while the army was away. As Zayd ibn Harithah rode into Madinah with news of the victory, the Muslims were returning from her burial. Both Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum had first been married to sons of Abu Lahab, who made them leave the two when the Prophet ﷺ began to preach; (one report says these were only betrothals, never consummated); Abu al-As refused the same pressure over Zaynab. Uthman later married Umm Kulthum, and was called Dhun-Nurayn, 'the possessor of the two lights'.
ruqayyah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 17–18.

p: Banu Qaynuqa, a Jewish tribe of goldsmiths and armourers inside Madinah, had signed the city's charter. After Badr they grew openly hostile. The Prophet ﷺ gathered them in their market and warned them; they replied: 'Do not be deceived because you defeated a people who knew nothing of war. If you fight us, you will learn that we are men.'

The breaking point, according to the Seerah works (the report's chain is weak), came in their market. A Muslim woman, fully covered, was sitting at a goldsmith's stall; a man of Qaynuqa' secretly pinned the hem of her dress to her back, so that when she stood up she was exposed, and they laughed. A Muslim who saw it killed the man, and the Jews then fell on the Muslim and killed him. That was a breach of the charter. The Prophet ﷺ marched on them, with Hamzah carrying the banner, and besieged their forts for fifteen days until they surrendered.

Abdullah ibn Ubayy, their old ally, who had declared Islam after Badr when he saw the Muslims' strength, seized the Prophet ﷺ by his armour and would not let go until he agreed to spare them: 'Four hundred unarmoured men and three hundred in mail protected me from every enemy, and you would cut them down in one morning?' The Prophet ﷺ, angered, let them go. They were given three days to leave Madinah with their families, under the supervision of Ubadah ibn as-Samit, and they settled in Adhri'at in Sham. Ubadah ibn as-Samit, who had also been their ally, renounced the alliance in favour of Allah and His Messenger.

Mufti Menk draws the lesson the Prophet ﷺ taught: believers are like one body, and the honour of one Muslim, man or woman, is the concern of all. 'Do not rejoice at your brother's misfortune, lest Allah have mercy on him and afflict you' (Tirmidhi).
qaynuqa.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 18.

p: In Shawwal of 2 AH, news came that Banu Sulaym and Ghatafan were gathering at Qarqarat al-Kudr to attack Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ marched with two hundred men. The tribes scattered before he arrived, and the Muslims returned with some five hundred camels left behind.
kudr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After Badr, Abu Sufyan vowed not to wash until he had avenged it. In Dhu al-Hijjah of 2 AH he led two hundred riders to the edge of Madinah, burnt some palm trees and killed two men in a field.

The Prophet ﷺ pursued him with two hundred men. Abu Sufyan's riders fled so fast that they threw away their provisions, mostly sacks of sawiq, a barley flour, to lighten their load. The Muslims picked them up, and the raid became known as Ghazwat as-Sawiq.
sawiq.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After Badr, Abu Bakr and Umar each asked for the hand of Fatimah, the Prophet's youngest daughter, and he declined gently. Ali, who had grown up in his house, was too shy and too poor to ask, until a servant told him she was of marriageable age and encouraged him. He came and sat before the Prophet ﷺ but could not speak, until the Prophet ﷺ asked: 'Have you come about Fatimah?' 'Yes.'

When he did, the Prophet ﷺ asked what he could give as mahr. Ali had nothing. 'Where is the shield I gave you?' Ali had only that armour; it was sold, for about four hundred (some say four hundred and eighty) dirhams, and the money used for the mahr and a simple household. Their home had a sheepskin, a leather pillow stuffed with fibre, a hand mill and two water skins.
The Prophet ﷺ visited them on their wedding night, poured water over them and prayed for blessings on them and their children. From this marriage came al-Hasan, al-Husayn, Zaynab and Umm Kulthum.

Mufti Menk stresses that the mahr in Islam is the groom's gift to the bride herself, not a payment to her family, and that the Prophet ﷺ married his daughter to a man with almost nothing because of his faith. He also said: 'Whoever raises two daughters until they come of age, he and I will come on the Day of Resurrection like this,' joining his fingers (Muslim).
ali-fatimah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 18.

p: Uthman ibn Maz'un was among the earliest Muslims and among those who emigrated to Abyssinia. Known for his devotion, he had once wished to give up worldly life entirely; the Prophet ﷺ forbade it.

He was the first of the Muhajirin to die in Madinah, and the first buried at al-Baqi'. Aisha narrated that the Prophet ﷺ kissed him after his death, and his tears fell on Uthman's face (Tirmidhi). He placed a stone at the head of the grave as a marker, saying: 'I mark my brother's grave with it, and bury beside him those of my family who die.' Later, when his son Ibrahim died, he said: 'Join our righteous predecessor Uthman ibn Maz'un' (Hayatus Sahaba 2:598).
ibnmazun.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 3 AH, news came that Banu Tha'labah and Muharib of Ghatafan were massing at Dhu Amarr in Najd. The Prophet ﷺ marched with 450 men. The tribes fled into the mountains, and he stayed most of a month before returning.

It is reported that during this expedition a man named Du'thur found the Prophet ﷺ resting alone, drew a sword over him and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' 'Allah,' he said. The sword fell from Du'thur's hand; the Prophet ﷺ took it and asked the same question. 'No one,' said Du'thur. The Prophet ﷺ forgave him, and he accepted Islam and called his people (reported by al-Waqidi; a similar incident is in Bukhari at Dhat ar-Riqa').
dhuamarr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, a wealthy poet of the Jews of Madinah, went to Makkah after Badr, mourned the Quraysh dead in verse and urged Quraysh to take revenge. Back in Madinah he wrote insulting verses about Muslim women.

The Prophet ﷺ asked: 'Who will deal with Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, for he has harmed Allah and His Messenger?' Muhammad ibn Maslamah volunteered. With a small party including Ka'b's foster-brother Abu Na'ilah, he lured Ka'b out of his fort at night and killed him (Bukhari, from Jabir). His death ended his campaign of incitement against the Muslims.
sr-kab.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Jumada al-Ula of 3 AH, the Prophet ﷺ led three hundred men to Bahran in the Hijaz, where Banu Sulaym were reported to be gathering. They had dispersed before he arrived, and he returned after about two months without fighting.
bahran.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After Badr, Quraysh feared the coastal road to Sham and tried a new route east through Najd to Iraq, with a rich caravan led by Safwan ibn Umayyah and guided by Furat ibn Hayyan.

The Prophet ﷺ sent Zayd ibn Harithah with a hundred riders. They surprised the caravan at the well of al-Qaradah; its men fled, and the Muslims took the goods. Furat was captured, later accepted Islam, and became a companion.
sr-qaradah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Quraysh returned from Badr forbidden even to weep for their dead, lest the Muslims rejoice. In Dar an-Nadwah they agreed to spend the whole profit of Abu Sufyan's caravan, some fifty thousand gold dinars, on revenge (8:36). They gathered three thousand men with two hundred horses, joined by allies from Kinanah and Tihamah, by Abu Amir 'the monk', who had fled Madinah when the Prophet ﷺ arrived, and by Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave whose master Jubayr ibn Mut'im promised him freedom if he killed Hamzah. They brought their women to shame them into standing firm. Al-Abbas, still in Makkah, did not march, and sent a letter warning his nephew. Abu Azzah had promised never to fight again, but was drawn in once more (reports differ on whether he was pressed into it).

The Prophet ﷺ consulted the Companions. He preferred to defend from within the city, as did older men and Abdullah ibn Ubayy, but younger companions who had missed Badr, and Hamzah, urged him to go out rather than let the enemy into their homes, and he agreed. He led Jumu'ah, told them victory came through obedience, and put on his armour. When they regretted pressing him, he said: 'It is not fitting for a prophet who has put on his armour to take it off until Allah judges between him and the enemy.' He gave the banners to Mus'ab ibn Umayr for the Muhajirin, and to Usayd ibn Hudayr and al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir for the Aws and Khazraj. As always he reviewed the volunteers and sent back the youngest. Rafi' ibn Khadij, though young, was allowed to stay because he was a skilled archer. His friend Samurah ibn Jundub wept, saying he could out-wrestle Rafi'; the Prophet ﷺ had them wrestle, Samurah threw Rafi' to the ground, and both were allowed to fight.

He marched with a thousand men. At ash-Shaykhayn he saw a large contingent of Ibn Ubayy's Jewish allies and sent them back: he would not fight idolaters with the help of men whose loyalty was uncertain. At dawn, near Uhud, Abdullah ibn Ubayy turned back with about three hundred: 'He obeyed the youngsters and disobeyed me.' Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram, Jabir's father, ran after them pleading, in vain. Some Muslims wanted to fight the deserters on the spot; Allah revealed: 'Why are you two groups about the hypocrites, when Allah has turned them back for what they earned?' (4:88). The remaining seven hundred camped with Mount Uhud at their backs, facing Madinah. Before battle he reminded them that no soul dies before receiving all the provision written for it, and that victory comes through obedience. The Prophet ﷺ placed fifty archers under Abdullah ibn Jubayr on a small hill, Jabal ar-Rumah, telling them: 'Do not leave your place, even if you see birds snatching us' (Bukhari 3039): whether the Muslims were winning or losing, they were to protect the army's back.

The battle opened well. The banner-bearers of Quraysh, the clan of Abd ad-Dar, came out one after another and fell one after another, the first, Talhah ibn Abi Talhah, killed by Ali (some say az-Zubayr). The Quraysh cavalry charged and was driven back by arrows. Abu Dujanah had asked for the Prophet's sword and its right, and was told: to strike the enemy with it until it bent. He tied on the red band he wore when he meant to fight to the death and strutted between the lines; the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This is a gait Allah hates, except in a place like this.' With Hamzah and Ali he cut through the ranks. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas saw two men in white fighting fiercely beside the Prophet ﷺ, whom he never saw before or after: Jibril and Mika'il (Bukhari, Muslim). Quraysh began to flee. Seeing the enemy camp abandoned, most of the archers left the hill to gather spoils despite their commander's pleas. Khalid ibn al-Walid, then leading the Quraysh cavalry, saw the gap, swept round the hill and attacked from behind.

Chaos followed. Wahshi, who had no other aim that day, waited behind a rock until Hamzah passed, then threw his spear into his lower body and killed him. A cry went up that Muhammad had been killed, and many Muslims lost heart. The Prophet ﷺ was struck; his helmet was driven into his cheek, a tooth was broken and he fell into a pit. A small band shielded him with their bodies: Abu Talhah, Talhah ibn Ubaydillah, who took arrow after arrow and lost the use of his hand protecting him (Abu Bakr would say: 'That whole day was Talhah's'), Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas shooting arrows, and Nusaybah bint Ka'b fighting with a sword. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, carrying the banner, had his right hand cut off, held it in his left, and when that too was cut, clasped it to his chest until he was killed (Ibn Sa'd); because he resembled the Prophet ﷺ, the cry spread that Muhammad had been killed. Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas's stone broke the Prophet's tooth, and Ibn Qami'ah struck his helmet into his cheek. Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who had long vowed to kill him, charged at him; the Prophet ﷺ took a spear and grazed his neck, and Ubayy died of it on the way home. He is the only person the Prophet ﷺ ever killed with his own hand. Fatimah and other women came to give water and tend the wounded.

The Muslims regrouped on the slope of the mountain and Quraysh withdrew without taking Madinah. About seventy Muslims were martyred and some twenty-two to thirty-seven of Quraysh were killed, most of them Ansar, among them Hamzah, whose body was mutilated by Hind bint Utbah, whose father he had killed at Badr: she cut out his liver and chewed it. The Prophet ﷺ forbade mutilation of any body, living or dead. He did not want women to see their mutilated relatives and keep that image forever; but Hamzah's sister Safiyyah promised to be patient and was allowed to see him, and she said: 'All this is for the sake of Allah.' The Prophet ﷺ grieved over him deeply; Hanzalah, who had come straight from his wedding night, was seen being washed by angels. The martyrs were buried in the clothes they died in, unwashed, two or three to a grave, the one who knew more Quran placed first; the Prophet ﷺ said they would rise with their wounds bleeding, the colour of blood and the scent of musk. Mus'ab, once the richest youth of Makkah, had a shroud so short that when it covered his head his feet showed, and they covered his feet with idhkhir grass (Bukhari). The Prophet ﷺ recited: 'Among the believers are men who have been true to their covenant with Allah; some have fulfilled their vow, and some are still waiting' (33:23).

Hamnah bint Jahsh was told her brother Abdullah ibn Jahsh had been martyred, and she prayed for him; then her uncle Hamzah, and she prayed for him; then her husband Mus'ab, and she cried out. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A woman's husband holds a special place with her.' A woman of Banu Dinar was told that her husband, brother and father were all killed. She asked only: 'What of the Messenger of Allah?' When she saw him alive she said: 'Every calamity after you is small.' Those who survived married many of the widows and cared for the orphans; the Prophet ﷺ himself would soon do the same.

As Quraysh left, Abu Sufyan called from the mountain: 'A day for a day: this is for Badr. You will find some of your dead mutilated; I did not order it, nor does it grieve me. We meet again at Badr next year.' The Prophet ﷺ had Umar answer: 'Allah is the Highest and Most Majestic. Our dead are in Paradise and yours in the Fire.' Neither side had won outright: Quraysh did not dare enter Madinah.

About sixty ayat of Surah Al Imran (3:121–179) were revealed about Uhud, teaching that the setback came from disobedience: 'Allah fulfilled His promise to you while you were cutting them down, until you lost heart and disputed and disobeyed after He had shown you what you loved. Among you are some who want this world and some who want the Hereafter' (3:152), that it exposed the hypocrites (3:166–167), and consoling the believers: 'If a wound has touched you, a like wound has touched them' (3:140); 'Do not weaken and do not grieve; you will be superior if you are believers' (3:139). 'Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?' (3:144). Scholars and Mufti Menk draw two lessons from the day: disputing among themselves (tanazu') and disobeying the Messenger's order cost them dearly. 'The disbelievers are allies of one another; unless you do the same, there will be great corruption on earth' (8:73).
uhud.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 18–19.

p: Hafsah, daughter of Umar ibn al-Khattab, was widowed when her husband Khunays ibn Hudhafah, a veteran of Badr, died of his wounds (most reports say from Badr; some say Uhud). Umar went himself to look for a husband for her. Umar offered her in marriage to Uthman, who declined, and to Abu Bakr, who stayed silent. Umar felt hurt.

Then the Prophet ﷺ asked for her hand. Abu Bakr later told Umar he had kept silent because he knew the Prophet ﷺ had mentioned her, and he would not reveal his secret (Bukhari). Hafsah was known for fasting and night prayer, and the first compiled copy of the Quran was later kept with her.

Mufti Menk draws the lesson: there is no shame in a father seeking a good husband for his daughter or sister; Umar, one of those promised Paradise, did exactly that. Culture that makes families wait in silence has no basis in Islam.
hafsah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 19.

p: In Ramadan of 3 AH, Fatimah gave birth to her first son. The Prophet ﷺ called the adhan in his ear, named him al-Hasan, and on the seventh day sacrificed for him, shaved his head and gave its weight in silver in charity.

He loved al-Hasan dearly. He would carry him on his shoulders and say: 'O Allah, I love him, so love him' (Bukhari). Once, from the minbar, he said: 'This son of mine is a sayyid; through him Allah may reconcile two great groups of Muslims' (Bukhari 2704), words fulfilled in 41 AH.
hasan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: The day after Uhud, though the Muslims were wounded and exhausted, the Prophet ﷺ ordered them to pursue Quraysh, allowing only those who had fought at Uhud to come. He feared Quraysh would turn back to finish off Madinah.

They marched about eight miles to Hamra al-Asad and camped for three nights, lighting many fires so they seemed a great army. Ma'bad al-Khuza'i, passing the Quraysh camp, warned Abu Sufyan of a huge Muslim force, and Quraysh hurried back to Makkah.

Allah praised those who answered: 'Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the injury had struck them… to whom people said: the people have gathered against you, so fear them. But it increased them in faith, and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs' (3:172–173). Aisha told Urwah that his father az-Zubayr and his grandfather Abu Bakr were among them (Bukhari). Allah also taught them to say: 'Do you await for us anything but one of the two best things,' victory or martyrdom (9:52).
hamra.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 19.

p: In Muharram of 4 AH, news came that Banu Asad under Tulayhah were preparing to raid Madinah, encouraged by Uhud. The Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Salamah with 150 men to strike first.

They reached Qatan in Najd by surprise; the tribe scattered, leaving camels and sheep. Abu Salamah's wound from Uhud reopened on the journey, and he died soon after his return. The Prophet ﷺ closed his eyes and prayed for him, and later married his widow, Umm Salamah.
sr-qatan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Safar of 4 AH, two tragedies struck within days. Men from Adal and al-Qarah asked for teachers; the Prophet ﷺ sent six (some say ten) companions under Asim ibn Thabit. At ar-Raji' they were betrayed and surrounded by Banu Lihyan. Some fought to the death; Khubayb ibn Adi and Zayd ibn ad-Dathinah were sold to Quraysh and executed in Makkah. Before his death Khubayb prayed two rak'ahs and recited verses of faith.

At the same time, Abu Bara' Amir ibn Malik asked for companions to teach the people of Najd under his protection. The Prophet ﷺ sent about seventy reciters, men who gathered wood by day and prayed at night. At the well of Bi'r Ma'unah, Haram ibn Milhan carried the Prophet's letter to Amir ibn at-Tufayl, who had him killed without reading it, though envoys were never to be harmed. Banu Amir refused to break Abu Bara's protection, so Amir ibn at-Tufayl gathered tribes of Sulaym (Ri'l, Dhakwan and Usayyah), who killed almost all of them; one or two survived by lying among the dead. Haram ibn Milhan, struck by a spear, cried: 'I have won, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!'

The Prophet ﷺ grieved as never before. For a month he made qunut in the dawn prayer, praying against the tribes that had killed them (Bukhari, from Anas). This is the origin of qunut an-nazilah, the supplication in times of calamity; it was made sometimes in Fajr and sometimes in other prayers, sometimes before ruku' and sometimes after, and all of these are valid.
maunah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 20.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 4 AH, the Prophet ﷺ went to Banu Nadir, a Jewish tribe bound by treaty, to ask their help paying blood money. They seated him beside a wall and, according to the Seerah reports, plotted to drop a millstone on him from the roof. He was informed by revelation and left at once.

He sent Muhammad ibn Maslamah to tell them they had broken the treaty by plotting to kill him, and must leave Madinah within ten days. Abdullah ibn Ubayy urged them to refuse and promised two thousand men: 'If you are expelled we will leave with you, and if you are fought we will help you.' Allah exposed him: 'Allah bears witness that they are liars. If they are expelled, they will not leave with them; if they are fought, they will not help them' (59:11–12). They refused. The Muslims besieged their forts for about fifteen days (Mufti Menk says six nights), and some of their palm trees were cut down. Ibn Ubayy's help never came, and fear struck them 'from where they did not expect' (59:2). They surrendered and were allowed to leave with whatever their camels could carry except weapons; some went to Khaybar and some to Sham. They pulled down their own houses as they left so the Muslims could not live in them: 'They destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers; so take a lesson, O people of vision' (59:2). Some, like Huyayy ibn Akhtab, settled at Khaybar.

Surah al-Hashr was revealed about them, so that Ibn Abbas called it Surah Banu Nadir (Bukhari 4029). Since no battle was fought, their property was fay', not ghanimah (spoils of war), and Allah set its rule: it belongs to Allah and the Messenger, for relatives, orphans, the poor and travellers (59:7). It was given mainly to the poor Muhajirin. Two men of Banu Nadir accepted Islam and kept their property. The Ansar's children who had been raised as Jews among them led to the revelation: 'There is no compulsion in religion' (2:256).
nadir.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 20.

p: Drinking was deeply rooted among the Arabs of Makkah and Madinah. They traded in wine, fought when drunk and regretted it when sober, and Quraysh even carried it to their battles. Some, like Abu Bakr, never touched it even before Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ was protected from it.

Wine was prohibited in stages. First Allah revealed that wine and gambling hold some benefit but their sin is greater (2:219), after Umar asked for a clear ruling. The question itself showed that they sensed something wrong in it; many Companions stopped from then on. Then, after a companion led the prayer while drunk and misrecited, 'Do not approach prayer while intoxicated, until you know what you are saying' (4:43). With five prayers a day, little time was left for drinking except after Isha.

Finally Allah revealed: 'O believers, wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows are filth from the work of Shaytan; avoid them (literally, keep far away from them, which is stronger than a simple ban, as with 'do not come near zina'), that you may succeed… Will you not then desist?' (5:90–91). Shaytan wants to stir enmity and hatred through them and turn people from prayer. Anas was serving drinks at Abu Talhah's house when the caller announced the prohibition. Abu Talhah told him to pour it out. No one stopped to think what it was worth or to sell it to others; and wine flowed in the streets of Madinah (Bukhari).
People asked about those who had died before the ban with wine in them, and Allah revealed 5:93: there is no blame on believers for what they consumed before the ruling, if they had taqwa.

The 'benefit' in 2:219, many commentators explain, included the profit of trade, and the old Arab habit of giving gambling winnings to the poor.
