Mufti Menk warns that the same excuse is still heard ('if I win, I will give it to charity'); one who wants to give charity should give from his own lawful wealth.
khamr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 19.

p: The Prophet ﷺ led an expedition into Najd against Banu Muharib and Banu Tha'labah of Ghatafan. The companions had so few mounts that they took turns riding; their feet became so worn that they wrapped them in rags, so it was called Dhat ar-Riqa', 'the expedition of rags' (Bukhari 4128, from Abu Musa).

The two forces met but did not fight. Fearing a surprise attack, the Prophet ﷺ led the prayer of fear (Salat al-Khawf), with the army praying in groups while others stood guard. Allah had revealed it when the enemy hoped to fall on the Muslims while they were bowed in prostration: one group prays with the imam while the other stands armed, then they change places (4:101–102).

Jabir narrated that on the way back the Prophet ﷺ rested alone under a tree, hanging up his sword. A bedouin took it, drew it over him and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' 'Allah,' he answered. The sword fell, and the Prophet ﷺ forgave the man (Bukhari). Scholars differ on whether this expedition was in 4 or 7 AH.
riqa.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 22.

p: At the end of Uhud, Abu Sufyan had called out: 'We will meet again at Badr next year.' In Sha'ban of 4 AH, the Prophet ﷺ marched to Badr with 1,500 men to keep the appointment.

Abu Sufyan, reluctant to fight, set out from Makkah with two thousand, and hired Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud to go ahead to Madinah and frighten the Muslims with tales of a vast army. It only increased their faith, and they said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs' (3:173), the words Ibrahim said when thrown into the fire (Bukhari). Mufti Menk urges Muslims to say this at bad news, rather than swearing. Abu Sufyan turned back after two days, saying it was a year of drought. The Muslims waited at Badr for eight days, traded profitably at its seasonal market, and 'returned with grace and bounty from Allah, untouched by harm' (3:174), their reputation restored after Uhud.
badr2.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 20.

p: In Sha'ban of 4 AH, Fatimah gave birth to her second son, al-Husayn, about a year after al-Hasan. The Prophet ﷺ called the adhan in his ear and named him. He said of the two brothers: 'Al-Hasan and al-Husayn are the leaders of the youth of Paradise' (Tirmidhi), and 'Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn' (Tirmidhi). He would shorten or lengthen his prostration if they climbed on his back.
husayn.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 20.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 5 AH, news came that tribes at Dumat al-Jandal, on the route to Sham, were robbing caravans and gathering to approach Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ marched a thousand men north, travelling by night.

The tribes fled before he arrived, leaving their livestock. He stayed some days and sent out patrols, then returned. It was the furthest north he had marched so far, and it showed the tribes on the Syrian border the reach of the new state.
dumah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Banu al-Mustaliq, a branch of Khuza'ah, had fought for Quraysh at Uhud, waylaid travellers, and now, news came, their chief al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar was gathering men against Madinah. Their spy was caught and executed. The Prophet ﷺ marched with about seven hundred men and thirty horses; Aishah went with him, chosen by lot as was his custom with his wives. For the first time Abdullah ibn Ubayy and many hypocrites came along, hoping for spoils now that the Muslims were winning. At their well of al-Muraysi' the two sides exchanged arrows for about an hour; then the Muslims charged and defeated them without loss. Many were taken captive, with much livestock, among them al-Harith's daughter Juwayriyah.

Juwayriyah came to the Prophet ﷺ to arrange her ransom. One report adds that her father came with camels for it, hid two of them on the way, and accepted Islam when the Prophet ﷺ asked him about the two he had left in the valley. The Prophet ﷺ married her, and changed her name from Barrah (Muslim). When the companions heard, they said: 'These are now the in-laws of the Messenger of Allah,' and freed all their captives; Aishah said no woman was a greater blessing to her people, and Banu al-Mustaliq accepted Islam. Juwayriyah was devoted to worship. Once the Prophet ﷺ left her sitting in her place of prayer after Fajr and found her still there late in the morning. He said: 'After leaving you I said four phrases three times which, if weighed against all you have said today, would outweigh it: Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi, adada khalqihi, wa rida nafsihi, wa zinata arshihi, wa midada kalimatihi' (Glory and praise be to Allah, as many times as the number of His creation, as much as pleases Him, as much as the weight of His Throne, and as much as the ink of His words) (Muslim).

On the way back, a quarrel at the well between a Muhajir and an Ansari led each to call on his own people: 'O Ansar!' 'O Muhajirin!' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Leave it; it is rotten' (Bukhari): no tribe or race is above another, 'the most honoured of you with Allah is the most pious' (49:13). It also let Abdullah ibn Ubayy say: 'When we return to Madinah, the honourable will expel the lowly,' and: 'Do not spend on those with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse.' Young Zayd ibn Arqam reported it; Ibn Ubayy denied it, and the Prophet ﷺ gave him the benefit of the doubt. To stop the talk he ordered the army to march at once, in the heat of the day. Usayd ibn Hudayr asked why, and when told, said: 'You are the honourable, by Allah, and he is the lowly.' Then Surah al-Munafiqun confirmed Zayd (63:1, 7–8) (Bukhari), adding: 'Do not let your wealth and children distract you from the remembrance of Allah' (63:9).

On the same journey Aisha lost a necklace while the army camped without water, and the ayah of tayammum was revealed (5:6). Later she lost it again and was left behind, which led to the slander described in the next event.
muraysi.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 20–21.

p: In Shawwal of 5 AH, leaders of Banu Nadir who had settled in Khaybar, among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab, went to Quraysh and Ghatafan. Ghatafan was promised a whole year's date harvest of Khaybar; Quraysh needed no payment to settle scores. They and formed a great alliance, the Ahzab (confederates), of about ten thousand men, to destroy Madinah.

The Prophet ﷺ consulted the companions, and Salman al-Farisi suggested a trench, a Persian tactic unknown to the Arabs. Madinah was protected on other sides by lava fields, hills and palm groves, so the trench was needed only on the open northern approach. The Prophet ﷺ rode out to mark it, and assigned each ten men forty cubits. The Muslims dug it in about six days in bitter cold and hunger, wide and deep enough that horses would not attempt it (some reports put its length at several kilometres). The Prophet ﷺ dug with them, a stone tied to his stomach for hunger, and carried earth until his body was covered in dust. When a huge rock blocked the work, he struck it three times; with each blow sparks flew, and he spoke of the keys of Sham, Persia and Yemen being given to the Muslims (Bukhari 4101; Ahmad). The diggers would not leave even to relieve themselves without asking his permission, and Allah praised them: 'The believers are those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a common matter, do not leave until they ask his permission' (24:62). The hypocrites slipped away without asking, and when they heard him speak of the keys of Sham, Persia and Yemen, they mocked: 'He promises us the treasures of Khosrow and Caesar, while we cannot go out to relieve ourselves in safety!'

Jabir saw signs of hunger on him and quietly slaughtered a small goat and cooked a little barley for a few people. The Prophet ﷺ announced to the whole army of diggers that Jabir had invited them, and told Jabir's wife not to take the pot off the fire or the bread out of the oven. He kept serving from them, and by his blessing all were fed and food remained (Bukhari).

The confederates arrived, astonished by the trench, and besieged the city for nearly a month. Some of the hypocrites called: 'People of Yathrib, you cannot hold out; go back!' and others asked leave, saying 'Our houses are exposed,' when they were not; they only wanted to flee (33:13). Allah answered: 'Say: flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing' (33:16). Khalid ibn al-Walid, then on the other side, would later die in his bed after a lifetime of battles, saying there was no handspan of his body without a wound: 'So let the eyes of cowards never sleep.' Then Banu Qurayzah, the last Jewish tribe in Madinah, broke their treaty, believing the Muslims were finished. The Prophet ﷺ sent az-Zubayr to see what they were doing, then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Sa'd ibn Ubadah and Abdullah ibn Rawahah to confirm it; it was true, leaving the Muslims attacked from both sides. He sent Salamah ibn Aslam with two hundred men and Zayd ibn Harithah with three hundred to guard the city behind them, and Usayd ibn Hudayr with two hundred to watch for Khalid's cavalry. A Qurayzah spy came to the fort where the women and children were sheltered; Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's aunt, struck him dead with a tent pole, and Qurayzah, thinking it well guarded, did not attack it. The Quran describes it: 'when eyes grew wild and hearts reached the throats… there the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking' (33:10–11). Ikrimah and others tried to force a crossing and were driven back. Amr ibn Abd Wudd crossed the trench and was killed in single combat by Ali. Another of their horsemen, Nawfal ibn Abdullah, fell into the trench and was killed; Quraysh offered money for his body, and the Prophet ﷺ refused to take any price for a corpse and gave it back.

The Prophet ﷺ secretly offered two chiefs of Ghatafan, Uyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn Awf, a third of Madinah's dates to withdraw. First he asked Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn Ubadah: 'Is this a command from Allah, or your own view?' 'My own view, to protect you.' They said: 'When we were idolaters they never ate a date of ours except as guests or by buying it. Now that Allah has honoured us with Islam, shall we give them our wealth? We will give them nothing but the sword.' He dropped the offer. Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud of Ghatafan accepted Islam secretly and, with the Prophet's permission, sowed mistrust, telling Qurayzah to demand hostages from Quraysh before fighting, and telling Quraysh and Ghatafan that Qurayzah meant to hand their hostages to Muhammad. Each side began to doubt the other. The Prophet ﷺ prayed: 'O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the confederates; O Allah, defeat them and shake them' (Bukhari). Then Allah sent a fierce, freezing wind, while the Muslim side of the trench was spared, that overturned their pots, put out their fires and tore their tents. Hudhayfah, sent to spy at night and told not to provoke them, sat so close to Abu Sufyan that he could have killed him with an arrow. When Abu Sufyan, suspecting a spy, told each man to ask the name of the one beside him, Hudhayfah quickly seized the hands of the men on either side and asked them first. Then he heard Abu Sufyan order the retreat (Muslim). 'O believers, remember Allah's favour upon you when armies came against you and We sent against them a wind and forces you did not see' (33:9). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Now we will go out against them, and they will not come against us.' Mosques mark places on Jabal Sal' where the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions camped during the siege. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ would say: 'There is no god but Allah alone. He fulfilled His promise, helped His servant, honoured His army, and defeated the confederates alone' (Bukhari). Mufti Menk's lesson: Allah's help comes when hardship is at its peak, 'when eyes grew wild and hearts reached the throats', so never despair.
khandaq.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 21–22.

p: On the day the confederates left, Jibril came and said: 'Have you laid down your weapons? The angels have not. Go to Banu Qurayzah.' The Prophet ﷺ told the companions: 'None of you should pray Asr except at Banu Qurayzah' (Bukhari). On the way the time of Asr began to run out. Some said: 'We will pray only at Banu Qurayzah, as he said,' and prayed after sunset; others said: 'He only meant us to hurry,' and prayed on the road. When told, the Prophet ﷺ did not blame either group (Bukhari). Scholars take from this that where a text bears two sound interpretations, both followers can be right, and neither should force his view on the other.

The Muslims besieged Qurayzah for about 25 days. They asked to leave as Qaynuqa' and Nadir had, and were refused. First they asked for Abu Lubabah ibn Abd al-Mundhir, their old ally, to advise them. When they asked whether to accept the Prophet's judgement, he said yes, but pointed to his throat. At once he knew he had betrayed a trust. Too ashamed to face the Prophet ﷺ, he went straight to the masjid and tied himself to a pillar, swearing not to free himself until Allah forgave him. His wife untied him only for prayer. After six nights Allah accepted his repentance; Umm Salamah gave him the news from her door, but he would not untie himself until the Prophet ﷺ did it with his own hand (Ibn Ishaq). About men like him Allah revealed: 'Others have admitted their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will turn to them' (9:102). The Pillar of Abu Lubabah still stands in the Rawdah of the Prophet's Masjid. Qurayzah then surrendered and asked to be judged by their old allies the Aws. The Prophet ﷺ let Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, chief of the Aws, decide. Sa'd, dying of a wound from the Trench, was carried from the tent in the masjid where the wounded were nursed. Qurayzah expected leniency from their old ally, but he judged according to their treachery in wartime: the fighting men to be executed and the women and children taken captive. The Prophet ﷺ said he had judged by the judgement of Allah (Bukhari).

Mufassirin note that this judgement matched the law of their own scripture for a besieged city that breaks faith. Some of Qurayzah who accepted Islam were spared. Al-Ahzab 33:26–27 refers to these events.

Sa'd ibn Mu'adh died of his wound soon after. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh' (Bukhari, Muslim), and that seventy thousand angels came down for his funeral who had never come down before (an-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar). When the Companions admired a silk garment given to the Prophet ﷺ, he said: 'The handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise are better than this' (Bukhari). At his burial he said that if anyone were spared the squeeze of the grave, it would have been Sa'd (Ahmad, an-Nasa'i).
qurayzah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 22.

p: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, chief of the Aws, had been struck in the arm by an arrow at the Trench. He prayed: 'O Allah, do not let me die until You have cooled my eyes concerning Banu Qurayzah.' The bleeding stopped until he had judged them.

The Prophet ﷺ had a tent pitched for him in the masjid so he could visit him often. After the judgement his wound burst open and he died. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh' (Bukhari, Muslim). His bier was strangely light, and the Prophet ﷺ said the angels were carrying it. When a fine silk garment was shown to the companions, he said: 'The handkerchiefs of Sa'd in Paradise are better than this' (Hayatus Sahaba 1:397, 2:472).
sad-death.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Zaynab bint Jahsh, the Prophet's cousin, had at first refused when he asked her to marry Zayd ibn Harithah, his freed slave and adopted son, who was then called Zayd ibn Muhammad. Allah revealed: 'It is not for a believing man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair' (33:36), and she said: 'I hear and obey.' She married Zayd, a marriage willed by Allah to show that nobility of lineage counts for nothing before taqwa. But the two were never compatible. Zayd came to the Prophet ﷺ to complain more than once, and he told him: 'Keep your wife and fear Allah' (33:37). In the end Zayd divorced her.

Allah then commanded the Prophet ﷺ to marry her, to end the jahiliyyah custom of treating adopted sons as real sons: 'We married her to you so that there would be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons' (33:37). The mahr was four hundred dirhams, and a wedding feast was held. Zaynab would say to the other wives: 'Your families married you off; Allah married me from above the seven heavens' (Bukhari).

Allah also abolished adoption as the Arabs practised it: 'He has not made your adopted sons your sons… Call them by their fathers' names; that is more just with Allah. If you do not know their fathers, they are your brothers in religion' (33:4–5). From then on he was called Zayd ibn Harithah, and his is the only name of a Companion in the Quran. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever claims to be the son of someone other than his father, knowing it, Paradise is forbidden to him' (Bukhari). Caring for a child who is not one's own remains a great virtue; what ended was changing his lineage. Mufti Menk urges families today to tell adopted children the truth about their parents, while loving and raising them as their own. Of all people, only Isa is called by his mother's name in the Quran, because he had no father.

At the wedding feast some guests stayed long after eating, sitting in the house. Allah then revealed the ayah of hijab (33:53), teaching manners for entering the Prophet's house and speaking with his wives from behind a screen (Bukhari, from Anas). Zaynab was known for her generosity to the poor and worked with her hands to give in charity. Allah also told the Prophet ﷺ: 'Tell your wives, your daughters and the believing women to draw their outer garments (jalabib) over themselves' (33:59). Umm Salamah said that when it was revealed, the women of the Ansar came out covered in dark cloaks, 'as if there were crows on their heads' (Abu Dawud).
zaynab.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 22.

p: In Muharram of 6 AH, Muhammad ibn Maslamah led thirty riders against a clan of Banu Bakr at al-Qurata' in Najd. On the way back they captured Thumamah ibn Uthal, chief of Banu Hanifah in Yamamah, and tied him to a pillar in the masjid.

Each day the Prophet ﷺ asked him: 'What do you have, Thumamah?' He replied: 'If you kill, you kill one whose blood will be avenged; if you are kind, you are kind to one who is grateful; if you want wealth, ask.' On the third day the Prophet ﷺ freed him. Thumamah washed, returned and accepted Islam, saying: 'No face on earth was more hateful to me than yours, and now it is the most beloved.' He went on to Umrah and cut off Yamamah's grain to Makkah until the Prophet ﷺ asked him to resume it (Bukhari).
sr-qurata.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 6 AH, the Prophet ﷺ set out with two hundred riders to punish Banu Lihyan for betraying the companions at ar-Raji'. He made as if heading north toward Sham, then turned south.

Banu Lihyan learnt of it and fled into the mountains. The Prophet ﷺ camped at Usfan and sent riders toward Makkah to show Quraysh his strength, then returned. It is reported that the ayat on shortening prayer and the prayer of fear (4:101–103) were revealed at Usfan (Abu Dawud, an-Nasa'i).
lihyan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Uyaynah ibn Hisn of Ghatafan raided the Prophet's milch camels grazing at al-Ghabah, killed the herdsman and took his wife. Salamah ibn al-Akwa', heading out early, saw them. He climbed a hill, shouted three times to Madinah, 'Ya Sabahah!', and then chased the raiders on foot alone, shooting arrows and calling out: 'I am Ibn al-Akwa'; today is the day of the wretched!'

He kept them running until they dropped the camels and much of their own gear to escape. Horsemen from Madinah caught up, and the Prophet ﷺ arrived with more at the spring of Dhu Qarad. He said: 'The best of our horsemen today is Abu Qatadah, and the best of our foot soldiers is Salamah,' and gave Salamah a double share (Bukhari 4194, Muslim).
dhuqarad.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 6 AH, Ukkashah ibn Mihsan led forty men against Banu Asad at al-Ghamr. The tribe fled at their approach, and the Muslims returned with two hundred camels without fighting.
sr-ghamr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Akhir of 6 AH, Muhammad ibn Maslamah led ten men to Dhul-Qassah against Banu Tha'labah. At night about a hundred tribesmen ambushed them as they slept. All were killed except Muhammad ibn Maslamah, who was left for dead with wounds; a passing Muslim carried him back to Madinah.
sr-qassah1.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In reply to the ambush at Dhul-Qassah, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah with forty men. They marched by night and reached the tribe at dawn; the men fled into the mountains, and the Muslims took their livestock and returned.
sr-qassah2.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Akhir of 6 AH, Zayd ibn Harithah led a party against Banu Sulaym at al-Jamum. A woman of Muzaynah guided them to a camp of the tribe, and they returned with captives and livestock. The woman was freed and married as a reward.
sr-jamum.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Jumada al-Ula of 6 AH, Zayd ibn Harithah led 170 riders to al-Is to intercept a Quraysh caravan returning from Sham. They captured it, and among the captives was Abu al-As ibn ar-Rabi', husband of the Prophet's daughter Zaynab, who had stayed in Makkah unconverted.

Abu al-As slipped into Madinah by night and asked Zaynab for protection. At Fajr she called out: 'I have given protection to Abu al-As.' The Prophet ﷺ confirmed her protection and asked the companions to return his goods, which they did. Abu al-As took the goods back to Makkah, returned every trust to its owner, then declared Islam and came to Madinah, where Zaynab was returned to him.
sr-is.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Jumada al-Akhirah of 6 AH, Zayd ibn Harithah led fifteen men to at-Taraf against Banu Tha'labah. The tribe fled, fearing a larger army behind them, and Zayd returned with twenty camels.
sr-taraf.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Dihyah al-Kalbi was returning from his embassy to Heraclius with gifts when men of Judham robbed him at Hisma. The Prophet ﷺ sent Zayd ibn Harithah with five hundred men. They defeated the raiders and recovered the goods. Leaders of Judham who had already accepted Islam then came to Madinah to ask for their people's release, and it was granted.
sr-hisma.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rajab of 6 AH, Zayd ibn Harithah led a party to Wadi al-Qura against Banu Fazarah. The Seerah works mention it briefly; it was followed by a clash with Fazarah that led to the expedition to Umm Qirfah.
sr-wadi.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Sha'ban of 6 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf with seven hundred men to Banu Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal. He tied the turban on Abd ar-Rahman's head himself and instructed him: 'Fight in the name of Allah. Do not steal from the spoils, do not betray, do not mutilate, and do not kill a child.'

Abd ar-Rahman called them to Islam for three days. Their Christian chief al-Asbagh ibn Amr accepted Islam, and many followed. Abd ar-Rahman married his daughter Tumadir, as the Prophet ﷺ had advised, and she became the mother of Abu Salamah ibn Abd ar-Rahman.
sr-dumah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Sha'ban of 6 AH, the Prophet ﷺ learnt that Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr at Fadak were gathering men to help the Jews of Khaybar. He sent Ali with a hundred men. Travelling by night, they captured a spy who led them to the tribe, which fled; the Muslims returned with five hundred camels and two thousand sheep.
sr-fadak.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Banu Fazarah attacked a trading party led by Zayd ibn Harithah at Wadi al-Qura, killed several of his companions and left Zayd badly wounded. When he recovered, the Prophet ﷺ sent him back with an army. In Ramadan of 6 AH they defeated Fazarah, including the household of Umm Qirfah, a noblewoman who had incited attacks on the Prophet ﷺ.
sr-qirfah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: A group of men from Uraynah and Ukl came to Madinah and accepted Islam, but fell ill in its climate. The Prophet ﷺ sent them to the grazing camels outside the city to drink their milk. When they recovered, they killed the herdsman Yasar, mutilated him and drove off the camels.

The Prophet ﷺ sent Kurz ibn Jabir with about twenty riders, who caught them and brought them back, and they were punished in kind for what they had done (Bukhari, from Anas). The ayat on the punishment for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread corruption (5:33–34) are reported to have been revealed concerning them.
sr-uraynah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Dhu al-Qa'dah of 6 AH, the Prophet ﷺ dreamt that he entered the Sacred Masjid in safety with his companions, some with heads shaved and some with hair cut short; a prophet's dream is revelation, so he announced Umrah. He called the Bedouin tribes around Madinah to come too, but many made excuses, sure that the Muslims would never return alive. Hajj was not yet obligatory. He set out with about 1,400 companions in ihram, carrying only travellers' swords and driving sacrificial camels, to show they came for worship, not war. The Arabs held sacrificial animals marked for the Ka'bah in such awe that even pagans would not touch them.

At Usfan his scout reported that Quraysh had sworn to stop them, as a matter of pride, though they had always let even their enemies come in the sacred months, and had sent Khalid ibn al-Walid with about two hundred horsemen. Khalid later said that whenever he moved against the Prophet ﷺ he felt he was a protected man. The Prophet ﷺ took a rugged route and camped at al-Hudaybiyyah, on the edge of the Haram, where his camel al-Qaswa knelt and would not move. 'The One who held back the elephant has held her back,' he said.

Envoys went back and forth, and each one Quraysh sent came back softened. Budayl ibn Warqa' of Khuza'ah, told that they had come only for Umrah, urged Quraysh to let them in, and they told him to sit down. Al-Hulays ibn Alqamah, chief of the Ahabish, revered sacrificial animals, so the Prophet ﷺ had them driven before him while the Companions raised the talbiyah. He turned back without even reaching the Prophet ﷺ: 'Glory be to Allah! These people should not be barred from the House,' and threatened to withdraw his men when Quraysh mocked him. Urwah ibn Mas'ud returned to Quraysh amazed: 'I have visited Caesar, Khosrow and the Negus, and never seen a king honoured by his people as Muhammad's companions honour him. When he speaks they lower their voices, and they do not look him full in the face out of respect.' Quraysh also sent Mikraz ibn Hafs with fifty men to raid the camp by night; Muhammad ibn Maslamah's guard captured them, and the Prophet ﷺ let them go. He sent Uthman to Makkah under the protection of his cousin Aban ibn Sa'id, to explain their purpose and to give the weak Muslims there good news of relief. Quraysh refused, offered Uthman alone the chance to make tawaf, which he refused while the Prophet ﷺ was barred, and held him. When a rumour spread that Uthman had been killed, the Prophet ﷺ took a pledge from the companions under a tree that they would not flee, and would fight to the death if need be, unarmed as they were: Bay'at ar-Ridwan. Quraysh were shaken. Allah declared: 'Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree' (48:18). Those who took the pledge are known as the People of the Tree; the Prophet ﷺ said none of them would enter the Fire (Muslim).

Quraysh then sent Suhayl ibn Amr to make a treaty. Uthman was found alive, but the pledge had done its work. When Ali wrote 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful', Suhayl objected and asked for 'In Your name, O Allah'. Uthman was found alive, but the pledge had done its work. When Ali wrote 'Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah', Suhayl said: 'If we accepted that, we would not have fought you.' Ali could not bring himself to erase it. The Prophet ﷺ, who could not read, asked him to point to the words, erased them with his own hand, and wrote 'Muhammad ibn Abdullah'. The terms: a ten-year truce; the Muslims would return this year and come for Umrah the next, when Quraysh would leave the city for three days and they could enter with only sheathed swords; travellers of each side would be safe; anyone from Quraysh who came to the Muslims without permission would be returned, but not the reverse; tribes could ally with either side. Khuza'ah at once allied with the Muslims and Banu Bakr with Quraysh (Bukhari 2731).

The terms seemed humiliating. Umar asked: 'Are we not on the truth and they on falsehood? Why accept lowliness in our religion?' Abu Bakr told him: 'He is the Messenger of Allah; hold fast to his stirrup.' When the Prophet ﷺ told the companions to slaughter their animals and shave, no one moved, in their grief, not from disobedience but hoping some revelation would still let them enter. Umm Salamah advised him to do it himself without a word; then they all followed.

On the way home Surah al-Fath was revealed: 'Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory' (48:1). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A surah has been revealed to me tonight that is dearer to me than everything the sun rises upon' (Bukhari). Umar asked: 'Is it a victory?' 'Yes.' Allah promised: 'Allah has fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills, in safety, heads shaved and hair cut short' (48:27). He exposed the Bedouins who stayed behind, thinking 'the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families,' and then came asking forgiveness 'with their tongues what is not in their hearts' (48:11–12). Within two years, under the peace, more people accepted Islam than in all the years before. For the first time the idolaters could mix freely with Muslims and see their worship, cleanliness and conduct; Mufti Menk says a Muslim praying calmly in a public place still teaches more than words.
hudaybiyyah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 23.

p: As the treaty was being written, Abu Jandal, Suhayl's own son, staggered into the camp in chains, having escaped from Makkah, and begged the Muslims to take him. Suhayl insisted on the new clause. The Prophet ﷺ returned him, telling him to be patient, for Allah would make a way out for him and the weak.

Allah also ruled that believing women who emigrated were not to be returned: 'O believers, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them… If you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers' (60:10); a woman's idolater husband was to be repaid what he had spent on her, and the marriage was dissolved. The first was Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Scholars also note that the clause was worded for men.

Back in Madinah, another Muslim, Abu Basir, escaped from Makkah. Quraysh sent two men to fetch him, and the Prophet ﷺ handed him over. On the road Abu Basir killed one of them and escaped to the Red Sea coast at Sif al-Bahr. Abu Jandal and other escapees joined him until they were about seventy, and they raided every Quraysh caravan passing to Sham.

Quraysh finally wrote to the Prophet ﷺ, begging him by their kinship to take these men into Madinah and dropping the clause they had insisted on. He sent for them (Bukhari 2731; Hayatus Sahaba 1:172–174).
abubasir.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 23.

p: With peace secured, the Prophet ﷺ sent letters to the rulers around Arabia, He was told that kings would not read a letter without a seal, so he had a silver ring made, engraved in three lines read from the bottom up: Muhammad, Rasul, Allah. It was a seal for state letters, not an ornament. Anas said he could still picture the white gleam of it on the Prophet's ﷺ hand (Bukhari). The letters were not sent all at once but over 7 and 8 AH. To Heraclius, Emperor of Rome, he sent Dihyah al-Kalbi, a Companion so handsome that Jibril sometimes came in his form, with the letter: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful… Peace on whoever follows guidance. I invite you to Islam. Accept Islam and you will be safe, and Allah will give you a double reward. If you turn away, you bear the sin of your subjects.'

Heraclius asked for anyone from that land and was brought Abu Sufyan, there with a Quraysh trading party. He asked who was closest in kinship to the man, seated Abu Sufyan in front and the others behind him, and told them to speak up if he lied; Abu Sufyan later said only shame at being caught lying kept him truthful. The questions and answers: Is his lineage noble? Yes. Did anyone among you claim this before him? No. Was any of his forefathers a king? No. Did you ever accuse him of lying? No. Are his followers the nobles or the weak? The weak. Are they increasing or decreasing? Increasing. Does anyone leave his religion out of dislike for it? No. Does he betray? No, and we are now in a truce with him. Have you fought him? Yes; sometimes he wins and sometimes we do. What does he command? To worship Allah alone without partners, to pray, to be truthful and chaste and to keep ties of kinship.

Heraclius explained each question: messengers come from noble lineage; had someone claimed it before, he might be copying; had a forefather been king, he might want the throne back; one who never lies about people would not lie about Allah; the weak are always the first followers of prophets; true faith grows and, once its joy enters the heart, no one leaves it; messengers do not betray; and messengers are tested, but the final victory is theirs. 'If what you say is true, he will rule the place beneath these two feet of mine. I knew he was coming, but did not think he would be from you' (Bukhari 7). His court erupted and the Arabs were sent out. Abu Sufyan said to his companions: 'Even the king of the Romans fears him,' and that was when he first felt Islam enter his heart. Later Heraclius gathered his nobles in a locked hall at Hims and invited them to follow the Prophet ﷺ; when they rushed for the doors, he told them he had only been testing their firmness in their religion, and did not accept Islam (Bukhari 7). Mufti Menk's lesson: knowing the truth is not enough; one must act on it.

Khosrow of Persia received his letter through Abdullah ibn Hudhafah as-Sahmi (reports differ on whether it reached him directly or through one of his officials). He was furious, tore it up and trampled it. When told, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'May Allah tear up his kingdom.' Before long Khosrow was murdered by his own son, Persia fell into civil war, and the empire soon collapsed. To the Negus of Abyssinia, Ashamah, the letter went with Amr ibn Umayyah ad-Damri; like the other letters, it spoke to the reader's own beliefs, here explaining who Isa (peace be upon him) truly was. The Negus affirmed it was the truth and accepted Islam, though some reports say he asked for time to win over his nobles before declaring it openly. To al-Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt, went Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. He understood the letter well but did not accept Islam. He wrote back courteously and sent gifts: two young women from noble Coptic families, Mariyah and her sister Sirin, a mule, and other goods. Mariyah became the mother of the Prophet's ﷺ son Ibrahim, who died in infancy. Al-Ala' al-Hadrami took a letter to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa of Bahrain, who accepted Islam with many of the Arabs there; the Prophet ﷺ kept him as ruler and guided him, as was his way with rulers who accepted. Badhan, ruler of Yemen, also accepted and was kept in place, and his son succeeded him. Amr ibn al-As, after his own Islam, took a letter to Jayfar and Abd, the sons of al-Julanda in Oman, and they too accepted. Al-Harith ibn Umayr, carrying a letter to the ruler of Busra, was seized and killed on the way, which led to the expedition of Mu'tah. Most rulers, Muslim or not, received the envoys with honour and sent replies and gifts. Khosrow alone insulted them; unlike the Christian rulers, Persia had no scripture that spoke of a coming prophet. Islam was now known far beyond anything Quraysh had imagined.
letters.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 4–24.

p: Khaybar, an oasis of fortresses about 150 km north of Madinah, had become the centre of plotting against the Muslims since Banu Nadir settled there; its leaders had organised the Confederates who besieged Madinah at the Trench. Quraysh, now bound by the treaty, stayed out. Its people were skilled builders and fighters: their forts stood in three clusters, linked so defenders could slip from one to the next, some reportedly by tunnels, and they knew the Muslims would come. In Muharram of 7 AH, soon after Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ marched on it with about 1,600 men, only those who had been at Hudaybiyyah.

He arrived at night and attacked at dawn. At the first forts, the Muslims cut down some palm trees to show they had come in earnest, and when the defenders were beaten they fled to the next fort. During one siege, Umar caught a man slipping out at night; in return for safety he told them of a planned attack the next day and of a house stored with catapults, armour and weapons. The Muslims won the next day's fighting and took the weapons. The strong fort of al-Qamus held out for days. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger and whom Allah and His Messenger love; Allah will give victory through him.' Everyone spent the night hoping it would be him; Umar said he never wished for leadership except that day (Muslim). In the morning the Prophet ﷺ asked for Ali, who had sore eyes; he spat lightly in them and they healed at once. He gave him the banner and told him to invite them to Islam first: 'If Allah guides one man through you, that is better for you than red camels' (Bukhari 4210). Ali killed the champion Marhab in single combat, and the fort fell. Another fort was besieged for three days until a man showed where its water came in; the Prophet ﷺ cut it off, the defenders came out to fight and were beaten. Ali, az-Zubayr and Abu Dujanah were remembered for their courage. Some forts were taken by battle, some after siege, and the last two surrendered without fighting. The siege lasted around twenty days, the whole stay just under a month; about 93 of the defenders were killed and 15 Muslims martyred, as reported. Every fort held wealth, each kind stored in its own place.

The people of Khaybar pleaded not to be killed or expelled. The Prophet ﷺ let them stay and farm the land for half the harvest, on condition that the Muslims could end the arrangement whenever they chose (Bukhari). It suited the Muslims too: the Muhajirun had no farming skill, and the men were needed for the spread of Islam. Abdullah ibn Rawahah was sent each year to assess the crop. When they tried to bribe him to under-count it, he refused: neither his love for the Prophet ﷺ nor his dislike of them would make him unjust, and they said that by such justice the heavens and earth stand. Kinanah ibn ar-Rabi' was asked about the treasure of Banu Nadir, with its jewellery and perfume, and claimed it had been spent on war; it was later found hidden, and he was executed, the only one not forgiven. Fadak, a nearby oasis, made peace on the same half-share terms; its income was set aside for the Prophet's ﷺ household and the poor of his clan. Safiyyah bint Huyayy, daughter of the chief of Banu Nadir (Huyayy had been executed with Banu Qurayzah), was among the captives. She accepted Islam, and he freed her and married her, keeping the honour she had known as a chief's daughter and raising it as a Mother of the Believers. She is remembered as gentle-spoken and devout. At Khaybar the Prophet ﷺ also announced two prohibitions: temporary marriage (mut'ah), a pre-Islamic custom of marriage for a fixed period, and the meat of domestic donkeys (Bukhari, Muslim, from Ali); Sahih Muslim also reports a final, permanent prohibition of mut'ah in the year of the Conquest. A Jewish woman, Zaynab bint al-Harith, served him a poisoned roast sheep; he chewed a little, spat it out and said it was poisoned; some reports say the meat itself told him. She admitted it: 'If you are a prophet, you would know; if not, we would be rid of you.' Bishr ibn al-Bara', who had eaten from it, died. The Prophet ﷺ forgave her for the attempt on his own life; reports say she was later executed in retribution for Bishr (Abu Dawud). He said years later that he still felt its effect (Bukhari).
At Khaybar, Ja'far and the emigrants returned from Abyssinia, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I do not know which makes me happier, the conquest of Khaybar or the return of Ja'far.'
khaybar.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 24–25.

p: After more than ten years in Abyssinia, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the remaining emigrants, about sixteen men with their families, sailed home on two ships. With them came Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his people from Yemen, whose ship had been blown to Abyssinia; they had stayed with Ja'far ever since. Abu Musa, who later narrated many hadith, said he was the youngest of his group. Umm Habibah, now the Prophet's ﷺ wife, came with them.

They reached the Prophet ﷺ just as Khaybar was conquered. He embraced Ja'far, kissed his forehead and said: 'I do not know which makes me happier, the conquest of Khaybar or the arrival of Ja'far.' He gave them a share of the spoils. When Umar told Asma bint Umays that those who made the Hijrah to Madinah had more right to the Prophet, she complained, and he said: 'You, the people of the ship, have two hijrahs' (Bukhari, from Abu Musa).
jafar-return.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 24.

p: Abu Hurayrah of the tribe of Daws, guided to Islam through at-Tufayl ibn Amr, came to Madinah during Khaybar and joined the Prophet ﷺ there. He had no wealth and lived among the people of the Suffah, often hungry, sometimes fainting from hunger in the masjid.

He devoted himself to staying close to the Prophet ﷺ, while others were busy in the markets and fields. He complained of forgetting, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to spread his cloak; he spoke, Abu Hurayrah gathered it to his chest, and he said he never forgot anything after that (Bukhari). Though he was with the Prophet ﷺ for only about four years, he narrated more hadith than any other companion. His mother, at first hostile, accepted Islam after the Prophet ﷺ prayed for her (Muslim).
abuhurayrah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After Khaybar, Umar received a piece of land there, the most valuable property he had ever owned. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked what to do with it. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If you wish, keep the land itself and give its produce in charity.'

Umar made it a charity that could not be sold, given away or inherited, its income going to the poor, relatives, freeing slaves, the cause of Allah, travellers and guests, with the caretaker allowed to eat from it reasonably (Bukhari, from Ibn Umar). It is counted as the first waqf in Islam and became the model for endowments for centuries (Hayatus Sahaba 2:187).
umar-waqf.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: On the return from Khaybar, the Prophet ﷺ came to Wadi al-Qura, a valley of Jewish farmers. He called them to Islam; they refused and fought. After a short siege they surrendered on the same terms as Khaybar, farming the land for half its produce. Tayma, further north, then made peace without fighting.

A slave named Mid'am who served the Prophet ﷺ was killed by a stray arrow. People said: 'Congratulations on Paradise.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'No; the cloak he stole from the spoils of Khaybar is burning on him' (Bukhari), a lesson on the gravity of theft from the spoils.
wadiqura.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 24.

p: In Sha'ban of 7 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Bakr with a party against Banu Fazarah in Najd. They attacked at dawn and took captives. Salamah ibn al-Akwa', who took part, captured a woman and her beautiful daughter; the Prophet ﷺ later asked him for the girl and sent her to Makkah to ransom Muslim prisoners (Muslim).
sr-najd.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Sha'ban of 7 AH, Umar ibn al-Khattab led thirty men against Hawazin at Turabah, near Makkah. They travelled by night and hid by day, but Hawazin learnt of them and fled; Umar returned without fighting.
sr-turabah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Sha'ban of 7 AH, Bashir ibn Sa'd led thirty men against Banu Murrah near Fadak. They took livestock, but the tribe pursued them at night and killed most of the party. Bashir fought until he fell and was left for dead; he recovered and made his way back to Madinah.
sr-fadak2.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Ramadan of 7 AH, Ghalib ibn Abdullah al-Laythi led a party against Banu Uwal and Banu Abd ibn Tha'labah at al-Mayfa'ah. Usamah ibn Zayd took part, and in the fighting he and an Ansari overtook a man who said 'La ilaha illa Allah'. The Ansari held back, but Usamah killed him.

When the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said: 'Did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah?' Usamah said the man had said it only out of fear of the sword. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Did you split open his heart to know whether he said it sincerely?' and kept repeating it, until Usamah wished he had only accepted Islam that day (Muslim, from Usamah).
sr-huruqat.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Shawwal of 7 AH, news came that Ghatafan were gathering at Yumn and Jabar with Uyaynah ibn Hisn to attack Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ sent Bashir ibn Sa'd with three hundred men. They scattered the tribe and returned with livestock and two prisoners, who accepted Islam.
sr-yumn.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Dhu al-Qa'dah of 7 AH, as agreed at Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ came to Makkah for Umrah with about two thousand companions. He had them bring their weapons in case Quraysh broke faith, leaving them with a guard at Ya'jaj, outside the Haram, and drove sixty sacrificial camels. When Quraysh's scouts reported the Muslims armed, envoys came to say he had never broken his word; he replied that no weapons would enter Makkah. Quraysh's leaders left the city for three days and watched from the hills.

They had said the Muslims were weakened by the fever of Madinah, so the Prophet ﷺ told the companions to uncover their right shoulders and walk briskly in the first three rounds of tawaf, to show their strength. He made tawaf on his camel, touching the Black Stone with his staff and kissing the staff. Once the onlookers left after three rounds, the companions walked normally for the rest. This became the sunnah for men in Umrah: the right shoulder uncovered (idtiba') for all seven rounds and the brisk walk (raml) for the first three. It is called Umrat al-Qada, the Umrah made up for the one they were barred from. Abdullah ibn Rawahah walked before him reciting verses, and Bilal later climbed the Ka'bah (at the Conquest) to call the adhan.

During this visit the Prophet ﷺ married Maymunah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah, an early Muslim and a widow, aunt of Khalid ibn al-Walid and Ibn Abbas. Al-Abbas arranged it, so that she would go to Madinah under his protection. (She is not related to Juwayriyah bint al-Harith.) When Quraysh demanded he leave after three days, he left and sent the guards to perform their Umrah, and consummated the marriage at Sarif, outside the Haram, where the walimah was held. Maymunah's marriage was his last.
qada.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 24.

p: In Dhu al-Hijjah of 7 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Ibn Abi al-Awja' with fifty men to call Banu Sulaym to Islam. They answered: 'We have no need of what you call us to,' and attacked. Most of the party were killed; Ibn Abi al-Awja' returned wounded.
sr-awja.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Khalid ibn al-Walid, the commander who had turned Uhud against the Muslims, said he always knew in his heart he was fighting on the losing side, at Uhud, at the Trench and at Hudaybiyyah, where he felt the Prophet ﷺ was protected. When the Muslims came for Umrat al-Qada he left Makkah so as not to face them. His brother al-Walid, already Muslim, searched for him and, not finding him, left a letter: 'You are on the wrong side and missing so much good. The Prophet ﷺ asked, "Where is Khalid? Someone like him cannot remain ignorant of Islam," and he hopes you will come.'

Khalid set out for Madinah and met Amr ibn al-As, who had decided the same after his time in Abyssinia, and Uthman ibn Talhah, keeper of the Ka'bah's key. They arrived together in Safar of 8 AH. His brother told him to hurry, as the Prophet ﷺ was expecting him; he bathed, put on good clothes and went, and the Prophet ﷺ smiled at him as he declared the shahadah. Khalid asked him to pray for forgiveness for every time he had fought against Islam. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Makkah has thrown to you the pieces of its liver.' When Amr made the same request, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Islam wipes out what came before it' (Muslim 121); Khalid was told the same. Amr said Islam had first entered his heart at the Negus's court, and some reports say he accepted Islam there. With these leaders of Quraysh's army now Muslim, delegations and individuals came to Islam while Quraysh's support shrank: 'Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders?' (13:41). Within months Khalid was called the Sword of Allah.
khalid.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 24.

p: In Safar of 8 AH, Ghalib ibn Abdullah al-Laythi led a party against Banu al-Mulawwah at al-Kadid. They attacked by night and drove off their camels; the tribe pursued them, but a flash flood filled the valley between them, and the Muslims returned safely.
sr-kadid.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 8 AH, Shuja' ibn Wahb led twenty-four men against Banu Amir at as-Siyy. They surprised the tribe and returned with camels and sheep, each man's share being fifteen camels.
sr-siyy.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 8 AH, Ka'b ibn Umayr al-Ghifari led fifteen men to Dhat Atlah on the borders of Sham to call the people to Islam. The people refused and shot at them; all were killed except one wounded man who made his way back to Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ planned to send an army in response, but heard that the tribe had moved away.
sr-atlah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: The Prophet ﷺ sent al-Harith ibn Umayr with a letter to the ruler of Busra. A Ghassanid governor, Shurahbil ibn Amr, seized and killed him, an act of war against the custom of protecting envoys. These tribes were under Roman rule and were themselves preparing to move against Madinah. In Jumada al-Ula of 8 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent an army of three thousand north, the largest Muslim army up to then. Seeing them off at the edge of Madinah, he told them to fight in Allah's name, and not to attack people worshipping in their churches, nor kill women, children or old men who took no part, nor cut down trees or destroy buildings.

He appointed Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed slave who had chosen him over his own family, to lead; if Zayd fell, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib; if Ja'far fell, Abdullah ibn Rawahah. He had never before named a chain of commanders, and the companions sensed all three would be martyred. As they left, Abdullah ibn Rawahah, the poet who defended Islam in verse, wept; asked why, he said he was thinking of the verse about every soul passing over the Fire (19:71) and wondering how he would cross. At Ma'an they learnt that Heraclius had gathered a vast force of Romans and Arab allies, reports range from about 150,000 to 200,000 or more, Romans and Christian Arabs together. They debated writing for reinforcements, but Abdullah ibn Rawahah urged them on: 'We do not fight by numbers or strength, but by this religion,' and either victory or martyrdom would be theirs. They all agreed to go on.

They met at Mu'tah, east of the Dead Sea. Zayd carried the banner until he fell. Ja'far took it; when his right hand was cut off he held it in his left, and when that was cut off he hugged it with his arms until he was killed, with more than ninety wounds on his front. Abdullah ibn Rawahah took it and was martyred. Thabit ibn Aqram took up the banner and told them that if they fled they would be cut down anyway, with wounds in their backs. They chose Khalid ibn al-Walid, newly Muslim and there as an ordinary soldier, for his skill in war, who broke nine swords in his hand that day (Bukhari).

Khalid reorganised the army in the night, swapping the wings and moving the rear forward so the Romans thought reinforcements had arrived, and drew back step by step over several days; fearing a trap in the desert, the Romans did not follow. Twelve Muslims were martyred; Roman losses are reported to have been far greater. The graves of the three commanders are in southern Jordan. In Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ told the people of each death as it happened, his eyes flowing with tears, and said: 'Then the banner was taken by a sword of the swords of Allah, and Allah gave them victory' (Bukhari). He said Ja'far had been given two wings in Paradise, and he was called Ja'far at-Tayyar; Ibn Umar would greet his son: 'Peace be upon you, son of the one with two wings' (Bukhari). He went to Ja'far's wife Asma bint Umays, asked for her children, and when she asked, told her Ja'far was martyred, before the army had returned. (She later married Abu Bakr, bearing Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, and after his death Ali.) When the army reached Madinah some people shouted, 'Runaways!' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'They are not runaways; they will return to fight, if Allah wills' (Ibn Ishaq).
mutah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 25.

p: The tribe of Abd al-Qays lived in Bahrain, on the eastern side of Arabia. A delegation came to Madinah; the Prophet ﷺ welcomed them: 'Welcome to the people who have come without shame or regret.' They said that the hostile tribe of Mudar lay between them and Madinah, so they could only travel in the sacred months, and asked for clear commands to take home.

He commanded them four things: faith in Allah alone (the shahadah, prayer, zakat and fasting Ramadan) and giving a fifth of spoils; and forbade four kinds of vessels used for making wine (Bukhari, Muslim). To their leader al-Ashajj he said: 'You have two qualities Allah loves: forbearance and deliberation' (Muslim). Theirs was one of the first masjids where Jumu'ah was held after the Prophet's masjid (Hayatus Sahaba 1:145).
abdqays.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Jumada al-Akhirah of 8 AH, news came that tribes of Quda'ah were gathering near Sham. The Prophet ﷺ sent Amr ibn al-As with three hundred men; his grandmother was from those tribes, and it was hoped they would incline to Islam.

Finding the enemy large, Amr sent for help. The Prophet ﷺ sent two hundred more under Abu Ubaydah, including Abu Bakr and Umar. Amr insisted on keeping overall command, and Abu Ubaydah, gentle as always, agreed. Amr forbade the men to light fires in the cold night, and when the enemy fled within hours of the fighting, he would not let them give chase. Back in Madinah the men complained; Amr explained that their small numbers would have shown in the firelight and invited an attack, and that a pursuit risked an ambush. The Prophet ﷺ approved. Another cold night Amr led the prayer after tayammum instead of ghusl; when asked, the Prophet ﷺ smiled and approved. Amr later asked him: 'Who is most beloved to you?' 'Aisha.' 'And among men?' 'Her father' (Bukhari).

The name Dhat as-Salasil is usually explained as the name of a water there; Mufti Menk explains it as 'the chains', saying the enemy chained men together so they could not flee. After it, several tribes of the region made alliances with the Muslims and many accepted Islam.
salasil.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 25.

p: Zaynab, the Prophet's eldest daughter, had stayed in Makkah when he emigrated, as her husband Abu al-As was not yet Muslim. When she later set out for Madinah, Habbar ibn al-Aswad struck her camel; she fell and miscarried, and never fully recovered. Abu al-As later accepted Islam and was reunited with her; he spoke of her with praise, saying he would not choose any woman of Quraysh over her.

She died in Madinah early in 8 AH. The Prophet ﷺ instructed Umm Atiyyah and the women washing her body: 'Wash her three, five or more times, with water and lotus leaves, and put camphor in the last,' and gave his own waist-wrap to be placed next to her body (Bukhari). Her daughter Umamah, whom he used to carry in prayer, later married Ali.
zaynab-d.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: In Rajab of 8 AH, Abu Ubaydah led three hundred men to the Red Sea coast to watch a Quraysh caravan. Their food ran out until each man had one date a day, which they sucked like a child, then drank water; then they ate leaves, so the expedition was called al-Khabat, 'the leaves'. Qays, son of the generous Sa'd ibn Ubadah, had brought camels borrowed from his father; he slaughtered one a day for three days, until Abu Ubaydah stopped him, as the camels were not his.

Then the sea threw up a huge creature, a whale called al-Anbar. They ate from it for half a month and grew strong, and Abu Ubaydah had a camel walk under one of its ribs. Back in Madinah they told the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'It was provision Allah brought out for you. Do you have any of its meat to give us?' and ate some (Bukhari, Muslim, from Jabir).
sr-khabat.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 25.

p: In Sha'ban of 8 AH, Abu Qatadah led fifteen men against Ghatafan at Khadirah in Najd. They attacked by night and returned with camels and sheep after fifteen days.
sr-khadirah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Ramadan of 8 AH, before the march on Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Qatadah with eight men toward Batn Idam, in the opposite direction, so that the news would spread that he was heading there and Quraysh would not learn of the real destination.
sr-idam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: The Muslim army of ten thousand camped at Marr az-Zahran, a day from Makkah, and lit ten thousand fires. Al-Abbas, who had just joined the Muslims, rode out on the Prophet's white mule hoping to persuade Quraysh to ask for safety before the city was taken by force. He found Abu Sufyan out scouting and brought him to the Prophet ﷺ under his protection. Umar wanted to kill him; al-Abbas shielded him.

The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Woe to you, Abu Sufyan, is it not time for you to know there is no god but Allah?' Abu Sufyan said: 'If there were another god besides Allah, he would have helped me.' 'Is it not time to know that I am the Messenger of Allah?' 'About that I still have some doubt.' Al-Abbas, his close friend, urged him, reminding him that Islam wipes out all that came before it, and he declared the shahadah. Mufti Menk stresses this was not a threat: it was the assurance that with Islam his past was forgiven.

Al-Abbas said: 'Abu Sufyan loves honour; give him something.' The Prophet ﷺ declared: 'Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe; whoever closes his door is safe; whoever enters the Sacred Masjid is safe.' At the Prophet's ﷺ instruction, al-Abbas stood Abu Sufyan at a narrow point where he watched the army march past tribe by tribe, then hurried to Makkah to announce the amnesty (Ibn Ishaq, at-Tabarani; Hayatus Sahaba 1:183–184).
abusufyan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 25.

p: In Sha'ban of 8 AH, the treaty of Hudaybiyyah was broken. A man of Banu Bakr, allies of Quraysh, is reported to have insulted the Prophet ﷺ, a man of Khuza'ah, allies of the Muslims, objected, and a quarrel between the two became an attack by Banu Bakr on Khuza'ah. Khuza'ah fled into the Haram and pleaded, 'Your god!' Their attackers replied, 'There is no god today.' Quraysh quietly helped with weapons and men, and some of Khuza'ah were killed. Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i rode to Madinah to plead for help, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'You will be helped.' Quraysh, worried, sent Abu Sufyan to Madinah to renew the treaty. He went first to his daughter Umm Habibah, the Prophet's ﷺ wife; when he went to sit, she folded away the Prophet's ﷺ bedding: 'This is the bedding of the Messenger of Allah, and you are a polytheist.' He said: 'You have changed since you left us.' He spoke to the Prophet ﷺ, then to Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali, and all of them turned him away. He returned with nothing.

The Prophet ﷺ told only Abu Bakr, who asked, 'Do we not have a treaty with them?' 'They have broken it.' He called all the tribes that had accepted Islam to come to Madinah for Ramadan and prepared them for war without naming the destination, and sent a small party in the opposite direction. He prayed: 'O Allah, keep the news from Quraysh until we surprise them.' Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a veteran of Badr and Hudaybiyyah with family in Makkah, wrote to warn Quraysh and sent the letter with a woman. Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ, and he sent Ali, az-Zubayr and al-Miqdad: 'Go to Rawdat Khakh; there is a woman there with a letter.' She denied it, and Ali said: 'Bring out the letter, or we will search your clothes.' She took it from her braids. Umar asked leave to kill Hatib as a traitor. Hatib said: 'I have not doubted my faith; I only wanted a favour from them for my family.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'He has told you the truth,' and: 'Perhaps Allah looked at the people of Badr and said, "Do as you wish, I have forgiven you"' (Bukhari 3007). Surah 60:1 was revealed.

On 10 Ramadan he marched with ten thousand men, leaving Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum in charge of Madinah. On the way, his cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith (not the Quraysh leader) and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah met the army and accepted Islam. At al-Kadid, as the fast became hard, he broke his fast and told the people to do the same, showing that travellers may break the fast and make it up later. His uncle al-Abbas, travelling to Madinah with his family to emigrate, met the army and accepted Islam; the Prophet ﷺ sent the family on and took al-Abbas with him. Al-Abbas had long known his nephew was right, and left as soon as he heard rumours of the march. On 20 Ramadan the army entered Makkah from several directions, the Prophet ﷺ from Kada' in the north and Khalid from the south; only Khalid's column met resistance, and two Muslims and some of the attackers were killed. The Prophet ﷺ entered riding his camel with Usamah ibn Zayd behind him, his head bowed so low in humility that his beard almost touched the saddle, reciting Surah al-Fath. Watching their old enemy enter so humbly, many declared the shahadah; many had held back only out of fear of Quraysh.

He rested a while in a tent pitched for him, then went to the Ka'bah and performed tawaf on his camel, touching the Black Stone with his staff, and struck the 360 idols around it with a stick, reciting: 'The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; falsehood is bound to vanish' (17:81), and they fell on their faces (Bukhari 4287). He had the images inside the Ka'bah removed, prayed inside, and Bilal climbed onto its roof and called the adhan. The pagans who gathered to watch saw a man who had been a slave and tortured in Makkah honoured above them all.

Standing at the door of the Ka'bah, he addressed the Quraysh who had persecuted him for twenty years: 'What do you think I will do with you?' 'Good; you are a noble brother and the son of a noble brother.' He said: 'I say to you as Yusuf said to his brothers: no blame on you today. Go, you are free.' He gave the key of the Ka'bah back to Uthman ibn Talhah and his family forever. People came one by one to pledge allegiance, among them Mu'awiyah and Abu Bakr's father Abu Quhafah. One man trembled before him, and he said: 'Relax; I am not a king. I am the son of a woman of Quraysh who ate dried meat' (Ibn Majah). It was his character, not the sword, that drew people to Islam that day.

He then addressed the people: Allah had removed the arrogance of the days of ignorance and its pride in ancestry; people are the children of Adam, and Adam was created from dust. He recited: 'O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you nations and tribes so that you may know one another. The most honoured of you with Allah is the most mindful of Him' (49:13; Tirmidhi 3270). Mufti Menk links to it the saying that no Arab has virtue over a non-Arab, nor a white person over a black, except by piety. While he made tawaf, Fadalah ibn Umayr crept up meaning to kill him. The Prophet ﷺ stopped: 'Fadalah?' 'Yes.' 'What were you saying to yourself?' 'Nothing, I was remembering Allah.' He laughed, said 'Ask Allah's forgiveness,' and placed his hand on Fadalah's chest. Fadalah said: 'He had not lifted his hand before no one on earth was dearer to me than him' (Ibn Hisham). As he prayed on Safa, some of the Ansar whispered that now he had his homeland back he might stay in Makkah. He called them and said: 'I live where you live and I die where you die' (Muslim), and they wept with joy. He stayed in Makkah about eighteen or nineteen days.
Only a handful of people guilty of grave crimes were excluded from the amnesty, and most of them were later forgiven too. People came in crowds to give the pledge, as Surah an-Nasr describes.
fath.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 1–26.

p: Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, fought against the Muslims to the last, and on the day of the Conquest he fled for the coast, to take any boat that would carry him, sure he would never survive. His wife Umm Hakim accepted Islam and asked the Prophet ﷺ to grant him safety, which he did. She caught up with Ikrimah and brought him back: 'He is the most generous of men; he will not harm you.' The Prophet ﷺ smiled and welcomed him. The Prophet ﷺ told the companions not to insult his father in front of him, and rose to greet him warmly. Ikrimah accepted Islam and later fought bravely until he was martyred at Yarmuk.

Safwan ibn Umayyah, whose father Umayyah had tortured Bilal, also fled to the coast, intending to throw himself into the sea though he could not swim. His cousin Umayr ibn Wahb obtained safety for him, and the Prophet ﷺ gave his turban as a sign; Safwan came back and asked for two months to think, and the Prophet ﷺ gave him four. Safwan lent the Muslims weapons for Hunayn, and when he saw the Prophet ﷺ give him a valley full of livestock from the spoils, he said: 'No one gives like this except a prophet,' and accepted Islam (Muslim).

Suhayl ibn Amr, who had negotiated Hudaybiyyah, hid in his house and sent his son Abdullah to ask for safety. The Prophet ﷺ granted it and said: 'Whoever meets Suhayl, let him not stare at him; he is a man of intelligence and honour.' Suhayl accepted Islam and became known for his devotion (al-Hakim, Ibn Ishaq; Hayatus Sahaba 1:193–198).

Others on the list were forgiven too. Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh hid with his foster brother Uthman, who brought him to the Prophet ﷺ; he accepted Islam and his name was dropped. Al-Harith ibn Hisham and Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah took refuge with Umm Hani, who granted them protection, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'We protect whom you protect, Umm Hani' (Bukhari). Hind bint Utbah, who had mutilated Hamzah's body at Uhud, came veiled to the women's pledge. As he named its terms, not to steal and not to commit adultery, she asked whether she could take from her stingy husband Abu Sufyan's wealth without his knowledge; he said: 'Take what is enough for you and your child, reasonably' (Bukhari). Then he recognised her, and she sought forgiveness and was forgiven. Habbar ibn al-Aswad later came to him at al-Ji'ranah and accepted Islam, Wahshi came from Ta'if and accepted Islam, and Abu Lahab's sons also declared the shahadah.
ikrimah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 25.

p: After the Conquest, the Prophet ﷺ sent companions to destroy the great idols of the region. Khalid ibn al-Walid went to Nakhlah and cut down al-Uzza, the chief idol of Quraysh. Amr ibn al-As went to Ruhat and broke Suwa', the idol of Hudhayl. Sa'd ibn Zayd al-Ashhali went to al-Mushallal near Qudayd and destroyed Manat, the idol of the Aws and Khazraj in jahiliyyah.
Herald after herald also went through Makkah announcing: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him not leave an idol in his house without breaking it.'
sr-idols.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 26.

p: After the Conquest, the Prophet ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to call Banu Jadhimah to Islam. Unable to say 'aslamna' (we have accepted Islam), they said 'saba'na, saba'na' (we have changed religion). Khalid took this as refusal, killed some of them and took others captive. Ibn Umar and others with him refused to kill their captives.

When the Prophet ﷺ heard, he raised his hands and said twice: 'O Allah, I am free of what Khalid has done' (Bukhari). He sent Ali with money to pay blood money for every life and compensation for all lost property, even a dog's drinking bowl, and Ali gave them what was left over as a precaution.
sr-jadhimah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: After the Conquest, the great tribe of Hawazin and Thaqif gathered about twenty thousand men under Malik ibn Awf to march on Makkah; among them was Banu Sa'd, the clan of his foster-mother Halimah. Malik made them bring their women, children and herds so that no one would flee. Durayd ibn as-Simmah, an old war expert too frail to fight, warned him that a beaten man is not stopped by anything, but Malik would not listen. In Shawwal of 8 AH the Prophet ﷺ marched out with twelve thousand: the ten thousand from Madinah and two thousand from Makkah, some newly Muslim and some, like Safwan ibn Umayyah, not yet Muslim. It was the largest Muslim army yet. On the way they passed Dhat Anwat, a tree on which the pagans hung their weapons and tokens for blessing, and some new Muslims asked for one like it. He said: 'Allahu Akbar! You have said what the people of Musa said: "Make for us a god as they have gods" (7:138)' (Tirmidhi 2180). Some said: 'We will not be defeated today because of small numbers.'

Hawazin hid in the narrow valley of Hunayn. At dawn, as the Muslims descended, the archers rained arrows on them from both sides. The vanguard broke and fled, and the panic spread through the army. There was no opening duel; before the army understood, it was under attack. Only a small band stayed with the Prophet ﷺ, among them Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, al-Abbas and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, who rode his white mule toward the enemy, calling: 'I am the Prophet, that is no lie; I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib!' He was the bravest of people that day (Bukhari 3042). Some newly Muslim Makkans said Muhammad's defeat had come. Mufti Menk reports that Ikrimah, Muslim only days, silenced them: victory belongs to Allah, and even if they retreat, the final victory will be theirs.

He told al-Abbas, who had a powerful voice, to call out: 'O people of the Tree! O people of Surah al-Baqarah!' The companions returned like cows to their calves, crying 'Labbayk!' The Prophet ﷺ threw a handful of dust toward the enemy, saying 'May their faces be disfigured,' and the battle turned. Hawazin fled, leaving their families and herds, and the Muslims took them all; the silver was gathered too and everything was taken to al-Ji'ranah. The defeated split three ways: most to Ta'if, others to Nakhlah and Awtas. A force under Abu Amir al-Ash'ari defeated them at Awtas; Abu Amir was martyred and his nephew Abu Musa brought the men back (Bukhari).

Allah revealed: 'Allah has helped you on many battlefields, and on the day of Hunayn when your great numbers pleased you, but they availed you nothing… Then Allah sent down His tranquillity on His Messenger and the believers, and sent down forces you did not see' (9:25–26). The spoils were vast: six thousand captives, twenty-four thousand camels, more than forty thousand sheep and four thousand uqiyah of silver.
hunayn.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 26.

p: The defeated Thaqif retreated into their walled city of Ta'if. They had sealed the gates with weapons and food for a year. The Prophet ﷺ camped nearby with two tents for his wives Umm Salamah and Zaynab, where the main masjid of Ta'if stands today, and besieged the city for about eighteen nights, using the catapult and protective shields taken at Khaybar, but the walls were strong and the defenders shot volleys of arrows, and threw heated iron, killing several Muslims (about twelve fell at Hunayn and Ta'if, as reported). Khalid called for a champion to come out and duel, but no one would, and their leader Abd Yalil, who had driven the Prophet ﷺ out of Ta'if years before, shouted that they would never come down.

He announced that any slave who came down from the walls would be free, and about twenty did, including Abu Bakrah. When the siege brought no result, he consulted Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah, who said: 'They are a fox in its hole; if you stay you will catch it, if you leave it will not harm you.' Their aim, to break the army that had planned to attack them, was already achieved, so he lifted the siege. Asked to curse Thaqif, he prayed instead: 'O Allah, guide Thaqif and bring them' (Tirmidhi), just as, years before, he had refused the angel of the mountains' offer to crush them. Within a year they came to Madinah as Muslims.
taif-siege.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 26.
