p: Urwah ibn Mas'ud, a chief of Thaqif who had negotiated for Quraysh at Hudaybiyyah, was in Yemen during the siege of Ta'if. Afterwards he caught up with the Prophet ﷺ on the road to Madinah and accepted Islam. He asked to return and call his people. The Prophet ﷺ warned him: 'They will kill you.' Urwah said: 'They love me more than their own eyes.'

He returned to Ta'if and called Thaqif to Islam from the roof of his house at dawn. They shot him with arrows. Dying, he said: 'This is an honour Allah has given me, and a martyrdom He has led to me,' and asked to be buried with the martyrs who fell besieging Ta'if. The Prophet ﷺ said he was like the man in Surah Ya-Sin who called his people and was killed (Ibn Ishaq; Hayatus Sahaba 1:203, 219).
urwah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: The Prophet ﷺ brought the spoils of Hunayn to al-Ji'ranah and waited some days, hoping Hawazin would come as Muslims. Then he distributed them. He gave generously to the leaders of Quraysh and other new Muslims, such as Abu Sufyan, Safwan and Uyaynah, a hundred camels each, to win their hearts. Abu Sufyan received forty uqiyah of silver and a hundred camels, and his sons Yazid and Mu'awiyah the same; he said: 'You are generous in peace and in war.' Safwan, still not Muslim, gazed at a valley full of livestock, and the Prophet ﷺ gave it all to him. Hakim ibn Hizam asked, and was given; asked again, and was given; and a third time. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Hakim, this wealth is green and sweet. Whoever takes it without greed is blessed in it, and whoever takes it greedily is not blessed in it, like one who eats and is never full. The upper hand is better than the lower hand.' Hakim kept only the first share and swore never to take anything from anyone again; he refused even his due from Abu Bakr and Umar (Bukhari 1472). Before the distribution, Zayd ibn Thabit gathered the spoils; some had quietly taken small things, and the Prophet ﷺ warned that whatever was taken unlawfully would be fire on the Day of Judgement. Items were returned, and no one was named. Each soldier received four camels and forty sheep, and a horseman three shares, two for the horse. When a man said the distribution was unjust, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Who will be just if I am not?' Umar asked to kill him; he said: 'Perhaps he prays,' and 'I was not commanded to search people's hearts' (Bukhari). The Ansar received little and some among them grumbled.

He gathered the Ansar in a tent and said: 'O Ansar, did I not find you astray and Allah guided you through me, divided and Allah united you through me, poor and Allah enriched you through me?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger are most generous.' He said: 'If you wished you could say: you came to us rejected and we believed you, abandoned and we helped you… Are you not pleased, O Ansar, that people go home with sheep and camels while you go home with the Messenger of Allah? If all people took one valley and the Ansar another, I would take the valley of the Ansar.' They wept until their beards were wet, as if water had been poured on them, saying: 'We are pleased with the Messenger of Allah as our share' (Bukhari, Muslim). Because he returned with them, Madinah became the City of the Messenger, and a prayer in his masjid is better than a thousand elsewhere except the Sacred Masjid (Bukhari).

After more than ten days, a delegation of Hawazin came as Muslims, among them his foster-relatives from Banu Sa'd, reminding him of the women who had nursed him. He said: 'I was waiting for you,' and told them to choose either their families or their wealth; they chose their families. He returned at once the captives in his share and that of Banu Abd al-Muttalib, and told them to stand after Zuhr and ask the people; the Muhajirun and Ansar gave up theirs. A few refused, and he bought them back with compensation and returned them (Bukhari). He kept the family of Malik ibn Awf, honourably, until Malik came himself. Malik slipped out of Ta'if, came to al-Ji'ranah, accepted Islam and received his family and a hundred camels, and the Prophet ﷺ made him leader of the Muslims of his people. After about thirteen days at al-Ji'ranah he entered ihram there, performed Umrah by night, and returned to Madinah, about two and a half months after leaving it. The great tribal wars of Arabia were over.
jiranah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 26.

p: Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, son of a famous poet, had mocked the Prophet ﷺ and Islam in verse, and the Prophet ﷺ had declared his blood forfeit. His brother Bujayr, already Muslim, wrote warning him and urging him to come repentant.

Ka'b came to Madinah in disguise, sat before the Prophet ﷺ after Fajr and asked: 'If Ka'b came repentant and Muslim, would you accept him?' 'Yes.' 'I am Ka'b.' He then recited his ode Banat Su'ad, which includes the line: 'The Messenger is a sword from which light is sought, an Indian blade drawn from the swords of Allah.' It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ gave him his own cloak (burdah), which Mu'awiyah later bought from his family (Ibn Ishaq, al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim; Hayatus Sahaba 1:226).
kabzuhayr.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Muharram of 9 AH, Banu Tamim stopped tribes from paying zakat to the Prophet's collector. He sent Uyaynah ibn Hisn with fifty riders, who surprised them and took about fifty captives. Leaders of Banu Tamim then came to Madinah to negotiate; they called out loudly to the Prophet ﷺ from behind his rooms, leading to the revelation of the opening of Surah al-Hujurat (49:1–5), and they accepted Islam.
sr-tamim.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Safar of 9 AH, Qutbah ibn Amir led twenty men against Khath'am near Tabalah. They fought a hard battle in which many on both sides were wounded, and returned with livestock.
sr-tabalah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Awwal of 9 AH, ad-Dahhak ibn Sufyan al-Kilabi led a party to Banu Kilab to call them to Islam. They refused and fought; they were defeated. Ad-Dahhak's own father was among those who fought against him.
sr-kilab.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Akhir of 9 AH, news came that Abyssinian ships had been seen off the coast near Jeddah. The Prophet ﷺ sent Alqamah ibn Mujazziz with three hundred men; the raiders fled to sea.

On the way back, Alqamah let a group go ahead under Abdullah ibn Hudhafah, who was known for his humour. He lit a fire and ordered his men to jump into it, to test them; some were about to, until he stopped them, saying he was joking. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If anyone tells you to disobey Allah, do not obey him,' and 'Obedience is only in what is right' (Bukhari). Ibn Abbas linked 4:59 to Abdullah ibn Hudhafah.
sr-alqamah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: In Rabi' al-Akhir of 9 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Ali with 150 men to destroy al-Fuls, the idol of Tayy. They destroyed it and took captives, among them the sister of Adiyy ibn Hatim, son of Hatim at-Ta'i, the pagan Arab famed for generosity: it was said that with nothing left in his house he would slaughter the camel he rode rather than let a guest go hungry. Adiyy fled to Sham.

His sister told the Prophet ﷺ whose daughter she was; for her father's generosity he freed her, clothed her and provided for her journey. She went to Adiyy and urged him to go to Madinah. Adiyy came, a Christian of high rank, and was struck by the Prophet's humility: on the way he stopped a long time for an old woman who wanted to talk to him, and Adiyy thought, 'This is no king.' At his house he gave Adiyy his only cushion and sat on the floor. The Prophet ﷺ told him a woman would one day travel from al-Hirah to the Ka'bah fearing no one but Allah, and the treasures of Khosrow would be opened. He told him: 'Accept Islam and you will be safe.' Adiyy accepted Islam and lived to see both (Bukhari).
sr-fuls.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: In Rajab of 9 AH, traders coming from Sham brought news that the Byzantines were gathering an army to attack Madinah, alarmed by the rise of Islam and stung by Mu'tah. The Prophet ﷺ chose to meet them rather than be attacked at home. It was a time of extreme heat, drought and poverty, just as the dates were ripening. The Prophet ﷺ, who usually concealed his destination, announced it openly and called every able-bodied man, so people could prepare for the long march far to the north. Mounts were so few that up to eighteen men shared one camel in turns, and the Prophet ﷺ took his turn walking like the rest. It became known as the 'expedition of hardship' (Jaysh al-Usrah).

He urged the companions to spend. Uthman brought a hundred saddled camels, then another hundred, then another (some reports say up to nine hundred or a thousand), and a thousand dinars; the Prophet ﷺ turned the coins over in his lap and said: 'Nothing Uthman does after today will harm him' (Tirmidhi). Abu Bakr brought all his wealth, and when asked what he left for his family, said: 'Allah and His Messenger.' Umar brought half his wealth, hoping that day to outdo Abu Bakr, and said: 'I will never compete with him again' (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi). Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, Talhah, Muhammad ibn Maslamah and others gave large amounts. A poor man worked through the night for a measure of dates and brought half; the hypocrites laughed that Allah had no need of it, and called those who gave much show-offs, and Allah revealed 9:79 against those who mock the givers. The Prophet ﷺ never belittled any charity, however small. Hypocrites came with excuses and he excused them, until Allah said: 'May Allah pardon you; why did you excuse them before it became clear who was truthful?' (9:43–45). The weak, the sick and those with nothing to spend were excused, and so were those who came asking for mounts and, when told there were none, turned away weeping (9:91–92). 'Had it been near and easy gain, they would have followed you' (9:42). They told others, 'Do not go out in the heat'; Allah replied: 'The fire of Hell is hotter… let them laugh a little and weep much' (9:81–82), and called the believers: 'What is wrong with you, that you cling heavily to the earth?' (9:38).

About thirty thousand men marched north, with some ten thousand horses; six years earlier at Badr there had been 313 men and two horses. Abu Bakr carried the main banner, and az-Zubayr, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Abu Dujanah those of the Muhajirun, Aws and Khazraj, as reported. As men were reported missing, he would say: 'Leave him; if there is good in him, Allah will bring him to you, and if not, Allah has spared you of him.' Abu Dharr's camel gave out, so he carried his things on his back and walked; when a lone figure was seen approaching, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Be Abu Dharr,' and then: 'May Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, will die alone, and will be raised alone.' At al-Hijr, the ruins of the people of Thamud, he told them not to drink its water or use it in cooking, and to pass through weeping, lest what befell them befall the travellers (Bukhari). Soon after, in thirst and heat with no cloud in the sky, he prayed for rain; it poured until they drank and filled every container. When his camel strayed, a hypocrite sneered that a man who claimed news from heaven did not know where his camel was; the Prophet ﷺ said he knew only what Allah taught him, and that Allah had shown him the camel caught by its rein on a tree in a nearby valley, where they found it. He warned that a violent wind would blow that night and told them to stay seated and tie their camels; a man who stood was blown away to the mountains of Tayy (Muslim). When food ran low, Umar suggested pooling everyone's leftovers; he prayed over them, everyone ate, and they filled their containers (Muslim). Near Tabuk he told them not to touch the spring until he came. It was barely a trickle; he washed his face and hands in a little of its water and poured it back, and it gushed. He told Mu'adh: 'If you live long, you will see this place filled with gardens' (Muslim). Some hypocrites in the army said they had never seen people greedier or more cowardly in battle than these reciters. When asked, they said they were only joking; Allah revealed: 'Was it Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking? Make no excuse; you disbelieved after your belief' (9:65–66).

They reached Tabuk and camped there about twenty days. Hearing of the size of the Muslim army, the Byzantines withdrew and did not come out, and there was no battle. Rulers of Aylah, Jarba and Adhruh came, made treaties and agreed to pay jizyah in return for the Muslims' protection, and Khalid was sent to capture Ukaydir of Dumat al-Jandal. Mufti Menk explains jizyah as a tax for protection; when Muslim armies later could not protect a people, they returned it.

Large parts of Surah at-Tawbah were revealed about the expedition, exposing the hypocrites. Three sincere believers who had stayed behind without excuse, Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn ar-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayyah, told the truth and were boycotted for fifty days, until Allah accepted their repentance (9:118). Their story is told in its own event.
tabuk.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 27–28.

p: From Tabuk, the Prophet ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid with 420 riders to Ukaydir ibn Abd al-Malik, the Christian ruler of Dumat al-Jandal. He told Khalid: 'You will find him hunting wild cattle.' On a moonlit night a wild cow scratched at the gates of Ukaydir's fort; he rode out after it with his brother, and Khalid's men captured him. Ukaydir was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who spared him on condition of paying jizyah. The companions marvelled at his gold-embroidered brocade, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise are better than this' (Bukhari).
sr-ukaydir.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: In Rajab of 9 AH, the Negus Ashamah, King of Abyssinia, died. He had protected the Muslim emigrants for years and had accepted Islam secretly.

On the day he died, the Prophet ﷺ announced his death to the companions in Madinah, though no news had arrived: 'Your brother an-Najashi has died; pray for him.' He led them out to the prayer ground, lined them up in rows and prayed the funeral prayer over him in absentia with four takbirs (Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah). There was no one where he died to pray over him, which is why the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him in his absence.
negus.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: In Sha'ban of 9 AH, Umm Kulthum, the Prophet's daughter and wife of Uthman, died after six years of marriage. Uthman had married her after her sister Ruqayyah died at the time of Badr. The Prophet ﷺ sat by her grave with tears in his eyes. He said: 'If I had a third daughter, I would marry her to Uthman.' Of his daughters, only Fatimah now remained.
ummkulthum.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: After the Conquest of Makkah and Tabuk, the tribes of Arabia, who had been waiting to see the outcome between the Prophet ﷺ and Quraysh, came to Madinah in delegations to accept Islam. The year 9 AH became known as the Year of Delegations, with more than seventy delegations reported in all; some came to accept Islam, some to pledge, some to stay and learn, and some were a single man who went home and brought his whole people to Islam, and Surah an-Nasr describes people 'entering the religion of Allah in crowds'.

Delegations came from Thaqif, Banu Tamim, Banu Asad, Tayy, Hamdan, Kindah, the kings of Himyar and many more. The Prophet ﷺ received them in the masjid, at the pillar still known as the Pillar of Delegations, sent teachers back with them, and wrote letters setting out their duties. When the delegation of Kindah accepted Islam, he asked about the silk they wore around their necks, and they tore it off and threw it away at once; he had taught that gold and silk are forbidden to the men of his ummah (Abu Dawud, an-Nasa'i). Tamim ad-Dari, a former Christian who had lived in Palestine, came with his people and accepted Islam; he is remembered as the first to light lamps in the Prophet's ﷺ masjid. A delegation of Ghassan, the people whose governor had killed the Prophet's ﷺ envoy, also came and accepted Islam, as reported.
Banu Tamim came with their poet and orator to boast, and called out to him loudly from behind his rooms; the opening of Surah al-Hujurat taught manners with the Messenger (49:1–5).
wufud.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: Dimam ibn Tha'labah came from Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, tied his camel in the masjid and asked: 'Which of you is Ibn Abd al-Muttalib?' He said: 'I will ask you questions harshly; do not be offended.' Then he asked by Allah, one by one: 'Did Allah send you to all people? Did Allah command you that we pray five prayers? Fast this month? Take this charity from our rich and give it to our poor?' To each the Prophet ﷺ answered: 'By Allah, yes.'

Dimam said: 'I believe in what you have brought, and I am the messenger of my people.' As he left, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'If he is truthful, he will enter Paradise.' He went home, first condemned al-Lat and al-Uzza before his people, and by evening every man and woman of his tribe had accepted Islam (Bukhari, Muslim, from Anas; Hayatus Sahaba 1:215). Mufti Menk draws the lesson: never compromise the obligatory, and build up voluntary worship, which on the Day of Judgement will make up what is lacking in the obligatory (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi).
dimam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: The people of Ta'if, who had stoned the Prophet ﷺ in 619 and killed Urwah ibn Mas'ud, found themselves surrounded by Muslim tribes. In Ramadan of 9 AH Abd Yalil, who had rejected the Prophet ﷺ at Ta'if years before, came with a delegation of six. Al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah saw them first, and Abu Bakr ran ahead to give the Prophet ﷺ the good news. He pitched a tent for them in or beside the masjid so they could hear the Quran and watch the believers; for the first time, they listened.

Abd Yalil asked about fornication, usury and wine: their people were steeped in them and could not give them up. Each time the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse forbidding it, and said it was Allah's command, not his own. Then they reasoned among themselves: everyone here once did these things and left them, so we can too, and they accepted Islam. They asked to keep al-Lat for three years, then one year, then one month, and to be excused from prayer. He refused all of it except that they would not have to break their idol with their own hands. He sent Abu Sufyan and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah to destroy al-Lat. The people of Ta'if gathered, sure the idol would kill whoever struck it. Al-Mughirah, known for his humour, struck it and deliberately fell down; as they cried out, he jumped up laughing and told them it was only stone that could neither harm nor help even itself. Then they broke it apart, and Thaqif soon came fully to Islam. He appointed Uthman ibn Abi al-As, the youngest of them but the keenest to learn the Quran, as their leader.
thaqif.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: Wahshi, the Abyssinian slave who killed Hamzah at Uhud and was freed for it, stayed in Makkah, but his crime gave him no peace; by his own account he could not sleep and took to drink, and after the Conquest fled to Ta'if. When Ta'if sent its delegation, he was told the Prophet ﷺ did not harm envoys, and he came with them.

He stood before the Prophet ﷺ and declared the shahadah. The Prophet ﷺ asked: 'Are you Wahshi? Tell me how you killed Hamzah.' He told the story, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Can you keep your face away from me?' Wahshi stayed out of his sight. After the Prophet's death he fought at al-Yamamah and killed Musaylimah the false prophet with the same spear, saying: 'I killed the best of people and the worst of people' (Bukhari; Hayatus Sahaba 1:80).
wahshi.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 19.

p: Abdullah ibn Ubayy had been about to be crowned king of Madinah before the Prophet ﷺ arrived. He outwardly accepted Islam but led the hypocrites: he withdrew a third of the army at Uhud, spread the slander against Aisha, and said 'the honourable will expel the lowly'.

In Dhu al-Qa'dah of 9 AH he fell ill and died. His son Abdullah, a sincere believer, asked the Prophet ﷺ for his shirt to shroud him in and to pray over him. The Prophet ﷺ gave his shirt and stood to pray. Umar pulled at his garment: 'Will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you?' The Prophet ﷺ said Allah had given him a choice ('ask forgiveness for them or not', 9:80) and prayed over him.

Then Allah revealed: 'Never pray over any of them who dies, nor stand at his grave' (9:84), and he never prayed over a hypocrite again (Bukhari, from Ibn Umar and Umar). The Prophet ﷺ gave Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman the names of the hypocrites, and he kept the secret. Umar begged him only to say whether his own name was among them, and was told no; Umar would not pray the funeral prayer over anyone unless Hudhayfah prayed too.
ibnubayy.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: In Dhu al-Qa'dah of 9 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Bakr to lead the Hajj with three hundred Muslims; the idolaters still performed Hajj in their own way. The Prophet ﷺ did not go himself that year: pagans still circled the Ka'bah naked, men and women, sometimes in fulfilment of vows, and Quraysh would not go on to Arafah but stayed at Muzdalifah, making Hajj more a market and festival than worship. Abu Bakr taught the rites as they should be done and preached at Arafah, Mina and on the Day of Sacrifice. After he left, the opening ayat of Surah at-Tawbah (Bara'ah) were revealed, ending the treaties with the idolaters.

The Prophet ﷺ sent Ali after him to proclaim them, since such declarations were made by a member of the leader's own family. At Mina on the Day of Sacrifice, Ali and others proclaimed: 'After this year no idolater shall perform Hajj, and no one shall circle the House naked' (Bukhari). Treaties were not ended without notice: idolaters were given four months; after that, Hajj belonged to the Muslims alone, preparing the way for the Farewell Hajj.
abubakr-hajj.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: In 10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to Yemen to teach and judge, and later Ali as well. Before Mu'adh left, he walked beside his camel, giving advice: 'You are going to a People of the Book. First call them to bear witness that there is no god but Allah. If they accept, tell them Allah has prescribed five prayers… then zakat, taken from their rich and given to their poor. Beware of the prayer of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and Allah' (Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas). To both he said: 'Make things easy, not hard; give good news and do not drive people away' (Bukhari).

He asked Mu'adh how he would judge: 'By the Book of Allah.' 'If you do not find it there?' 'By the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah.' 'If not there?' 'I will strive to form my own judgement.' The Prophet ﷺ praised Allah for guiding his messenger's messenger (Abu Dawud). He also said: 'O Mu'adh, perhaps you will not meet me after this year; perhaps you will pass by my masjid and my grave.' Mu'adh wept. He never saw the Prophet ﷺ again.
yemen.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: In Rabi' al-Akhir of 10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b in Najran, telling him to call them to Islam for three days before any fighting. Khalid sent riders through the land calling: 'Accept Islam and you will be safe.' They accepted, and Khalid stayed to teach them. They sent a delegation to Madinah, led by Qays ibn al-Husayn.
sr-najran.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Each Ramadan, Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and reviewed the whole Quran with him. In his last Ramadan, 10 AH, Jibril reviewed it with him twice, and the Prophet ﷺ spent twenty days in i'tikaf instead of his usual ten.

He told Fatimah privately: 'Jibril used to review the Quran with me once a year, and this year he did it twice. I think my time has come.' She wept; then he told her she would be the first of his family to follow him, and she smiled (Bukhari, from Aisha). The final review is important to scholars, as it fixed the order of the Quran as it was later compiled.
lastramadan.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited.

p: Mariyah al-Qibtiyyah, sent as a gift by al-Muqawqis of Egypt, bore the Prophet ﷺ a son in 8 AH, his only child after Khadijah's. He named him Ibrahim after his forefather and gave him to a wet nurse in Awali, whose husband was a blacksmith; some suggest the smoke of the forge harmed the child.

In 10 AH, at about eighteen months, Ibrahim fell ill and died. The Prophet ﷺ held him as he breathed his last, and tears flowed from his eyes. Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf asked: 'Even you, O Messenger of Allah?' He blamed no one. He said: 'This is mercy that Allah places in the hearts of His servants' and: 'The eyes weep and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. We are saddened by your parting, Ibrahim' (Bukhari).

On the same day the sun eclipsed, and people said it was because of Ibrahim's death. He corrected them: 'The sun and moon are two signs of Allah; they do not eclipse for anyone's death or life. When you see that, pray and call upon Allah' (Bukhari, from al-Mughirah).
ibrahim.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: In Dhu al-Qa'dah of 10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ announced that he would perform Hajj, the only Hajj he made after the Hijrah. Hajj had been made obligatory on all who are able (3:97). People came from all over Arabia to accompany him and learn from him; reports put the crowd at a hundred thousand or more.

He left Madinah five days before the end of Dhu al-Qa'dah and spent the night at Dhul-Hulayfah, the miqat of Madinah. There he bathed, put on the two plain garments of ihram, perfumed himself, prayed, entered ihram for Hajj and Umrah together (qiran), mounted his camel and began the talbiyah: 'Labbayk Allahumma labbayk, labbayka la sharika laka labbayk, inna al-hamda wa an-ni'mata laka wal-mulk, la sharika lak.' The crowd around him stretched as far as the eye could see (Muslim 1218a, from Jabir).
hulayfah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: After eight days of travel, the Prophet ﷺ reached Makkah on 4 Dhu al-Hijjah and entered from the north after spending the night at Dhu Tuwa and bathing, and went to the Sacred Masjid. He kissed the Black Stone, performed seven circuits of tawaf, with his right shoulder uncovered, walking briskly in the first three, and prayed two rak'ahs behind Maqam Ibrahim reciting 'Take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer', with Surah al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in the two rak'ahs. He kissed the Stone again and drank Zamzam.

He then went to Safa, recited 'Indeed Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah' (2:158), saying 'I begin with what Allah began with', faced the Qiblah, declared Allah's oneness and supplicated, then walked seven times between the two hills, hastening in the valley bottom (marked today by green lights), praising and glorifying Allah on each. He told those who had not brought sacrificial animals to end their ihram after Umrah, and said: 'Had I known then what I know now, I would not have brought the sacrificial animals, and would have made it an Umrah'; they did (Muslim 1218a). Scholars differ over whether qiran, which he did, or tamattu', which he wished for, is better.
tawaf.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: On 8 Dhu al-Hijjah, the day of Tarwiyah, the Prophet ﷺ and the pilgrims went to Mina. He prayed Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha and the next Fajr there, shortening the four-rak'ah prayers. After sunrise on the 9th he set out for Arafah. Quraysh expected him to stop at Muzdalifah, as they used to, but he passed on to Arafah (Muslim 1218a).
tarwiyah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: On 9 Dhu al-Hijjah, a Friday, the Prophet ﷺ rode to Arafah and a tent was pitched for him at Namirah. After midday he rode his camel al-Qaswa into the valley of Uranah and addressed more than a hundred thousand people. Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah repeated his words so all could hear.

He said: 'O people, listen to my words, for I do not know whether I will meet you after this year in this place. Your blood, your property and your honour are sacred to one another, like the sacredness of this day, in this month, in this city.' On the Day of Sacrifice he asked them in turn: 'What day is this? Is it not the sacred day? Which month? Is it not the sacred month? Which city? Is it not the sacred city?' before saying the same (Bukhari). ' All the practices of jahiliyyah are under my feet. The blood feuds of jahiliyyah are abolished, beginning with the blood of Ibn Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith. The riba of jahiliyyah is abolished, beginning with that of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib; you are owed only your capital.' He warned: 'Do not turn back after me into disbelievers, striking one another's necks' (Bukhari).

'Fear Allah concerning women; you have taken them as a trust from Allah. They have rights over you and you over them. I leave among you something which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah' (Muslim); another narration adds 'and my Sunnah' (Malik, al-Hakim). ' You will be asked about me; what will you say?' They said: 'We bear witness that you conveyed, fulfilled and advised.' He raised his finger to the sky and pointed to the people, saying: 'O Allah, bear witness,' three times (Muslim 1218a). He told those present to convey his words to those absent.

He prayed Zuhr and Asr together, then stood by the rocks at the foot of the hill now called Jabal ar-Rahmah, without climbing it, facing the Qiblah in supplication for his ummah until sunset. On that day Allah revealed: 'This day I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as your religion' (5:3). A Jewish man told Umar: 'If that ayah had been revealed to us, we would have taken that day as a festival.' Umar said he knew exactly when and where it was revealed: on Friday at Arafah (Bukhari 45). It is reported that Umar wept when he heard it, saying that after completion there is only decline, sensing that the Prophet ﷺ would soon leave them.
farewell.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: After sunset on 9 Dhu al-Hijjah, the Prophet ﷺ left Arafah with Usamah riding behind him, urging the people: 'Calmly, calmly.' At Muzdalifah he prayed Maghrib and Isha together with one adhan and two iqamahs, and slept until dawn.

After praying Fajr early he went to al-Mash'ar al-Haram, where a masjid stands today, and stood in dua until the sky was bright, then moved on to Mina before sunrise, with al-Fadl ibn Abbas riding behind him. He allowed the weak and women to leave Muzdalifah earlier in the night (Muslim 1218a).
muzdalifah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: On 10 Dhu al-Hijjah, the Day of Sacrifice, the Prophet ﷺ had seven small pebbles gathered for him, as reported by Ibn Abbas, and threw them at Jamrat al-Aqabah, saying 'Allahu akbar' with each. He then sacrificed sixty-three camels with his own hand, one for each year of his life, and Ali sacrificed the rest of the hundred. He had his head shaved and prayed three times for those who shaved; asked about those who trimmed, he included them the fourth time (Bukhari). He then rode to Makkah for tawaf al-ifadah, drank Zamzam and returned to Mina.

He stayed in Mina for the days of tashriq, stoning the three jamarat each day after midday, and addressed the people again, repeating the sanctity of blood, property and honour. 'Learn your rites from me, for I may not perform Hajj after this year' (Muslim). It is reported that Surah an-Nasr was revealed in these days; the companions rejoiced, but when asked its meaning Ibn Abbas wept, which Ibn Abbas understood as a sign that his life's mission was complete. After the days of tashriq he made the farewell tawaf in Makkah and set out for Madinah.
mina.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: On the way back to Madinah, on 18 Dhu al-Hijjah, the Prophet ﷺ stopped at Ghadir Khumm, a pool near al-Juhfah between Makkah and Madinah, and addressed the companions.

Zayd ibn Arqam narrated that he praised Allah and said: 'O people, I am a man and the messenger of my Lord is about to come and I will answer. I leave among you two weighty things: the first is the Book of Allah, in which is guidance and light, so hold fast to it. And the people of my household; I remind you of Allah regarding the people of my household' (Muslim 2408a).

Other narrations (at-Tirmidhi, Ahmad) report that he took Ali's hand and said: 'Of whomever I am the mawla, Ali is his mawla.' Some companions returning from Yemen had complained about Ali's strictness, and scholars of the Ahl as-Sunnah understand the words as affirming love and support for Ali and his standing.

He spent the last night outside Madinah at Dhul-Hulayfah and sent word home that he was back. Entering in the morning he said: 'There is no god but Allah alone. He fulfilled His promise, helped His servant, and alone defeated the Confederates' (Bukhari). It was Dhu al-Hijjah of 10 AH.
ghadir.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: After returning from Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ heard that the Byzantines were again preparing to attack, and prepared an army to march toward Sham, where Zayd ibn Harithah had been martyred at Mu'tah. He appointed Zayd's son Usamah, not yet twenty, to command it, with senior companions including Umar under him.

Some objected to so young a commander. The Prophet ﷺ, already unwell, said from the minbar: 'If you question his command, you questioned his father's before him. By Allah, he was fit for command, and this one is among the dearest of people to me' (Bukhari). The army camped at al-Jurf outside Madinah, but when his illness grew worse, it waited. It set out only after his death, when Abu Bakr insisted on sending it.
usamah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: In his last months he often visited the martyrs' graves and al-Baqi', greeting them: 'Peace be upon you, dwellers of the abode of the believers; we will join you soon, if Allah wills' (Muslim). In late Safar of 11 AH, returning from a funeral at al-Baqi', the Prophet ﷺ fell ill with fever and headache, tying a cloth around his head as he did when it ached; the illness lasted under two weeks. He kept leading the prayers. In his last week he kept asking, 'Where will I be tomorrow?' until his wives, understanding, let him stay where he wished. He asked to be nursed in Aisha's room, a single small room like each of his wives', and walked there leaning on al-Abbas and Ali, his feet dragging.

Five days before his death the fever grew so high that he fainted. Waking, he asked for seven skins of water from different wells to be poured over him, then went out with his head bound and sat on the minbar. He said: 'Allah cursed the Jews and Christians, who took the graves of their prophets as places of worship. Do not make my grave an idol that is worshipped' (Bukhari, Malik). 'If I have struck anyone's back, here is my back; let him take his due.' A man said he was owed a few dirhams, and the Prophet ﷺ had them paid. He urged them to honour the Ansar, who would grow few. Then he said: 'Allah gave a servant the choice between this world and what is with Him, and he chose what is with Allah.' Abu Bakr wept, understanding that he meant himself. 'No one has done more for me in companionship and wealth than Abu Bakr. If I were to take a khalil, a most intimate friend, besides my Lord, I would take Abu Bakr' (Bukhari). Four days before, he again urged them: 'The prayer, the prayer,' and to hold to the Book of Allah and his Sunnah.

On Thursday night he fainted repeatedly while the people waited for Isha, each time asking whether they had prayed. Then he said: 'Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people,' and insisted though Aisha said her father was too tender-hearted. Abu Bakr led seventeen prayers in his lifetime. A day or two later, feeling a little better, he came out and prayed sitting beside Abu Bakr, who repeated the takbir aloud for the people. Three days before his death Jabir heard him say: 'None of you should die except thinking well of Allah' (Muslim). When a companion remarked on his pain, he said that the illness of a patient believer makes sins fall away as leaves fall from a tree (Bukhari). On his last Monday morning he lifted the curtain of his room, looked at the companions praying in rows behind Abu Bakr and smiled. Abu Bakr began to step back, but the Prophet ﷺ signed to him to continue; Aisha said it was as if he rejoiced to see his message fulfilled. They thought he had recovered. That morning he whispered to Fatimah and she wept, then whispered again and she laughed: first that he would not recover, then that she would be the first of his family to join him. He told her: 'There will be no more pain for your father after today' (Bukhari). He kissed Hasan and Husayn and asked the people to be kind to his family, advised his wives, and told Aisha he still felt the effect of the poisoned meat of Khaybar.

The day before, he freed his slaves, gave away his last six or seven coins in charity and gave his weapons to the Muslims; his armour was pledged with a Jewish man for some food. His last instructions were about prayer and those under one's authority. He rested his head on Aisha's chest; when her brother Abd ar-Rahman came in with a miswak, he looked at it; she softened it with her teeth and he used it. Dipping his hand in water and wiping his face, he said: 'La ilaha illa Allah; death has its agonies.' He raised his finger and his eyes. Aisha leaned close and heard: 'With those You have favoured, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69). O Allah, forgive me, have mercy on me and join me to the highest companion,' and he passed away (Bukhari 4463, 4440). Every prophet is shown his place in Paradise and given the choice before he dies. It was Monday, 12 Rabi' al-Awwal, 11 AH; he was 63. Anas said: 'The brightest day we saw was the day he entered Madinah, and the darkest was the day he died' (Tirmidhi).

The companions were stunned. Umar stood with his sword, saying the Prophet ﷺ had not died but had gone to his Lord like Musa and would return. Abu Bakr came from his house in as-Sunh, uncovered the Prophet's face, kissed his forehead and said: 'May my father and mother be sacrificed for you. How pure you were in life and in death. You will not taste death twice.' He told Umar to sit; Umar would not. He went out and said: 'Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died. Whoever worships Allah, Allah is alive and does not die,' and recited: 'Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?' (3:144). Umar said his legs gave way; it was as though people had never heard the ayah before (Bukhari 4452–4454).

On Tuesday he was washed three times with water and lotus leaves, without removing his clothes, by Ali, with al-Abbas and his sons turning him, and Usamah and the freed slave Shuqran pouring the water; Aws ibn Khawli of the Ansar was also present. He was shrouded in three white Yemeni sheets, and the companions prayed over him in groups of about ten, without an imam: first his relatives, then the Muhajirun, then the Ansar, then the women, then the children. Abu Bakr reported that prophets are buried where they die, so his bed was moved and a lahd (a grave with a side niche) was dug where he had died, in Aisha's room, where his grave now lies within al-Masjid an-Nabawi.
wafat.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: While the Prophet's family prepared his body, word came that the Ansar had gathered at the Saqifah (meeting hall) of Banu Sa'idah, today a small garden beside the King Abdulaziz Library in Madinah, to choose a leader, proposing Sa'd ibn Ubadah. Abu Bakr, Umar and Abu Ubaydah hurried there.

An Ansari speaker praised the Ansar's role and some proposed: 'A leader from us and a leader from you.' Abu Bakr spoke calmly, acknowledging all the Ansar's virtues, and said the Arabs would accept leadership only from Quraysh. He offered Umar or Abu Ubaydah. Umar said: 'Rather we pledge to you; you are our master, the best of us and the most beloved to the Messenger of Allah,' and took his hand and pledged. The Muhajirin and then the Ansar followed (Bukhari 6830). They recalled his closeness to the Prophet ﷺ: his companion in the cave, chosen to lead the prayer and to lead the Hajj.

The next day the general pledge was given in the masjid. Abu Bakr addressed the people: 'I have been given authority over you, though I am not the best of you. If I do well, help me; if I do wrong, correct me. Truthfulness is a trust, and lying is betrayal. The weak among you is strong with me until I take back his right, and the strong among you is weak with me until I take the right from him. Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger; if I disobey them, you owe me no obedience' (Ibn Ishaq; Hayatus Sahaba 2:50–58, 3:439).

Ali and Banu Hashim delayed their pledge while caring for Fatimah, and Ali gave it publicly later (Bukhari). Abu Bakr was given the title Khalifat Rasul Allah, the successor of the Messenger of Allah.
saqifah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 29.

p: The Prophet's death shook Arabia, and many tribes turned away. Senior companions urged Abu Bakr to keep Usamah's army in Madinah to defend the city, or at least to replace the young commander.

Abu Bakr refused: 'By Allah, I will not untie a knot the Messenger of Allah tied. Even if dogs dragged the wives of the Prophet ﷺ by their feet, I would send it.' When Umar conveyed the request to replace Usamah, Abu Bakr seized his beard: 'The Messenger of Allah appointed him, and you tell me to remove him?'

He walked beside Usamah as the army left while Usamah rode, and asked his permission to keep Umar in Madinah. The army raided the borders of Sham and returned safely after about forty days. The tribes concluded that the Muslims must still be strong, and some held back from rebellion.
usamah-returns.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Fatimah never recovered from her grief at the Prophet's passing. He had told her privately in his last illness that she would be the first of his family to join him, and that she was the leader of the women of Paradise, and she had smiled (Muslim 2450a; Bukhari).
She died about six months after him, at about 28 or 29. Ali buried her at night, as she had wished, and prayed over her. Their children al-Hasan, al-Husayn, Zaynab and Umm Kulthum were young.
fatimah-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After the Prophet's death, much of Arabia rebelled. Some tribes left Islam altogether. Others followed false prophets who had appeared in his last days: Musaylimah in Yamamah, Tulayhah among Banu Asad, al-Aswad al-Ansi in Yemen and Sajah among Tamim. Others kept the prayer but refused to pay zakat to Madinah. Only Madinah, Makkah, Ta'if and a few loyal tribes held firm.

Umar and others advised Abu Bakr to be lenient with those refusing zakat, since they still prayed. Abu Bakr said: 'By Allah, I will fight whoever separates prayer and zakat, for zakat is the right of wealth. By Allah, if they withhold even a hobbling cord they used to give the Messenger of Allah, I will fight them for it.' Umar later said: 'Then I saw that Allah had opened Abu Bakr's heart to fighting, and I knew it was right' (Bukhari 6924).

Abu Bakr repelled tribes that attacked Madinah, then sent out eleven armies under commanders including Khalid ibn al-Walid, Ikrimah, Shurahbil ibn Hasanah, al-Ala' al-Hadrami and Amr ibn al-As. Within about a year Arabia was united again under Islam.
riddah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: The most dangerous of the false prophets was Musaylimah of Banu Hanifah in Yamamah, with an army of some forty thousand. Two Muslim armies were defeated before Abu Bakr sent Khalid ibn al-Walid.

The battle at Aqraba' was the fiercest of the riddah wars. The Muslims wavered at first; Thabit ibn Qays dug himself in up to his knees and fought to the death, and the ranks were reorganised by tribe so each knew where its weakness lay. Musaylimah's men retreated into a walled garden, later called the Garden of Death. Al-Bara' ibn Malik had himself thrown over the wall to open the gate.

Musaylimah was killed by Wahshi's spear, the same that had killed Hamzah. Hundreds of Muslims were martyred, among them many who had memorised the Quran, which led directly to its compilation (Hayatus Sahaba 1:517, 546).
yamamah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After al-Yamamah, where many huffaz were martyred, Umar came to Abu Bakr and said: 'I fear that more reciters will be killed in other battles and much of the Quran will be lost. I suggest you order the Quran to be collected.' Abu Bakr said: 'How can I do something the Messenger of Allah did not do?' Umar kept urging until Allah opened Abu Bakr's heart to it.

They called Zayd ibn Thabit, the young scribe of revelation. Zayd said: 'By Allah, if they had asked me to move a mountain, it would not have been heavier than this.' He gathered the Quran from palm stalks, flat stones, pieces of leather and bone, and from the memories of men, accepting each written passage only with two witnesses that it had been written in the Prophet's presence. He found the last ayat of Surah at-Tawbah only with Abu Khuzaymah al-Ansari (Bukhari 4986).
The complete copy (the suhuf) stayed with Abu Bakr until his death, then with Umar, then with Hafsah, and was later used by Uthman to make the standard copies.
quran-compiled.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After the riddah wars, Abu Bakr sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to Iraq, then under Sasanian Persia, joining al-Muthanna ibn Harithah, who had been raiding the border. Khalid wrote to the Persian commander Hurmuz: 'Accept Islam and you will be safe, or accept protection and pay jizyah; otherwise I have brought you people who love death as you love life' (Hayatus Sahaba 1:227–228).

In a series of battles in 633, at Kazimah (the Battle of Chains), al-Madhar, al-Walajah and Ullays, Khalid defeated the Persians and their Arab allies. Al-Hirah, the Arab capital of Iraq, made a treaty and paid jizyah; Khalid called its leaders to Islam first (Hayatus Sahaba 1:233). He then took al-Anbar and Ayn at-Tamr.
iraq.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In 634, Abu Bakr sent four armies to Sham under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, Shurahbil ibn Hasanah, Amr ibn al-As and Abu Ubaydah. He walked beside Yazid as he left and advised him: 'Do not kill a woman, a child or an old man. Do not cut down fruit trees or destroy buildings. You will pass people who have devoted themselves to worship in hermitages; leave them' (Hayatus Sahaba 1:434; Malik's Muwatta).

As the Byzantines gathered a huge force, Abu Bakr ordered Khalid from Iraq to Sham. Khalid crossed the waterless desert in a famous march, watering the camels and then slaughtering them for the water in their stomachs. The armies united and defeated the Byzantines at Ajnadayn in Palestine in Jumada al-Ula, 13 AH, the first great battle with Rome.
ajnadayn.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In Jumada al-Akhirah of 13 AH, Abu Bakr fell ill with fever after bathing on a cold day. He consulted senior companions about appointing Umar. Some feared Umar's harshness; Abu Bakr said: 'He was harsh because he saw me soft; when the matter is his, he will soften.' He dictated his appointment of Umar to Uthman (Hayatus Sahaba 2:68, 152).

He advised Umar: 'Fear Allah, Umar. Allah has deeds by day that He does not accept at night, and deeds by night He does not accept by day.' He asked that the stipend he had taken from the treasury be repaid from his land, and that he be shrouded in his own worn garments: 'The living need new clothes more than the dead.' His last words included: 'Make me die a Muslim and join me with the righteous' (Hayatus Sahaba 3:74).
He died at 63, the same age as the Prophet ﷺ, after two years and three months as Khalifah. He was buried beside the Prophet ﷺ in Aisha's room, his head at the level of the Prophet's shoulders.
abubakr-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Early in Umar's khilafah, he sent Abu Ubayd ath-Thaqafi to Iraq. In Sha'ban of 13 AH, at the Euphrates near al-Hirah, the Persian commander offered him the choice of crossing the river. Against advice, Abu Ubayd crossed by a bridge of boats.

The Persians attacked with elephants, which terrified the Arab horses. Abu Ubayd tried to cut the trunk of the white elephant and was crushed. A man cut the bridge to stop the retreat, and many drowned. Al-Muthanna held the rear and saved part of the army. It was the heaviest defeat of the conquests, and Umar comforted the survivors.
bridge.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After Ajnadayn, the Muslim armies besieged Damascus for several months. In 14 AH (635), Khalid entered from one side by force at night, while Abu Ubaydah, at another gate, accepted the city's surrender on terms. The commanders agreed to apply the peace terms to the whole city.
Its people were granted safety for their lives, property and churches in return for jizyah. Damascus became the centre of Muslim Sham.
damascus.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Heraclius gathered a massive army, reports say well over a hundred thousand, to drive the Muslims from Sham. The Muslims withdrew from Damascus and Homs, returning the jizyah they had collected since they could no longer protect those cities, and gathered about thirty-six thousand men at the Yarmuk river.

Before the battle, the Byzantine commander Jarajah rode out and asked Khalid why he was called the Sword of Allah. Khalid explained Islam to him; Jarajah accepted Islam and fought on the Muslim side until he was martyred (Hayatus Sahaba 1:234). Women such as Asma bint Yazid fought and drove back fleeing men (Hayatus Sahaba 1:571).

The battle lasted six days in Rajab 15 AH (August 636). Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and four hundred men pledged to fight to the death and most were martyred. On the last day the Muslim cavalry cut off the Byzantine retreat, and their army broke and fell into the ravine.

As al-Harith ibn Hisham, Ikrimah and Ayyash lay dying, water was brought to the first; he signalled to give it to the next, who signalled to the third, and all three died without drinking (Hayatus Sahaba 1:331). Heraclius left Sham, saying: 'Farewell, Syria, a farewell with no meeting after it.' Sham was opened to Islam.
yarmuk.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 1.

p: Umar sent Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas to Iraq with about thirty thousand men. The Persian commander Rustam faced them at al-Qadisiyyah with a much larger army and war elephants. Umar told Sa'd to call the Persians to Islam for three days before fighting (Hayatus Sahaba 1:236).

Envoys went to Rustam. Al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah sat beside him on his throne and was pulled down; he said: 'We Arabs are equal; we do not enslave one another.' Rib'i ibn Amir rode into the decorated tent on his horse, in simple clothes, leaning on his spear and cutting the carpets. Asked why they had come, he said: 'Allah has sent us to bring whomever He wills from the worship of servants to the worship of Allah, from the narrowness of this world to its vastness, and from the injustice of religions to the justice of Islam' (Hayatus Sahaba 1:237–239).

The battle lasted three or four days. Sa'd, ill with boils, directed it from a castle. Al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr arrived with reinforcements; the elephants were blinded and driven back. On the last day Rustam was killed and the Persian army fled (Hayatus Sahaba 1:440–441). The way to the Persian capital was open.
qadisiyyah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After al-Qadisiyyah, Sa'd marched on al-Mada'in (Ctesiphon), the Sasanian capital on the Tigris. The Persians destroyed the bridges. Sa'd prayed and led his army into the flooded river on horseback, reciting 'Allah is sufficient for us'; they crossed, and it is said not one man was lost (Hayatus Sahaba 3:604).

The Persian king Yazdegerd fled. Sa'd entered the white palace of Khosrow, prayed eight rak'ahs of victory, and recited: 'How many gardens and springs they left behind…' (44:25). Before entering, Salman al-Farisi called the people of al-Qasr al-Abyad to Islam for three days (Hayatus Sahaba 1:236). The vast treasures, including Khosrow's carpet, were sent to Umar.
madain.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After Yarmuk, Abu Ubaydah and Amr ibn al-As besieged Jerusalem. Its patriarch Sophronius agreed to surrender only to the Khalifah himself. Umar travelled from Madinah with a single camel and one servant, taking turns to ride; it was the servant's turn as they reached the city, so Umar entered leading the camel on foot, his clothes patched (Hayatus Sahaba 2:573).
When Abu Ubaydah suggested he wear finer clothes to impress the Romans, Umar said: 'We are a people whom Allah honoured with Islam; if we seek honour in anything else, Allah will humiliate us.'

He granted the people a covenant of safety for their lives, property, churches and crosses, and they would not be forced in religion. Invited to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, he declined, so that Muslims would not later claim it as a masjid. He cleared the rubbish from the site of the Temple Mount and prayed there, where a masjid was later built.
jerusalem.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: As the state grew, letters arrived undated or with confusing dates. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari wrote to Umar: 'Letters come to us from you without dates.' Umar gathered the companions to choose a starting point for a calendar.

Some suggested the Prophet's birth, others his first revelation or his death. Ali suggested the Hijrah, the moment that separated truth from falsehood, and the companions agreed. They chose Muharram as the first month, as the month the pilgrims returned from Hajj. Years have been counted from the Hijrah, AH (Anno Hegirae), ever since.
hijri.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In 18 AH a severe drought struck Arabia for nine months; the land turned ash-coloured, so it was called the Year of Ramadah (ashes). Bedouins flooded into Madinah. Umar organised relief, wrote to his governors in Egypt, Sham and Iraq for food, and fed thousands daily. He swore not to eat meat, butter or milk until the people could; he ate bread and oil until his skin darkened. He led the prayer for rain with al-Abbas, and rain came.

In the same year, plague struck Sham at Amwas. Umar was travelling there; at Sargh he heard of it and, after consulting, decided to turn back. Abu Ubaydah asked: 'Are you fleeing from Allah's decree?' Umar said: 'Yes, from Allah's decree to Allah's decree,' and Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf reported the Prophet's instruction not to enter or leave a land of plague (Bukhari; Hayatus Sahaba 2:125).

Umar wrote asking Abu Ubaydah to come to Madinah; he understood the intent and declined to leave his men. Abu Ubaydah died, advising the Muslims at his death in Jordan (Hayatus Sahaba 2:166). Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who called the plague a mercy and a martyrdom (Hayatus Sahaba 2:594), died after him, as did about twenty-five thousand others.
ramadah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After the Prophet's death, Bilal could not bear to call the adhan in Madinah; he broke down at 'Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah'. He asked to go to Sham to fight in Allah's cause.

It is reported that when Umar visited Sham, the people asked Bilal to call the adhan once more; when he did, everyone wept, remembering the Prophet ﷺ. As he lay dying in Damascus his wife cried 'What grief!', and he said: 'What joy! Tomorrow I will meet the beloved ones, Muhammad and his companions.' He was buried in Damascus.
bilal-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: With the treasures of Persia and Rome reaching Madinah, Umar set up a register (diwan) in about 20 AH, recording every Muslim's name and a yearly stipend from the treasury, based on the Persian model.

He began with the Prophet's family, al-Abbas first, then the people of Badr, then those who accepted Islam before Hudaybiyyah, and so on, giving precedence for early Islam and sacrifice rather than tribe. The Prophet's wives received the highest stipends, Aisha most of all. When people suggested he put his own family first, he refused: 'Begin with the relatives of the Messenger of Allah, and put Umar where Allah put him.' Even infants were given a stipend from birth.
diwan.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Amr ibn al-As persuaded Umar to let him march on Egypt and set out with about four thousand men in 639. After capturing al-Farama and other towns, he besieged the great fortress of Babylon (near today's Cairo) for seven months, with reinforcements under az-Zubayr, who climbed its wall. Before fighting, Amr called the Romans to Islam (Hayatus Sahaba 1:245).

Alexandria, the second city of the Roman empire, surrendered by treaty in 21 AH (641–642) after a long siege (Hayatus Sahaba 1:252). Amr founded the city of al-Fustat by his tent, where the Masjid of Amr ibn al-As still stands. The Coptic Christians, persecuted under Byzantine rule, were given protection and freedom of worship.

A story is reported that the Nile used to be given a girl in sacrifice each year until Umar wrote a letter to be thrown into it, and it flowed without a sacrifice; its chain is weak (Hayatus Sahaba 3:601).
egypt.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Early in his khilafah, Umar removed Khalid from supreme command in Sham and placed Abu Ubaydah over him, saying he feared people would think victory came from Khalid rather than from Allah. Khalid served under Abu Ubaydah without complaint.

Khalid died in his bed in Homs in about 21 AH. He said: 'I have fought in a hundred battles, and there is no part of my body without a sword, spear or arrow wound, yet here I am dying in my bed like a camel. May the eyes of cowards never sleep.' He left only his horse, his weapons and a slave, all given in the cause of Allah. Umar wept for him.
khalid-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Yazdegerd made a final effort to recover Persia, gathering an army said to number 150,000 at Nahawand in the Zagros mountains. Umar wished to lead the Muslims himself, but Ali advised him to stay in Madinah as the centre of the ummah. He appointed an-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin.

The Persians stayed behind their trenches. The Muslims feigned a retreat, drew them out, and then turned. An-Nu'man was killed early in the battle; his brother covered him with a cloak and carried the banner so the army would not lose heart. The Persians were routed. Umar wept at the news of an-Nu'man's death (Hayatus Sahaba 2:487). The Muslims called it the 'victory of victories', since after it the Persian empire never again fielded a great army.
nahawand.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: As new cities grew, Umar sent companions to teach the Quran and Sunnah. To Kufa he sent Ammar ibn Yasir as governor and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud as teacher and treasurer, writing: 'I have preferred you over myself by sending Abdullah.' Ibn Mas'ud founded the school of learning in Kufa, from which Abu Hanifah's teachers came.

To Basrah he sent Imran ibn Husayn and others; Abu Musa al-Ash'ari taught the Quran in its great masjid. To Sham he sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ubadah ibn as-Samit and Abu ad-Darda, who spread out to Homs, Damascus and Palestine (Hayatus Sahaba 3:238, 268).
teachers.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In Dhu al-Hijjah of 23 AH, as Umar led the Fajr prayer, Abu Lu'lu'ah Fayruz, a Persian slave of al-Mughirah, stabbed him several times with a two-headed dagger and stabbed others before killing himself. Umar pulled Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf forward to finish the prayer (Bukhari 3700).

Told who had stabbed him, Umar said: 'Praise be to Allah, who did not make my death at the hands of a man claiming Islam.' He sent his son to ask Aisha's permission to be buried beside his two companions; she gave up the place she had kept for herself. Ali, among others, praised him at his deathbed (Hayatus Sahaba 3:92).

Asked to name a successor, he named six of the companions with whom the Prophet ﷺ was pleased when he died: Uthman, Ali, Talhah, az-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, to choose one among themselves within three days, with his son Abdullah present only as an adviser. He advised his successor to look after the Muhajirin, the Ansar, the people of the cities and the dhimmis. He died three days later, after ten and a half years as Khalifah, and was buried beside the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr. Abu Talhah said on that day that every Muslim household had lost something (Hayatus Sahaba 2:489).
umar-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: The council of six met. Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf withdrew his own name and offered to choose for them, and they agreed. For three days and nights he consulted the people of Madinah, the companions, the army commanders and even travellers, hardly sleeping.

On the morning of 1 Muharram 24 AH, after Fajr in the masjid, he called Ali and asked whether he would rule by the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger and the practice of the two Khalifahs before him. Ali said he would act by his own ability and judgement. He asked Uthman, who said yes. Abd ar-Rahman pledged allegiance to Uthman, and Ali and all the people followed (Bukhari 7207; Hayatus Sahaba 1:273).
uthman-khilafah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In 27 AH Uthman sent Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi as-Sarh, governor of Egypt, west into Ifriqiya (today's Tunisia) with an army that included young companions such as Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, Abdullah ibn Umar and Abdullah ibn Amr.

The Byzantine governor Gregory met them near Sbeitla with a large army and offered his daughter and a fortune to whoever killed the Muslim commander. Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr led a surprise attack in the heat of the afternoon, killed Gregory and won the battle. The cities paid a large sum for peace, and the way west was opened.
ifriqiya.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Years earlier, the Prophet ﷺ had slept at the house of Umm Haram bint Milhan and woke smiling. He said he had seen people of his ummah sailing the sea in the cause of Allah 'like kings on thrones'. She asked him to pray that she be among them, and he said she would be among the first (Bukhari 2894).

Mu'awiyah, governor of Sham, had long asked to build a navy; Umar refused, fearing for the Muslims at sea. Uthman allowed it, on condition that only volunteers went. In 28 AH the first Muslim fleet sailed to Cyprus, and the island agreed to pay tribute. Umm Haram sailed with her husband Ubadah ibn as-Samit; on the island she fell from her mount and died, fulfilling the prophecy. Her grave is in Cyprus.
cyprus.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: As Islam spread, people in different lands recited the Quran in different dialects and readings and began to dispute which was correct. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, returning from campaigns in Armenia and Azerbaijan, came to Uthman alarmed: 'O Commander of the Believers, save this ummah before they differ over the Book as the Jews and Christians differed' (Bukhari 4987).

Uthman sent for the volume compiled under Abu Bakr, kept by Hafsah. He appointed Zayd ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As and Abd ar-Rahman ibn al-Harith to copy it, telling them that where they differed they should write it in the dialect of Quraysh, in which it was revealed. Copies were sent to Kufa, Basrah, Sham, Makkah and other centres, each with a reciter, and other private copies were burned.

Ali said: 'Do not say anything about Uthman except good. By Allah, he did what he did with the Mushaf only after consulting all of us.' The Uthmani rasm (script) is the basis of every copy of the Quran today.
mushaf.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After Nahawand, Muslim armies advanced across Persia, taking Isfahan, Fars, Kirman and Khurasan. Yazdegerd III, the last Sasanian king, fled from city to city with his court.

In 31 AH (651), at Merv in Khurasan, he was killed, reportedly by a miller in whose mill he hid, after his own governor turned against him. With his death the Sasanian empire, which had ruled Persia for over four centuries, came to an end, fulfilling the Prophet's words that the treasures of Khosrow would be spent in the path of Allah.
yazdegerd.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Abu Dharr, known for his asceticism and outspokenness, criticised the hoarding of wealth in Sham and Madinah, and asked Uthman's permission to live apart at ar-Rabadhah, a desert place outside Madinah.

The Prophet ﷺ had told him: 'May Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, will die alone and will be raised alone' (reported). In 32 AH he lay dying at ar-Rabadhah with only his wife and a servant, who had no cloth to shroud him. He told them a group of believers would come. A caravan from Iraq arrived, among them Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who wept, recalled the Prophet's words, and buried him (Hayatus Sahaba 3:106).
abudharr-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Salman al-Farisi had travelled from Persia through Sham searching for the true religion, was enslaved, and found the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Salman is one of us, the people of the house.'

As governor of al-Mada'in under Umar he received a large stipend but gave it all away, lived on what he earned by weaving palm leaves, and owned no house. As he lay dying, between 33 and 36 AH, he wept, saying the Prophet ﷺ had told them each should have of this world no more than a traveller's provisions, and he had around him a few utensils (Hayatus Sahaba 2:294, 3:68).
salman-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In about 34 AH (some say 31), the Byzantine emperor Constans II led a great fleet of several hundred ships against the young Muslim navy of Egypt and Sham under Abdullah ibn Sa'd off the coast of Lycia (southern Anatolia).

The Muslims tied their ships to the Byzantine ships so the fight became like a land battle, and fought hand to hand. The sea was said to turn red. The Byzantine fleet was defeated and Constans barely escaped. It was called Dhat as-Sawari, the Battle of the Masts, and it ended Byzantine control of the eastern Mediterranean.
masts.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: In Uthman's later years, groups from Egypt, Kufa and Basrah, stirred by complaints against some of his governors and by agitators, came to Madinah. Uthman answered their objections; they left, then returned claiming to have intercepted a letter ordering their punishment, which he swore he had not written.

They besieged his house for about forty days, even blocking water to the man who had bought the well of Rumah for the Muslims. Ali sent al-Hasan and al-Husayn to guard his door, and the companions offered to fight. Uthman refused: 'I will not be the first Khalifah to shed blood in the ummah of Muhammad,' and told them to go home (Hayatus Sahaba 2:411–412). He addressed the besiegers from his house, reminding them of his service, and gave his final address (Hayatus Sahaba 2:160, 3:470).

He had seen the Prophet ﷺ in a dream telling him he would break his fast with them. On Friday 18 Dhu al-Hijjah 35 AH he was fasting and reading the Quran when rebels broke in and killed him; his blood fell on the ayah 'Allah will suffice you against them' (2:137). His wife Na'ilah lost her fingers trying to protect him. The Prophet ﷺ had said of him: 'Shall I not be shy of a man of whom the angels are shy?' (Muslim).
uthman-martyr.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After Uthman's martyrdom, Madinah was in turmoil. The people turned to Ali, the most senior of the remaining council of six. He was reluctant, saying he would rather be an adviser than a ruler, but accepted when they insisted. The pledge was given in the masjid (Hayatus Sahaba 3:470 for his first address).

The most pressing question was justice for Uthman. Ali held that the state must first be stabilised before the killers, many mixed among the armies, could be pursued. Talhah, az-Zubayr and Aisha, and Mu'awiyah in Sham, wanted retribution first. This difference, held sincerely on both sides according to the Ahl as-Sunnah, led to the tragic events of the following years.
ali-khilafah.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman was the keeper of the Prophet's secret: the Prophet ﷺ had told him the names of the hypocrites of Madinah. Umar would watch whose funeral Hudhayfah attended before praying over anyone.

He served as governor of al-Mada'in. He died about forty days after Uthman's martyrdom, early in Ali's khilafah, having warned the people of the trials to come. On his deathbed he said: 'Welcome, death; a beloved has come at a time of need' (Hayatus Sahaba 3:77).
hudhayfah-death.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Talhah, az-Zubayr and Aisha went to Basrah with a group seeking to bring Uthman's killers to justice. Ali marched from Madinah to meet them. Negotiations through al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr nearly brought agreement, and both sides went to sleep expecting peace.

According to the historians, those involved in Uthman's killing, fearing a settlement, attacked both camps at night, each side believing the other had broken the agreement. Battle broke out in Jumada al-Akhirah of 36 AH, around the camel carrying Aisha's litter, which gave the battle its name. Az-Zubayr, reminded by Ali of a saying of the Prophet ﷺ, left the field and was killed treacherously on his way home. Talhah was killed by an arrow. When the camel was brought down the fighting ended.

Ali ordered that no one fleeing be pursued, no wounded man killed, and no property taken (Hayatus Sahaba 2:474). He prayed over the dead of both sides, and spoke of the other side as brothers who had rebelled against him (Hayatus Sahaba 2:475). He sent Aisha back to Madinah with honour, escorted by forty women of Basrah, and she later said she wished she had not gone out.
jamal.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After the Battle of the Camel, Ali moved his capital from Madinah to Kufa in Iraq in Rajab of 36 AH, to be nearer the centre of the eastern armies and the conflict with Sham. Kufa, founded under Umar, had many companions and a strong tradition of learning from Ibn Mas'ud.
He refused to live in the governor's palace, calling it the palace of ruin, and lived simply among the people. His sermons in Kufa were remembered for their eloquence (Hayatus Sahaba 3:479).
kufa.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Sham since Umar's time and a relative of Uthman, refused to give his pledge to Ali until Uthman's killers were punished. In 37 AH the two armies met at Siffin on the upper Euphrates.

For weeks they negotiated and skirmished, and in Safar a great battle was fought over several days. Thousands were killed on both sides, among them Ammar ibn Yasir, fighting for Ali; the Prophet ﷺ had said 'Ammar will be killed by the rebellious group' (Muslim).

When Ali's side seemed close to victory, soldiers of Sham raised copies of the Quran on their spears, calling for the Book of Allah to judge. Many in Ali's army demanded he accept; he agreed to arbitration. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari represented Ali and Amr ibn al-As represented Mu'awiyah. When they met at Dumat al-Jandal (or Adhruh) months later, the arbitration ended without resolving the dispute. The Ahl as-Sunnah hold that both sides were companions striving by their understanding, while Ali was in the right.
siffin.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: A group in Ali's army who had first demanded the arbitration then rejected it, declaring: 'Judgement belongs to Allah alone,' and that anyone who accepted human arbitration had disbelieved, including Ali. They withdrew to Harura' and then to an-Nahrawan, and were called the Khawarij (those who went out).

Ali debated them and sent Ibn Abbas, who brought back thousands. The rest began killing Muslims who disagreed with them; they murdered the companion Abdullah ibn Khabbab and his pregnant wife. Ali then fought them at an-Nahrawan in 38 AH and nearly all were killed.

Ali searched among the dead for a man with a deformed arm whom the Prophet ﷺ had described, and when he was found, Ali said 'Allahu akbar' and prostrated.
