The Prophet ﷺ had described the Khawarij as people who recite the Quran but it does not go beyond their throats, and who pass through the religion as an arrow passes through its target (Muslim 1066a).
nahrawan.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Three of the Khawarij plotted to kill Ali, Mu'awiyah and Amr ibn al-As on the same night. Only the attack on Ali succeeded. On 19 Ramadan 40 AH, as Ali went out to wake people for Fajr in Kufa, Abd ar-Rahman ibn Muljam struck him on the head with a poisoned sword.

Ali told his family not to kill anyone but the attacker, and if he survived, he would decide himself whether to forgive. He gave his last advice to al-Hasan and al-Husayn: to fear Allah, pray, give zakat, care for orphans and neighbours, and never abandon enjoining good. He died on 21 Ramadan, aged about 63, after nearly five years as Khalifah.
ali-martyr.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: After Ali's death, the people of Kufa pledged allegiance to al-Hasan. For about six months he ruled, while Mu'awiyah ruled Sham. As the armies faced each other, al-Hasan, seeing that his own followers were divided and that war would cost thousands of Muslim lives, chose peace.

In Rabi' al-Awwal of 41 AH he handed the khilafah to Mu'awiyah on conditions including the safety of the people of Iraq and Hijaz. The Muslims were united under one ruler again, and the year was called Am al-Jama'ah, the Year of Unity. Some of his supporters reproached him; he replied that he had done it to spare the blood of the ummah (Hayatus Sahaba 2:420, 3:486).

It fulfilled the Prophet's words from the minbar, with al-Hasan beside him: 'This son of mine is a sayyid; perhaps through him Allah will reconcile two great groups of Muslims' (Bukhari 2704). It also completed the thirty years of the Rightly Guided Khilafah mentioned in the hadith of Safinah: 'The khilafah will be for thirty years, then there will be kingship' (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi).
hasan-peace.src: Written from the standard histories (at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah, Ibn Sa'd) and the hadith cited.

p: Zamzam first gushed for Hajar and the infant Isma'il, when she ran seven times between Safa and Marwah searching for water. Over the centuries it silted up with floods, and it was filled in and forgotten when the tribe of Jurhum was driven out of Makkah. So Abd al-Muttalib's digging was its second appearance, not its first. In his time no one knew where it lay.

Abd al-Muttalib was sleeping in the Hijr beside the Ka'bah when he saw a dream telling him to dig 'Taybah'. He asked what it was, and the dream ended. On following nights he was told to dig 'Barrah' and then 'al-Madnunah', each time without explanation. On the fourth night he was told: 'Dig Zamzam,' a well that would never run dry and would give water to the pilgrims, and he was shown its place.

He began digging with his only son at the time, al-Harith. When he struck water he cried 'Allahu akbar'. The men of Quraysh gathered and claimed a share: 'It is the well of our father Isma'il; we have a right to it.' He refused, saying it had been given to him alone in his dream.

They agreed to take the dispute to a soothsayer of Banu Sa'd Hudhaym on the way to Sham. In the desert their water ran out, and believing they would die, each man began digging his own grave so that the last survivor alone would be left unburied. Then, as Abd al-Muttalib's camel rose, water burst out beneath its hoof. All drank, and the men of Quraysh said: 'Allah has judged for you. The One who gave you water in this desert gave you Zamzam.' They returned without reaching the soothsayer, and Abd al-Muttalib took charge of giving water to the pilgrims.

The Seerah works add that while digging, facing Quraysh with only one son, he vowed that if Allah gave him ten sons he would sacrifice one of them at the Ka'bah. When the lot later fell on his youngest, Abdullah, Quraysh persuaded him to cast lots between Abdullah and camels instead, until the lot fell on the camels at a hundred, and a hundred camels were sacrificed. Abdullah became the father of the Prophet ﷺ.

The Prophet ﷺ later said: 'The water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for' (Ibn Majah). Mufti Menk notes that Abd al-Muttalib had been told by more than one person, including a king of Yemen and a Jewish acquaintance, that a great leader would come from his descendants.
zamzam.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum). Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 2–5.

p: Abrahah al-Ashram, an Abyssinian who ruled Yemen for the Christian king of Abyssinia, built a magnificent church in San'a, called al-Qullays, and wanted the Arabs to make their pilgrimage there instead of to the Ka'bah. When an Arab defiled the church in protest, Abrahah swore to destroy the Ka'bah.

He marched on Makkah with a large army and an elephant; most narrations speak of one great elephant, named Mahmud, which matches the Quran's 'the people of the elephant', though some report several. Mufti Menk holds the one-elephant view as the correct one. Near Makkah his men seized livestock grazing outside the city, including about two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, and Abrahah sent word that he had come only to destroy the House, not to fight.

Abd al-Muttalib went to meet him. Abrahah was impressed by his dignity and seated him beside him, then asked what he wanted. 'My camels.' Abrahah was disappointed: 'I came to destroy the House that is your religion and your honour, and you speak to me of camels?' Abd al-Muttalib replied: 'I am the lord of the camels. The House has a Lord who will protect it.' He took back his camels, told Quraysh to withdraw to the mountains, and stood at the door of the Ka'bah praying to Allah to defend it.

When the army advanced, the elephant knelt and would not move toward the Ka'bah, however they beat it; turned toward Yemen or any other direction, it rose and hurried off. Then flocks of birds came from the sea, each carrying three stones of baked clay, one in its beak and one in each claw, no larger than a chickpea. They pelted the army, and every man struck was destroyed.

Abrahah himself was struck and was carried back toward Yemen as his body decayed, losing his fingers one by one, and he died on the way. Allah recorded it in Surah al-Fil: 'Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the people of the elephant?…' The Arabs called it the Year of the Elephant, and the Prophet ﷺ was born a few weeks later. The honour this event gave Quraysh is recalled in the next surah, Quraysh (106).
abrahah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum). Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 2.

p: From childhood he never bowed to an idol. Quraysh held a yearly festival at an idol called Buwana, where they shaved their heads and stayed a day. One year his aunts and Abu Talib pressed him to come and were angry when he refused; he went with them, then came back frightened. He said a tall figure in white had appeared and told him: 'Stand back, Muhammad, do not touch it.' After that he never attended (Ibn Sa'd).

He also kept away from the idle pleasures of the young men of Makkah. He said: 'I never thought of what the people of Jahiliyyah used to do except twice, and each time Allah came between me and it.' Grazing sheep with a friend, he asked him to watch the flock so he could go into town for the night entertainments, as the youths did. He reached a wedding with music, sat down to watch, and Allah struck his ears; he fell asleep and woke only with the morning sun. The same happened a second time. 'After that I never thought of evil until Allah honoured me with prophethood' (Ibn Ishaq; al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, whose chains scholars discuss).

So he grew up known for his truthfulness and trust, without a single lapse that his enemies could later throw at him. He would think about the wrongs of his people: worshipping stones, mistreating women, seizing the property of the weak. When he called them to Allah, the only answer left to them was denial out of pride, since they knew his character from his birth.
protected.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa'd) and the reports cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 3.

p: Long before he was sent, the world had been told to expect him. Ibrahim, building the Ka'bah with Isma'il, prayed: 'Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite Your verses to them, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them' (al-Baqarah 2:129). Every other prophet after Ibrahim came from the line of Ishaq; this prayer was for the line of Isma'il. The Quran describes the believers as those 'who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written in the Torah and the Gospel with them' (al-A'raf 7:157), and records Isa's words: 'O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming the Torah before me, and bringing good news of a messenger to come after me whose name is Ahmad' (as-Saff 61:6).

Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who had read the earlier scriptures, was asked how the Prophet ﷺ was described in the Torah. He said: 'By Allah, he is described in it with some of the qualities in the Quran: "O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner", a refuge for the unlettered; not harsh or coarse, nor loud in the markets; he does not repay evil with evil but pardons and forgives. Allah will not take him until through him He opens blind eyes, deaf ears and sealed hearts' (Bukhari). Muslim scholars also point to the 'Comforter' (Paraclete) promised in the Gospel of John as a reference to him, though Christians understand it as the Holy Spirit. Belief, every prophet taught, is the same from Adam to Muhammad: one God, the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell; only the laws changed with time, until the final Shari'ah. And only Muhammad ﷺ declared himself the last prophet.

Their books told the Jews that the awaited prophet would migrate to a land of date palms between two lava fields (harrah). Many Jewish clans had settled in and around Yathrib for this reason, and they would tell the Aws and Khazraj: 'A prophet will soon be sent; we will follow him and kill you as Ad and Iram were killed.' Salamah ibn Salamah ibn Waqsh, of the Ansar, remembered a Jewish neighbour who told them of the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell. When asked for a sign, he pointed to a prophet soon to come from the direction of Makkah, and, looking at Salamah, the youngest of them, said: 'If this boy lives out his life, he will meet him.' Salamah lived to see the Prophet ﷺ and believed; the neighbour, out of envy, did not (Ibn Ishaq, Ahmad).

A Jew from Sham called Ibn al-Hayyiban settled among Banu Qurayzah a few years before Islam. On his deathbed he asked them: 'Why do you think I left a land of bread and wine for a land of hardship and hunger? I came to await a prophet whose time has come, and this is the land he will migrate to. Do not let anyone get to him before you.' He died before the prophethood (Ibn Ishaq). When the Muslims later besieged Qurayzah, some young men of the tribe remembered his words and accepted Islam.

Some who knew the signs were held back by envy or pride. Umayyah ibn Abi as-Salt of Ta'if, a celebrated poet who had read the earlier books, avoided idols and wine, and spoke of one God, had hoped to be that prophet himself; when the Prophet ﷺ was sent he refused to believe. Years later the Prophet ﷺ listened to a hundred lines of his poetry and said: 'He very nearly became a Muslim' (Muslim). Heraclius, too, would tell Abu Sufyan that he had known a prophet was coming but did not think he would be from the Arabs. Many rejected him only because he was not of their own people. Mufti Menk draws the lesson: accept the truth whoever brings it.
awaited.src: Written from the Quran, the hadith cited and Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 4.

p: Salman al-Farisi was born to a noble Zoroastrian family near Isfahan, where his father kept him at the sacred fire. His father loved him so much he would not let him go out. Sent one day to the family's estate, he passed a church, went in, and was drawn by the Christians' prayer: 'This is better than our religion.' When he told his father, he was put in chains at home. He sent word to the Christians to tell him when a caravan left for Sham, broke free and went with it, and served a series of monks. The first was corrupt, hoarding the charity given to the poor; when he died Salman showed the people his hidden jars of gold and silver, and they refused him burial. The next was a truly pious man, and each teacher, dying, sent him on to another: in Damascus, Mosul, Nasibin and Amuriyah. The last of them, dying, told him: 'The time has come for a prophet sent with the religion of Ibrahim. He will migrate to a land of date palms between two lava fields. He will not eat from charity but will accept a gift, and between his shoulders is the seal of prophethood.'

Salman paid a party of Arab traders to take him to Arabia, but they betrayed him and sold him as a slave to a Jew, who sold him on to a man of Banu Qurayzah. When he was brought to Madinah he recognised the palm groves and the lava fields from the monk's description. He was at the top of a palm tree when he heard of the man who had arrived in Quba and claimed to be a prophet; he almost fell from the tree.

He tested the three signs. He brought dates as charity: the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions to eat and did not eat himself. He brought dates as a gift: the Prophet ﷺ ate with them. Then at a funeral in al-Baqi' he walked behind him, hoping to see his back; the Prophet ﷺ understood and let his cloak fall, and Salman saw the seal, kissed it and wept, and accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ helped him buy his freedom: his master demanded three hundred palm saplings planted and growing, plus forty uqiyyahs of gold. The Prophet ﷺ had the Companions dig the holes and help with saplings, then planted them by planting three hundred palm saplings with his own hands, every one of which took, although young palms often died; he gave Salman a piece of gold to pay the rest (Ahmad, Ibn Ishaq). Years later it was Salman who advised digging the trench around Madinah, as the Persians did. He later said: 'Salman is one of us, the people of the household.'
salman.src: Written from Salman's own account (Ahmad, Ibn Ishaq). Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 4–14.

p: For about three years the Prophet ﷺ called people to Islam quietly, one by one, starting with those closest to him. None of them rejected him. Khadijah had already believed. Ali, his ten-year-old cousin, was living in his house: Abu Talib had many children and little money, so the Prophet ﷺ had taken Ali to raise. Ali accepted Islam, the first of the young, and had never worshipped an idol. Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed slave who had refused to leave him even for his own father, also believed at once. His daughters, who knew their father better than anyone, believed too, and so did Umm Ayman, who had cared for him since the day he was born. Those who lived with him day and night were the first to testify to his truth. He later said: 'The best of you are those who are best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family' (Tirmidhi).

His closest friend was Abu Bakr, whose real name was Abdullah ibn Uthman; his father Uthman was known as Abu Quhafah. When the Prophet ﷺ told him what had happened, he declared at once: 'You are the most truthful; I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are His Messenger.' The Prophet ﷺ later said: 'I never invited anyone to Islam without his hesitating a little, except Abu Bakr; he did not hesitate when I told him' (Ibn Ishaq). Ahl as-Sunnah hold him to be the best of people after the prophets. He suffered much for it, and he never denied his faith when asked.

The message was passed quietly, by word of mouth, to people chosen with care. Still, whispers spread through Makkah that Muhammad had come with something new, though he had not yet announced anything in public. Abu Bakr now began inviting his own friends (see the next event).
secret-dawah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 5–6.

p: In the early days of his mission, Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ in the form of a man on the heights of Makkah. He struck the ground and a spring of water gushed out, and he performed wudu while the Prophet ﷺ watched. Then the Prophet ﷺ made wudu in the same way, and Jibril led him in prayer. The Prophet ﷺ went home and taught Khadijah, who made wudu and prayed with him (Ibn Ishaq).

At this stage the prayer was two rak'ahs, prayed in the morning and the evening, as voluntary worship. He and the Companions also stood in prayer at night, as Surah al-Muzzammil describes (73:1–4, 20). The five daily prayers became obligatory later, on the night of the Mi'raj. So salah was taught at the start of the mission and made compulsory at the Mi'raj.
Mufti Menk notes that the prayer was given as a gift, not a burden: there is a difference between praying because you have to and praying because you want to.
wudu-salah.src: Written from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and the Quran. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 6.

p: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud was a poor young shepherd who grazed the flocks of Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. One day the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, fleeing the idolaters, asked him for milk. He said the flock was a trust and not his to give. The Prophet ﷺ asked for a young ewe that had never been mated, stroked its udder and prayed, and it filled with milk; they drank and he gave it to Ibn Mas'ud. 'Teach me these words,' said Ibn Mas'ud, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'You are a young man who will be taught' (Ahmad).

He accepted Islam, among the first six, drawn by a message of honesty, good conduct and the worship of one God. He learnt seventy surahs directly from the Prophet's mouth, and became one of the greatest scholars of the Quran, tafsir, hadith and fiqh. He was the first after the Prophet ﷺ to recite the Quran aloud in public in Makkah: standing at the Maqam, he recited Surah ar-Rahman until Quraysh beat his face, and he said: 'The enemies of Allah have never been easier to me than now; if you wish, I will do it again tomorrow' (Ibn Ishaq). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever would like to recite the Quran as fresh as it was revealed, let him recite it as Ibn Umm Abd recites it' (Ibn Majah).
ibnmasud.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Ishaq) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 6.

p: When the call became public, Allah commanded: 'Proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists' (15:94): deliver the message, but do not fight back or retaliate. The Prophet ﷺ went wherever people gathered: to the Ka'bah, where many performed tawaf naked because of vows to their gods, and to the markets and fairs where the tribes came. Lowering his gaze, he would call: 'O people, say La ilaha illallah and you will succeed.' He never insulted their idols; he only said they could neither harm nor benefit.

Quraysh argued against four things. First, the Oneness of Allah: 'Has he made the gods into one God? That is a strange thing!' (38:5). They did not deny that Allah created them, and called on Him alone when in danger at sea, but refused to worship Him alone. Second, the Resurrection: 'Who will give life to bones when they have crumbled?' Allah answered: 'He who produced them the first time will give them life' (36:78–79). Third, the Messenger himself: 'Why was this Quran not sent down to a great man of one of the two cities?' (43:31), meaning a chief of Makkah or Ta'if rather than an orphan; 'Why is an angel not sent down with him?' (6:8); and 'What kind of messenger eats food and walks in the markets?' (25:7). Allah replied that had He sent an angel, it would come in the form of a man (6:9), and that if a demanded sign came and they still disbelieved, punishment would follow at once; and that every messenger before him ate food and walked in the markets (25:20).

Fourth, the Quran: 'Why was it not sent down all at once?' Allah answered: 'So that We may strengthen your heart with it' (25:32). It came in parts, often in response to events, so that each verse was remembered with its story. They said: 'Tales of the ancients he has had written down, dictated to him morning and evening' (25:5), yet he had never read a book nor written one with his hand (29:48). So Allah challenged them: to bring the like of the whole Quran, even if men and jinn helped each other (17:88); then ten surahs like it (11:13); then a single surah (10:38); then even a discourse like it (52:34). They could not. Mufti Menk notes that in the Quran's rhyming passages a change of rhyme usually marks a change of subject.

So they turned to a smear campaign, calling him in turn a madman, a man possessed by a jinn, a soothsayer, a poet, a man bewitched, and a sorcerer who split husband from wife. Allah reassured him: 'We are sufficient for you against the mockers' (15:95), and: 'We know that what they say grieves you; it is not you they deny, but the verses of Allah that the wrongdoers reject' (6:33).

Even their leaders could not resist the Quran. Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq each went secretly by night to listen to him reciting in prayer, none knowing the others were there. At dawn they met on the way back, blamed one another, and promised not to return; the next night all three came again, and the third night too. Then they swore a firm oath never to go back (Ibn Ishaq).
objections.src: Written from the Quran and Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 7.

p: Mufti Menk says we should know the names of those who harmed the Prophet ﷺ as well as those who believed. Chief among them was Abu Jahl (Amr ibn Hisham). One day he swore to Quraysh that he would crush the Prophet's head with a rock while he was in sujud, whatever Banu Hashim did to him. He came with the stone, then turned back pale, trembling, the stone stuck to his hand. 'A huge camel stood in my way,' he said. 'I have never seen anything like its head and teeth; it was about to eat me.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'That was Jibril; had he come closer, he would have seized him' (Ibn Ishaq). Again and again he tried to stop the Prophet ﷺ praying at the Ka'bah, and Allah revealed: 'Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays? … Let him call his council; We will call the guards of Hell. No! Do not obey him; prostrate and draw near' (96:9–19).

A man from Irash sold camels to Abu Jahl, who would not pay. Quraysh mockingly sent him to the Prophet ﷺ, expecting a scene. The Prophet ﷺ went with him to Abu Jahl's door and said: 'Pay this man his due.' Abu Jahl came out, pale, and paid at once. Asked why, he said he had seen the same terrifying camel behind him (Ibn Ishaq).

His uncle Abu Lahab and his neighbour Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt threw filth and rubbish at his door. He would clear it away, saying: 'O Banu Abd Manaf, what kind of neighbourliness is this?' Mufti Menk points out that in Islam one may not harm a neighbour, Muslim or not, even with smoke or noise. Once, as the Prophet ﷺ prostrated at the Ka'bah, Abu Jahl asked who would bring the entrails of a slaughtered camel. Uqbah brought them and laid them on his back while Quraysh laughed until they fell on one another. The Prophet ﷺ stayed in sujud until his young daughter Fatimah came running, lifted the filth off him and scolded them. He then said three times: 'O Allah, deal with Quraysh,' naming Abu Jahl, Uqbah and others. Ibn Mas'ud said he later saw every one of them dead at Badr (Bukhari).

Uqbah had once invited him to a feast, and the Prophet ﷺ said he would not eat until Uqbah said the shahadah, which he did to please his guest. His friend Ubayy ibn Khalaf rebuked him, and to prove himself Uqbah went and spat at the Prophet ﷺ. Of him Allah revealed: 'On the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands, saying: Would that I had taken a path with the Messenger… Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend' (25:27–28). Another day, as the Prophet ﷺ prayed, Uqbah twisted a cloth around his neck and choked him violently, until Abu Bakr pushed him away, saying: 'Will you kill a man because he says, My Lord is Allah, and he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord?' (40:28; Bukhari). Uqbah was captured at Badr and executed, as was an-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

Al-As ibn Wa'il owed money to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, a Muslim blacksmith, and kept avoiding him. When Khabbab pressed him he sneered: 'Don't you claim there is wealth and children in Paradise? Wait until I get there, and I will pay you then.' Allah revealed: 'Have you seen him who disbelieves in Our verses and says: I will surely be given wealth and children? Has he looked into the Unseen?' (19:77–78; Bukhari). Others simply laughed and winked at the believers as they passed, and Allah said: 'The criminals used to laugh at those who believed… Today the believers are laughing at the disbelievers' (83:29–34).

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl's uncle and a leader of Quraysh, heard the Quran and told his people: 'It has a sweetness and a grace; it is not the speech of a man, a soothsayer, a poet or a madman.' Abu Jahl came to him in tears: people were saying al-Walid had left his religion. Pressed to find something to say, al-Walid thought, frowned, and finally declared: 'Call it magic, for it separates a man from his father, his brother, his wife and his clan.' Allah revealed of him: 'He thought and determined… then he said: This is nothing but magic handed down' (74:18–25). An-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who had learnt the tales of the Persian kings in al-Hirah, would follow the Prophet's gatherings, telling those stories and claiming they were better. Of such men Allah revealed: 'Do not listen to this Quran; make noise during it, so that you may overcome' (41:26), and: 'Among people is he who buys idle tales to lead others astray from the path of Allah' (31:6).
mockers.src: Written from the Quran, the hadith cited and Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 7.

p: Abu Talib, though he never accepted Islam, was a just man and a leader of Quraysh, and he stood by his nephew. Because of him, Quraysh could not kill the Prophet ﷺ; others too were protected by relatives who stood up for them out of kinship even though they were not Muslims.

The leaders of Quraysh came to Abu Talib: 'Your nephew insults our gods, mocks our religion and calls our fathers misguided. Stop him, or step aside and leave him to us.' Abu Talib sent them away gently, but they came back with threats. He called his nephew: 'Spare me and spare yourself; do not burden me with more than I can bear.' The Prophet ﷺ thought his uncle might abandon him and said: 'O my uncle, by Allah, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left on condition that I give up this matter, I would not give it up until Allah makes it prevail or I die in its cause.' His eyes filled with tears and he turned to go. Abu Talib called him back: 'Go, my nephew, and say what you like. By Allah, I will never hand you over to them for anything' (Ibn Ishaq).

Later Quraysh tried bargaining with Abu Talib himself. They brought him Umarah ibn al-Walid, the finest young man of Quraysh: 'Take him as your son and give us your nephew to kill.' Abu Talib said: 'What a wicked bargain! You give me your son to feed and raise, and I give you mine to kill? By Allah, never.' Mufti Menk adds that they offered him blood money many times over, which he also refused (Ibn Ishaq).
Quraysh were forced to respect him, but hated him all the more, and as nearly every powerful family now had Muslims in it, they turned to other ways: offers, bargains and boycott.
abutalib-delegation.src: Written from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Days 7–8.

p: After the boycott, word of the Prophet ﷺ had spread far beyond Makkah. A group of about twenty Christians came to see him (Ibn Ishaq says from Abyssinia; others say from Najran). They sat with him at the Ka'bah, asked their questions and listened to the Quran. Their eyes filled with tears, and all of them believed.

Abu Jahl and some men of Quraysh stopped them as they left: 'What a foolish band you are! Your people sent you to bring back news of this man, and you abandon your religion after one sitting?' They answered: 'Peace be upon you. We will not argue with you in ignorance. We have our way and you have yours.' Allah revealed: 'Those to whom We gave the Book before it believe in it… When they hear idle talk they turn away from it and say: We have our deeds and you have yours. Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant' (28:52–55).

Mufti Menk draws the lesson: strangers who heard him once believed, while his own people, who had known him all his life, refused. Those near a source of knowledge must not be the last to benefit from it.
christians-listen.src: Written from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and the Quran. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 9.

p: Before the six men, two people of Yathrib had already been touched by Islam. Suwayd ibn as-Samit of the Aws, a poet so respected that his people called him al-Kamil (the perfect one), met the Prophet ﷺ at a fair. 'Perhaps what you have is like what I have,' he said. 'And what is that?' 'The wisdom of Luqman.' He recited some of it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This is good speech, but what I have is better: a Quran that Allah has revealed to me, a guidance and a light.' He recited it, and Suwayd said: 'This is fine speech.' He went back to Yathrib and was killed by the Khazraj soon after; his people used to say he died a Muslim (Ibn Ishaq). Luqman, after whom a surah is named, is held by most scholars to have been a wise man, not a prophet; many reports say he was from Nubia.

Later a delegation of the Aws led by Abu al-Haysar Anas ibn Rafi' came to Makkah to seek an alliance with Quraysh against the Khazraj. The Prophet ﷺ went to them and said: 'Shall I tell you of something better than what you came for?' and recited the Quran. Iyas ibn Mu'adh, a young man among them, said: 'By Allah, this is better than what we came for!' Abu al-Haysar threw a handful of dust in his face: 'Leave us; we did not come for this.' Iyas fell silent. He died soon after in Yathrib, and those with him said they heard him glorifying Allah and saying 'Allahu akbar' until he died (Ibn Ishaq, Ahmad).

Then came the Battle of Bu'ath between the Aws and the Khazraj, the last and bloodiest of their long wars. Most of their old leaders were killed. Aishah later said Bu'ath was a day Allah sent ahead for His Messenger: the men who would have resisted a new leader were gone, and Yathrib was ready (Bukhari).
yathrib-first.src: Written from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 10.

p: On the road they reached the tents of Umm Ma'bad, Atikah bint Khalid of Khuza'ah, at Qudayd, and asked to buy meat or milk. She had nothing: it was a year of drought, and the only ewe in the tent was too weak to go out with the flock and had no milk. The Prophet ﷺ asked if he could milk it. He passed his hand over its udder, said Bismillah and prayed, and it filled. He milked it into a large vessel; she drank until she was satisfied, then his companions, then he drank last. He milked it again, filled the vessel and left it with her.

In the common account, her husband Abu Ma'bad came home with his thin goats and was astonished by the milk. She described the guest so vividly ('radiant, with a handsome face, beautiful eyes with long lashes, a deep voice; when silent, dignified; when he spoke, it was as if pearls were falling') that he said: 'By Allah, this is the man of Quraysh we have heard about. I will join him if I can.' Mufti Menk prefers the report that Abu Ma'bad was present, recognised him at once, and asked to come with them, but was told to wait until he heard they had settled. Both later went to Madinah and accepted Islam (al-Hakim, Ibn Sa'd).

Along the way, when people asked Abu Bakr who the man with him was, he would say: 'A man who guides me on the way.' They took him to mean the road; he meant the path of goodness (Bukhari). Near Madinah, az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, returning from Sham with a trade caravan, met them and gave them both white garments (Bukhari).
umm-mabad.src: Written from the reports cited (al-Hakim, Ibn Sa'd, Bukhari). Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 12.

p: Once he was settled, the Prophet ﷺ sent Zayd ibn Harithah and Abu Rafi' back to Makkah to bring his family. They returned with his daughters Fatimah and Umm Kulthum, his wife Sawdah, and Umm Ayman, now Zayd's wife, with their little son Usamah. His eldest daughter Zaynab stayed behind: her husband Abu al-As ibn ar-Rabi' had not accepted Islam and would not let her go. Ruqayyah was with her husband Uthman.

Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr brought his father's family: his mother Umm Ruman, his sisters Aishah and Asma. Asma, wife of az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, was heavily pregnant. She gave birth at Quba to a son, Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr. The Jews had claimed they had bewitched the emigrants so no child would be born to them, and the Muslims cried 'Allahu akbar' at his birth. The Prophet ﷺ chewed a date and put it in the baby's mouth, so that the first thing to enter his stomach was the Prophet's saliva. He was the first child born to the Muhajirin in Madinah (Bukhari), and would one day rebuild the Ka'bah.
family-arrives.src: Written from Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Ishaq and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 13.

p: With the masjid built and the community organised, the Prophet ﷺ taught the new nation how to live together. His priorities were knowledge (after Badr, literate captives could ransom themselves by teaching ten Muslims to read and write), the purification of the heart from hatred, envy and malice, love and brotherhood, and the worship of Allah. Some of his early words in Madinah are among the best known in Islam.

Asked which part of Islam is best, he said: 'To feed others, and to greet with salam those you know and those you do not know' (Bukhari). 'He will not enter Paradise whose neighbour is not safe from his harm' (Muslim). 'When you cook a stew, add more water and share it with your neighbours' (Muslim). 'The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe' (Bukhari). 'None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself' (Bukhari).

'The believers in their love, mercy and compassion are like one body: when one limb aches, the whole body responds with sleeplessness and fever' (Muslim). 'A believer to a believer is like a building, each part strengthening the other' (Bukhari). 'Do not envy one another, do not hate one another, do not turn your backs on one another; be, O servants of Allah, brothers' (Muslim). 'Allah helps a servant as long as the servant helps his brother. Whoever relieves a believer of a hardship of this world, Allah will relieve him of a hardship of the Day of Resurrection; whoever covers a Muslim's faults, Allah will cover his faults in this world and the next' (Muslim). Mufti Menk contrasts this with the modern urge to expose: if you see a fault, go to your brother privately and help him correct it.

'Show mercy to those on earth, and the One above the heavens will show mercy to you' (Tirmidhi). 'He is not a believer who eats his fill while his neighbour beside him is hungry' (al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad). 'Removing something harmful from the road is a branch of faith' (Muslim), and he warned against relieving oneself on paths or in the shade where people rest (Muslim): the community was to be clean as well as kind. 'Any Muslim who clothes a Muslim who has nothing to wear, Allah will clothe him in the green garments of Paradise; any Muslim who feeds a hungry Muslim, Allah will feed him from the fruits of Paradise; and any Muslim who gives drink to a thirsty Muslim, Allah will give him to drink from the sealed nectar' (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi).
teachings.src: Compiled from the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: With Makkah emptied of Muslims, Quraysh turned on Madinah. They wrote to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and the idolaters of Madinah, who had been about to make him king: 'You have sheltered our man. Fight him or drive him out, or we will march on you with all the Arabs, kill your fighters and take your women.' Ibn Ubayy and his followers began gathering to fight. The Prophet ﷺ went to them: 'Quraysh's threat has carried you further than it should. Their plot against you is less than the harm you would do yourselves. Do you want to fight your own sons and brothers?' They understood and dispersed (Abu Dawud).

Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, chief of the Aws, went to Makkah for umrah and stayed with his old friend Umayyah ibn Khalaf. As he made tawaf, Abu Jahl confronted him: 'You perform tawaf safely after sheltering the apostates? Were you not with Abu Safwan, you would not go home alive.' Sa'd raised his voice: 'By Allah, if you stop me from this, I will stop you from something harder for you: your road to Sham past Madinah' (Bukhari). Quraysh now knew their trade route was at stake.

The Prophet ﷺ had a count taken of those who professed Islam, and they numbered about fifteen hundred (Bukhari). He visited the tribes around Madinah and made treaties: they would not be attacked, would not help the enemy, and would stand with the Muslims if Madinah were attacked. At first Companions guarded him at night; Aishah recalled a night he could not sleep until Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas came armed to stand guard (Bukhari, Muslim). Then Allah revealed: 'Allah will protect you from the people' (5:67), and he told the guards: 'Go, Allah has protected me' (Tirmidhi).

For thirteen years the Muslims had been told to be patient and not fight back, even when robbed and beaten. Now Allah revealed: 'Permission is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged, and Allah is able to give them victory: those driven from their homes unjustly only for saying, Our Lord is Allah' (22:39–40). Mufti Menk explains that the fighting that followed was not to force Islam on anyone, but to defend Madinah and recover what Quraysh had seized: the homes, wealth and goods of the Muhajirin, which Quraysh's caravans now carried north. Scholars describe the permission as coming in stages: first against Quraysh, then against those who joined them, then against any who broke treaties to fight the Muslims, and against any who began hostilities.
quraysh-threat.src: Written from the hadith cited and the Quran. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 15.

p: In Ramadan of 3 AH the Prophet ﷺ married Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, a widow (most reports say of Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, martyred at Badr; others say of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, martyred at Uhud). She was so generous to the poor, even with the little she had, that she had long been called Umm al-Masakin, 'mother of the poor'.

Many of the women he married at this time were widows of men who had fallen for Islam, left without a guardian. Zaynab lived only about eight months after the marriage and died in his lifetime, the second of his wives to do so after Khadijah. She was buried in al-Baqi'.
zaynab-khuzaymah.src: Written from Ibn Sa'd and the books of Seerah. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 19.

p: Before Islam, women in Arabia did not inherit; they could themselves be inherited, passed to a dead man's heir along with his property, or handed over to settle a debt. Islam gave women the right to own property in their own name, which no one may take from them.

Allah revealed the shares of inheritance in Surah an-Nisa' (4:11–12, 4:176). They were laid down by Allah Himself: 'Your parents and your children, you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit; these are obligations from Allah' (4:11). A person may leave a bequest (wasiyyah) of up to one third of his estate, but not to an heir whose share Allah has already fixed; the rest is divided by the Quran, whether he got on well with his children or not, unless an heir is excluded, for example by having murdered the deceased.

Scholars point out that more categories of female heirs than male receive fixed shares, and the largest fixed shares, two-thirds and one-half, are mostly given to women: a single daughter, for example, takes half the estate. Where a son receives twice a daughter's share, it is because the man is obliged to provide food, clothing and housing for his wife, children and the closest women of his family, including that same sister, while what she inherits is hers alone. Mufti Menk warns that many Muslims today cheat their sisters of their inheritance and leave estates undivided for years.
inheritance.src: Written from the Quran and the hadith on bequests. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 19.

p: Umm Salamah, Hind bint Abi Umayyah, had suffered as much as anyone for Islam: two hijrahs, to Abyssinia and to Madinah, and a year separated from her husband and child in Makkah. When her husband Abu Salamah died of his reopened Uhud wound in 4 AH, she remembered a conversation they had once had. She had told him: 'If you die, I will not marry again; I have heard that a woman will be with her husband in Paradise.' He answered: 'O Allah, if I die, give her a husband better than me.'

She was also taught to say at a calamity: 'O Allah, reward me for my affliction and give me something better in its place,' and she wondered: 'Who could be better than Abu Salamah?' (Muslim). After her waiting period Abu Bakr and then Umar proposed, and she gently declined. Then the Prophet ﷺ proposed. She told him she was no longer young, had children and was jealous by nature; he answered each concern, and they married in Shawwal of 4 AH. A widow honoured among the believers, she was not left without a guardian. She became one of the most learned of the Mothers of the Believers, and her counsel would prove decisive at Hudaybiyah.
umm-salamah.src: Written from Muslim, Ibn Sa'd and the books of Seerah. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 20.

p: In 3 AH Allah made clear that believers may not marry idolaters, men or women: 'Do not marry polytheist women until they believe; a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist, even if she pleases you. And do not marry your women to polytheist men until they believe' (2:221). Mufti Menk's explanation: if a couple cannot find common ground on faith, the most important thing of all, how will they find it on everything else?
mixed-marriage.src: Written from the Quran. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 20.

p: Returning from Banu al-Mustaliq, the army halted. Aishah went out to relieve herself and, coming back, found her necklace of Yemeni beads was missing and went to search for it. Meanwhile the order to march was given. She was young and light, and the men who lifted her curtained howdah onto her camel did not notice it was empty. When she returned, the camp was gone. Wrapped in her outer garment, she sat down where they had been, hoping they would come back for her, and fell asleep. Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, who followed behind the army, saw a dark shape, recognised her, and said only: 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.' She woke at his words. He did not speak to her; he made his camel kneel, she mounted, and he led it on foot until they reached the army at midday.

Abdullah ibn Ubayy saw his chance and began the slander, and it spread. People fell into three groups. Those who invented it: Ibn Ubayy and his circle. Those who repeated it without having invented it: among them Mistah ibn Uthathah, a poor relative whom Abu Bakr supported, Hassan ibn Thabit and Hamnah bint Jahsh. And those who rejected it outright: Abu Ayyub asked his wife: 'Would you do such a thing?' 'Never.' 'Then Aishah is better than you.'

Aishah fell ill on her return and knew nothing. She only noticed that the Prophet ﷺ, though he still visited her, was not as warm as before; he would come in and ask only: 'How is that one?' He knew in his heart it was false, but if he had declared her innocent himself, people would have said he was defending his wife; he waited for revelation, and for a month none came. One night Aishah went out with Umm Mistah, who stumbled and cursed her own son. 'How can you curse a man who fought at Badr?' 'Have you not heard what he is saying?' and she told her. Aishah went home weeping and asked leave to go to her parents. Her mother Umm Ruman told her to make light of it: a beautiful young wife loved by her husband always has rivals and talk. Abu Bakr could only say: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' She wept until she thought her heart would burst.

The Prophet ﷺ asked Ali and Usamah. Usamah said: 'We know nothing of your wife but good.' Ali said: 'Allah has not restricted you, and there are many women besides her; ask the servant girl.' Barirah said: 'By Him who sent you with the truth, I have never seen anything wrong in her, except that she is a young girl who falls asleep beside the dough and the goat comes and eats it.' The Prophet ﷺ then stood in the masjid: 'Who will excuse me for a man whose harm has reached my family?' Sa'd ibn Mu'adh of the Aws stood: 'If he is of the Aws, we will strike his neck; if of our brothers the Khazraj, command us.' Sa'd ibn Ubadah of the Khazraj angrily objected, Usayd ibn Hudayr answered him, and the two tribes almost came to blows until the Prophet ﷺ calmed them.

Then he came to her and said: 'O Aishah, if you are innocent, Allah will declare your innocence. If you have slipped, seek Allah's forgiveness and repent; when a servant admits his sin and repents, Allah accepts his repentance.' Her tears stopped. She said: 'If I say I am innocent, you will not believe me; if I confess to something I did not do, you will believe me. I can only say what the father of Yusuf said: Beautiful patience, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe' (12:18). Before anyone left the room, revelation came upon him. When it lifted he was smiling: 'Rejoice, O Aishah; Allah has declared your innocence.' Her mother told her to go to him; she said: 'I will thank no one but Allah' (Bukhari, Muslim).

Allah revealed: 'Those who brought the slander are a group among you. Do not think it bad for you; it is good for you. Each of them will bear the sin he earned, and the one who took the greater part of it will have a great punishment' (24:11). Why did the believers, on hearing it, not think well of their own people and say 'This is an obvious lie'? (24:12). 'You received it on your tongues and said with your mouths what you had no knowledge of, and thought it light, while with Allah it was grave' (24:15). Whoever accuses a chaste person must bring four witnesses or be flogged eighty lashes (24:4), and 'those who love that indecency should spread among the believers will have a painful punishment in this world and the next' (24:19). Mufti Menk applies this today: spreading tales of immorality, even true ones, spreads sin, and the slandered person gains from it, since the slanderers' good deeds pass to him.

Abu Bakr swore he would no longer support Mistah. Allah revealed: 'Let those of virtue and means among you not swear to stop giving to relatives, the poor and the emigrants. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?' (24:22). Abu Bakr said: 'Yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me,' expiated his oath, and resumed his support of Mistah for life (Bukhari). Aishah would later say that her innocence came down from above the seven heavens.
ifk.src: Written from Aishah's own account (Bukhari, Muslim) and Surah an-Nur. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 21.

p: Zayd ibn Thabit of the Ansar was only a boy when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, too young to fight at Badr, but he already knew many surahs and wrote beautifully. The Prophet ﷺ told him: 'Learn the writing of the Jews for me, for by Allah I do not trust them with my letters.' Zayd said: 'Half a month had not passed before I had learnt it; I used to write for him to them, and read their letters to him' (Tirmidhi; Bukhari mentions it). Later he learnt Syriac too in a few weeks.

He became one of the chief scribes of the revelation. After the battle of al-Yamamah, Abu Bakr chose him to gather the Quran into one copy, and under Uthman he led the committee that made the standard copies. Mufti Menk contrasts his dedication with ours: many say for years that they want to learn Arabic, yet learning a few words a day would soon add up.
zayd-thabit.src: Written from the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 22.

p: Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan, daughter of the leader of Quraysh, was among the very first believers. She emigrated to Abyssinia with her husband Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh, brother of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, and had a daughter there, Habibah, from whom she was called Umm Habibah. Ubaydullah died in Abyssinia; reports differ about his end, many saying he left Islam for Christianity before he died.

Widowed in a foreign land, she could not return to Makkah, where her father, still the enemy of Islam, would have persecuted her. The Prophet ﷺ sent Amr ibn Umayyah ad-Damri to the Negus, asking for her hand once her waiting period ended. The marriage was contracted in Abyssinia, with Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-As as her guardian, and the Negus paid her dowry on the Prophet's ﷺ behalf. She returned with Ja'far at Khaybar and became a Mother of the Believers, and the Prophet ﷺ became the son-in-law of Abu Sufyan himself.

Mufti Menk notes that almost all of the Prophet's ﷺ marriages were to widows or divorcees, women who had sacrificed for the faith, giving them protection and support; Aishah was his only previously unmarried wife. He urged his companions in the same way to care for widows, the divorced and orphans.
umm-habibah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum). Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 24.

p: Among the captives of Hunayn was a woman who insisted she was the Prophet's ﷺ sister. Brought to him, she said she was ash-Shayma' bint al-Harith, daughter of Halimah, his foster-sister, who had carried him as a child. As proof she showed a mark on her back where he had bitten her as a little boy, and he recognised it.

He spread his cloak for her to sit on and offered her a choice: to stay with him in honour, or to return to her people with gifts. She chose to go home, and he gave her gifts and sent her back. She accepted Islam (Ibn Ishaq).
shayma.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: During the days of the Conquest, a woman of the noble clan of Banu Makhzum stole. Her people, ashamed, wanted the penalty set aside and asked Usamah ibn Zayd, whom the Prophet ﷺ loved dearly, to intercede.

When Usamah spoke, the Prophet's ﷺ face changed colour: 'Do you intercede concerning one of the limits set by Allah?' Then he addressed the people: 'Those before you were destroyed because when a noble person among them stole they let him go, and when a weak person stole they punished him. By Allah, if Fatimah the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand' (Bukhari 4304, Muslim). The penalty was carried out; she later repented and Aisha said her repentance was sincere.
makhzumiyyah.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: The Prophet ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqbah to collect zakat from Banu al-Mustaliq, who had accepted Islam. Delighted, they rode out in a body to welcome him, armed as was their custom. Seeing them coming, he feared they meant to kill him, turned back and reported that they had refused zakat and wanted to kill him.

The Prophet ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to find out, telling him not to act in haste. Khalid camped near them by night and heard the adhan for the prayers, and in the morning they explained what had happened. Allah revealed: 'O you who believe, if a sinful person brings you news, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance and then regret what you have done' (49:6; Ahmad). Mufti Menk adds that one who comes carrying gossip about others has, by that, shown himself to be such a person.
walid-mustaliq.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: Some hypocrites built a masjid close to the Masjid of Quba, in league with Abu Amir 'the monk', a man of Madinah who had opposed Islam from the start and gone over to its enemies. They meant it as a base against the believers. As the Prophet ﷺ prepared for Tabuk, they asked him to pray in it to bless it, saying it was for the sick and for rainy nights. He said: 'When we return, if Allah wills.'

On the way back, Allah revealed: 'And those who took a masjid to cause harm, disbelief and division among the believers, and as an outpost for those who fought Allah and His Messenger before; they will swear they meant only good, but Allah bears witness that they are liars. Never stand in it. A masjid founded on piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it' (9:107–108). The Prophet ﷺ sent companions to burn it down. Allah described it as a building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapses with its builders into the Fire, and said it would remain a source of doubt in their hearts (9:109–110).
masjid-dirar.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 27.

p: Those who stayed behind from Tabuk fell into groups: those with real excuses; the hypocrites of Madinah and of the Bedouins, who came with false excuses and were exposed in Surah at-Tawbah: 'They will make excuses to you when you return; say: make no excuse, we will not believe you; Allah has informed us of your news' (9:94); and three sincere believers who had no excuse at all: Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn ar-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayyah.

When the Prophet ﷺ returned, Ka'b told him plainly: 'If I lied to please you, Allah would soon expose me; if I tell the truth you may be angry with me, but I hope for Allah's forgiveness. I had no excuse.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'This one has told the truth. Go until Allah decides about you.' Murarah and Hilal said the same.

The Muslims were told not to speak to the three. They came to the prayers and greeted the Prophet ﷺ, and he did not return the greeting; no one looked at them or answered them. After forty days their wives were told to keep away from them. Hilal's wife came to say her husband was very old and had no one to serve him, and the Prophet ﷺ allowed her to look after him. They held no grudge, kept praying for forgiveness and did not lose hope, until the wide earth felt narrow for them.

After fifty days, Allah revealed: 'And upon the three who were left behind, when the earth, vast as it is, closed in on them and their own souls closed in on them, and they knew there was no refuge from Allah except in Him; then He turned to them so that they might repent. Allah is the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful' (9:118). The Prophet ﷺ came out overjoyed. People ran to congratulate them and embrace them. Ka'b asked the Prophet ﷺ: 'Is it from you, or from Allah?' 'From Allah,' he said, his face shining, and recited the verses. Their names are remembered in the Quran to the end of time (Bukhari 4418, Ka'b's own account).
three-behind.src: Written from the standard Seerah sources (Ibn Hisham, Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum) and the hadith cited. Cross-checked with Mufti Menk, Life of the Last Messenger (Ramadan 2012), Day 28.

p: A delegation of the Christians of Najran came to Madinah and stayed by the masjid, listening. They said they had submitted to God before him, through Jesus. The Prophet ﷺ answered directly that three things kept them from Islam: worshipping the cross, eating pork, and calling Jesus the son of God, when Jesus called himself the Messenger of God. The discussion grew heated.

Allah revealed: 'The example of Isa with Allah is like that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him "Be", and he was' (3:59), and: 'If anyone disputes with you after the knowledge that has come to you, say: Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves, then pray earnestly and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars' (3:61). The Prophet ﷺ came out with his family, ready for the mubahalah.

The Christians conferred: if he is a prophet and we curse each other, we are ruined. They declined, and asked instead to live under Muslim protection, paying jizyah, and for a trustworthy man to be sent with them. He said: 'I will send with you a truly trustworthy man,' and sent Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah: 'Every ummah has its trustworthy one, and the trustworthy one of this ummah is Abu Ubaydah' (Bukhari). Some of them later accepted Islam.
